## Introduction

Nearly two centuries of Company and Crown rule bequeathed to India not merely a set of offices but an entire administrative grammar — the district as the unit of governance, the generalist civil servant as its pivot, codified law as the medium of authority, and audit as the discipline of the purse. Independent India retained this apparatus almost intact in 1950 but redirected it from extraction and control toward development and welfare. The legacy is therefore best assessed not by what was inherited, but by what was repurposed — and, increasingly, by what is being deliberately shed.

- 1. The constitutional and parliamentary frame. The Westminster model of a nominal head with a Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the legislature came through the Government of India Acts. The Government of India Act, 1935 is the largest single source of the Constitution — the federal distribution of powers in the Seventh Schedule, the office of Governor, the Federal Court (now the Supreme Court), emergency provisions and the Federal Public Service Commission all descend from it. The Act of 1919 introduced dyarchy and, crucially, the first devolution of subjects to the provinces.
- 2. The district and the Collector — the AP anchor. Warren Hastings created the Collector in 1772; Sir Thomas Munro, Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) from 1800 to 1807 and later Governor of Madras (1820–27), fused revenue, magisterial and developmental functions in one officer and designed the ryotwari settlement — direct assessment of the individual cultivator — in what are today Kurnool, Anantapur, YSR Kadapa and Chittoor districts. That office survives structurally as the District Collector and District Magistrate, still the fulcrum of disaster response, elections and revenue in Andhra Pradesh.
- 3. A permanent, neutral, generalist civil service. The Charter Act, 1853 opened the Covenanted Civil Service to open competition; the ICS became the “steel frame” of empire. Independent India retained the model through the All India Services under Article 312, insulated appointments through the UPSC (Articles 315–323) and protected tenure under Articles 310 and 311 — preserving the neutrality and hierarchy while replacing the imperial purpose.
- 4. Codified law and the hierarchy of courts. The Macaulay-drafted Indian Penal Code, 1860, the Criminal Procedure Code, the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and the Police Act, 1861 created a single legal order across the subcontinent, along with an appellate hierarchy of subordinate courts, High Courts (Indian High Courts Act, 1861) and a final appellate court. The legal method — codification, precedent, written judgment — is the deeper inheritance and remains intact.
- 5. Financial control and audit. British India institutionalised the annual budget (introduced by James Wilson in 1860), legislative appropriation and independent audit. The Auditor General under the 1919 and 1935 Acts became the Comptroller and Auditor General under Article 148, with reports laid before Parliament and examined by the Public Accounts Committee — the core accountability loop of Indian public finance.
- 6. Local self-government. Lord Mayo’s Resolution of 1870 began financial decentralisation and Lord Ripon’s Resolution of 18 May 1882 — which earned him the title “Father of Local Self-Government in India” — provided for elected majorities and non-official chairpersons in local boards. The lineage runs through the Balwantrai Mehta (1957) and Ashok Mehta (1978) Committees to the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, 1992 and the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules.

## The critical dimension — what is now being consciously decolonised
- Criminal law: the IPC, CrPC and Indian Evidence Act were repealed and replaced with effect from 1 July 2024 by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Ministry of Home Affairs; PIB, 2024) — sedition under the old Section 124A is gone, replaced by an offence framed around acts endangering sovereignty and integrity, and time limits have been introduced for filing charge-sheets and pronouncing judgment.
- Regulatory law: the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 decriminalised 183 provisions across 42 central Acts, dismantling the colonial reflex of criminalising minor procedural default; the Income-tax Act, 2025, effective from April 2026, replaces the 1961 Act whose lineage runs back to the Income-tax Act, 1922.
- Unfinished business: the Police Act, 1861 survives largely unreformed. In Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) the Supreme Court issued seven binding directives — State Security Commissions, a fixed two-year tenure for the DGP and key field officers, separation of investigation from law and order, and Police Establishment Boards — whose implementation across States remains partial. The Second ARC’s Public Order report (2007) reached the same conclusion.

›  The “Status” column is what converts a list into an evaluation — draw it even if pressed for time.

## Conclusion

The British legacy in Indian administration is best described as inherited machinery placed under new management. India retained the district, the generalist civil service, codified law and independent audit because they supplied continuity to a newly independent state, but it grafted onto them universal adult franchise, a justiciable Bill of Rights, constitutional local self-government and, more recently, a deliberate statutory decolonisation of criminal and regulatory law. The unfinished agenda — police reform under Prakash Singh, and the shift from a rule-based to a role-based bureaucracy under Mission Karmayogi — defines the next phase of that transition.

## Value addition
- Dateable milestones for rapid recall: Regulating Act 1773 (Governor-General of Bengal, Supreme Court at Calcutta) · Pitt’s India Act 1784 (Board of Control) · Charter Act 1833 (Governor-General of India; Section 87 bars discrimination on religion, birth, descent or colour) · Charter Act 1853 (open competition) · Government of India Act 1858 (Crown rule, Secretary of State) · Indian Councils Act 1909 (separate electorates) · GoI Act 1919 (dyarchy, first Public Service Commission recommended) · GoI Act 1935 (provincial autonomy, Federal Court, Federal PSC, RBI).
- Land revenue systems and their regional footprint: Permanent Settlement 1793 (Cornwallis — Bengal, Bihar, Odisha); Ryotwari (Munro — Madras Presidency including Andhra and Rayalaseema; Read in the Baramahal); Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie — North-Western Provinces). Andhra Pradesh’s land records, pattadar passbooks and the current re-survey under the Svamitva/land-titling programme rest on the ryotwari base.
- Andhra-specific institutional inheritances: Madras Presidency municipal and district board law shaped coastal Andhra’s early local bodies; the Andhra Pradesh High Court traces its jurisdiction lineage to the Madras High Court established under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861, before the Andhra High Court (1954), the AP High Court (1956) and the present bifurcated court at Amaravati (2019).
- Committee/commission tags: Second ARC — 5th Report Public Order, 10th Report Refurbishing of Personnel Administration, 15th Report State and District Administration; Ribeiro (1998), Padmanabhaiah (2000) and Soli Sorabjee’s Model Police Act (2006) on police reform.
- Sharp closing line to memorise: the colonial state was designed for control at minimum cost; the constitutional state is designed for service at maximum reach — and every unresolved administrative pathology in India sits somewhere on the seam between those two designs.

## Introduction

Education converts India’s demographic bulge into productive capacity, and the policy architecture has changed more in the last five years than in the preceding three decades. The National Education Policy, 2020 — the first education policy since 1986 — reset school structure, higher-education regulation and research funding simultaneously. The measurable direction of travel is positive: the Gross Enrolment Ratio in higher education has risen from 23.7 in 2014-15 to 30.0 in 2023-24, with total enrolment at 4.50 crore (AISHE 2023-24, Ministry of Education, released July 2026).

- 1. Restructuring school education. NEP 2020 replaced the 10+2 format with a 5+3+3+4 design aligned to cognitive stages and brought children aged 3–6 formally into the schooling system for the first time. The NIPUN Bharat Mission (July 2021) targets universal foundational literacy and numeracy by Class 3 by 2026-27, supported by the National Curriculum Framework for Foundational Stage (2022) and for School Education (2023). Outcome evidence: UDISE+ 2025-26 (Ministry of Education) records the secondary-stage dropout rate falling to 7.0% from 8.2% the previous year and the preparatory stage to 1.8% from 2.3%, with school internet connectivity rising to 67.4% and girls’ share of enrolment to 48.4%.
- 2. Measuring learning, not just enrolment. The PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024, conducted by NCERT on 4 December 2024 across roughly 781 districts for Classes 3, 6 and 9, replaced the National Achievement Survey with a competency-based assessment and now anchors the Holistic Progress Card. This matters because enrolment gains are meaningless without learning gains — the central critique of Indian schooling for two decades. PM SHRI (September 2022; outlay Rs 27,360 crore, central share Rs 18,128 crore, 2022-23 to 2026-27) is developing over 14,500 exemplar schools to demonstrate NEP practice, with more than 13,000 notified by early 2026.
- 3. Higher education — flexibility and quality. The Academic Bank of Credits and the APAAR student ID enable credit accumulation, multiple entry and exit and inter-institutional mobility; multidisciplinary universities, the four-year undergraduate programme and Institutions of Eminence pursue quality. Evidence: female GER reached 31.2 with a Gender Parity Index of 1.08, women now form 44% of STEM enrolment, and faculty strength stands at 17.32 lakh (AISHE 2023-24, PIB, July 2026). India had 54 universities in the QS World University Rankings 2026, up from 13 in 2015 (PIB, 2026).
- 4. Research and innovation. The Anusandhan National Research Foundation, established under the ANRF Act, 2023 and notified in February 2024, subsumed the Science and Engineering Research Board and is designed to channel roughly Rs 50,000 crore over five years, with a majority expected from non-government sources. Its flagship programmes — PAIR (hub-and-spoke partnerships pairing top institutions with weaker universities), MAHA (mission-mode research in strategic areas) and the ANRF Centres of Excellence — directly target the NEP’s diagnosis that Indian research is concentrated in a handful of institutions while State universities, which teach the bulk of students, remain research-poor.
- 5. Access and financing. Samagra Shiksha 2.0 integrates pre-school to Class 12; PM POSHAN extends hot cooked meals to pre-primary; PM Vidyalaxmi (approved November 2024) offers collateral-free, guarantor-free education loans with interest subvention for meritorious students in top institutions; and PM-USHA funds State higher-education institutions. SWAYAM, DIKSHA and PM e-Vidya carry the digital layer.

## The Andhra Pradesh layer — convergence and a candid weakness
- Demand-side support: Talliki Vandanam (G.O.Ms.No.27, School Education Department, Government of Andhra Pradesh, 12 June 2025) transfers Rs 15,000 per child per year to the mother or guardian for every eligible child from Class 1 to Intermediate — unlike its predecessor, it is not capped at one child per household. The 2026-27 release covered roughly 67.47 lakh students at an outlay of about Rs 10,120 crore (Government of Andhra Pradesh, July 2026).
- Supply-side response: Mega DSC-2025 (G.O.Ms.No.15, School Education Department, 19 April 2025) notified 16,347 teacher posts — the State’s largest single teacher recruitment — and the AP Budget 2025-26 extended free electricity to around 44,000 government schools.
- The weakness to acknowledge — this is what makes the answer credible: UDISE+ 2025-26 records that Andhra Pradesh has 16,357 single-teacher schools, the highest of any State. A single-teacher school cannot deliver the 5+3+3+4 stage-wise pedagogy NEP prescribes, so AP’s challenge is not enrolment or financing but school consolidation and teacher rationalisation — exactly the implementation gap the question’s syllabus heading is about.

- **Higher education GER** — 23.7 (2014-15) · 30.0 (2023-24) · AISHE, Ministry of Education, July 2026
- **Total HE enrolment** — 3.42 crore (2014-15) · 4.50 crore (2023-24) · AISHE 2023-24
- **Gender Parity Index (HE)** — Below 1 pre-2017-18 · 1.08 (2023-24) · AISHE 2023-24
- **Women in STEM enrolment** — 38.4% (2014-15) · 44% (2023-24) · AISHE 2023-24
- **Secondary dropout rate** — 8.2% (2024-25) · 7.0% (2025-26) · UDISE+, Ministry of Education
- **Schools with internet** — 63.5% (2024-25) · 67.4% (2025-26) · UDISE+ 2025-26
- **NEP target: HE GER — 50% by 2035** — NEP 2020

## Conclusion

Indian education policy has moved decisively from an input-and-access orientation to one built around learning outcomes, flexibility and research capacity, and the indicators bear this out. The binding constraint is now implementation rather than design: teacher availability and rationalisation, the digital divide, the fiscal capacity of States, and public spending that remains short of the 6% of GDP recommended since the Kothari Commission (1964-66) and reaffirmed by NEP 2020. Andhra Pradesh illustrates both sides — among the most generous demand-side transfers in the country, alongside the largest number of single-teacher schools. ## Introduction

Indian policy is drafted by expert committees, NITI Aayog task forces and departmental cells, yet outcomes routinely lag intent — what Pressman and Wildavsky termed the implementation deficit. The failure is rarely one of ideas; it lies in the chain that converts a sanction order into a service at the doorstep. The PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 (NCERT, national report released July 2025) illustrates this sharply: after a decade of foundational-literacy missions, only 55% of Class 3 students could arrange numbers up to 99 in order.

- **Stage** — What should happen · Where it leaks
- **1. Formulation** — Evidence-based, disaggregated design · Averaged national assumptions ignore regional diversity
- **2. Resourcing** — Predictable, front-loaded fund flow · Entitlement outlays crowd out monitoring and maintenance
- **3. Machinery** — Trained, stable cutting-edge staff · Vacancies, frequent transfers, no institutional memory
- **4. Interface** — Correct, complete beneficiary list · Exclusion errors from outdated databases
- **5. Feedback** — Real-time outcome tracking · Input audits only; no mid-course correction

## Major issues responsible for the formulation–implementation gap
- Design divorced from field diversity: Secretariat-drafted templates assume an average district that exists nowhere. Irrigation and crop-risk designs calibrated for assured-rainfall deltas travel badly to the Rayalaseema districts of Anantapuramu and YSR Kadapa, where rainfall variability and groundwater depletion produce a different risk profile altogether. Without granular disaggregation at the design stage, uniform schemes guarantee uneven outcomes.
- Capacity vacuum at the cutting edge: Delivery happens through the last functionary, not the first note-sheet. The 2nd ARC’s 15th Report (State and District Administration, 2009) identified tenure instability and frontline vacancies as core delivery failures. Andhra Pradesh’s Mega DSC-2025 teacher-recruitment drive was designed precisely to plug this cutting-edge gap — and the litigation it attracted shows recruitment integrity is itself part of implementation, not a precondition for it.
- Fiscal commitment outrunning fiscal capacity: Large recurring entitlements consume the very headroom that monitoring and maintenance need. AP budgeted Rs. 32,143 crore for NTR Bharosa pensions in FY 2025-26 (Govt. of AP, sspensions.ap.gov.in) and Rs. 10,090.74 crore for Talliki Vandanam covering 67.27 lakh students (AP School Education Dept. G.O., June 2025). When revenue slips, releases stagger and the promise thins at the margin.
- Targeting and exclusion errors: Lists built on obsolete databases misfire structurally. NFSA coverage still rests on Census 2011 ratios — against an intended 81.35 crore, about 80.67 crore persons actually draw grain (Dept. of Food & Public Distribution, December 2024) — leaving post-2011 urban migrants outside a right they legally hold. An error of enumeration becomes an error of justice.
- Absence of real-time feedback: Departments audit expenditure, not outcomes, so failure surfaces only at the annual review. AP’s Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) is the corrective template: its AWARE 2.0 platform fuses satellite, drone, IoT and CCTV feeds across 42+ applications under a five-year MoU with ISRO’s Satish Dhawan Space Centre (Govt. of AP/RTGS, June 2025), converting monitoring from retrospective audit into continuous alert.
- Weak, non-enforceable citizen interface: Citizens’ Charters remain non-justiciable and the Sevottam model voluntary (2nd ARC, 12th Report). Where the interface is redesigned, delivery visibly improves — AP’s Mana Mitra WhatsApp Governance (launched January 2025) now carries over 700 services with QR-verified, DigiLocker-linked certificates, removing the office visit that middlemen used to monetise.

## Conclusion

The implementation deficit is a governance-design problem, not an intelligence problem. Narrowing it requires outcome budgeting in place of expenditure budgeting, stable tenures tied to result-based appraisal, third-party concurrent evaluation, and statutory service guarantees that convert promises into enforceable claims. Andhra Pradesh’s pairing of a real-time data spine (RTGS/AWARE 2.0) with a citizen-facing delivery channel (Mana Mitra) indicates the direction of travel: policy succeeds when feedback is continuous and entitlement is enforceable.

## Value addition
- Conceptual toolkit: Pressman & Wildavsky’s implementation deficit; top-down (Sabatier–Mazmanian) versus bottom-up (Lipsky’s street-level bureaucracy) models — the latter explains why frontline discretion, not cabinet intent, decides the final outcome.
- 2nd ARC, 12th Report (Citizen Centric Administration): recommends the Sevottam service-delivery excellence model — Citizens’ Charter + Public Grievance Redress + Service Delivery Capability. India became the first country with a published public service delivery standard, IS 15700:2005.
- Enforceability instruments: State Right to Services Acts with penalty for delay (Karnataka Sakala Services Act, 2011); Social Audit under Section 17, MGNREGA; CPGRAMS for grievance escalation.
- Capacity instrument:Mission Karmayogi (NPCSCB) — shift from rule-based to role-based, competency-driven capacity building through the iGOT platform.
- AP institutional anchors to quote: RTGS (est. 2017), AWARE 2.0, State Data Lake, Mana Mitra, and the P4 ‘Zero Poverty — Bangaru Kutumbam’ platform (launched Ugadi, 30 March 2025) as a co-delivery experiment under Swarnandhra Vision 2047.

## Introduction
**Civil society** is the space between the state and the individual — voluntary organisations, community groups, social movements, professional associations, NGOs and citizens' collectives. In India it has been central to socio-political evolution, from Gandhi's mass mobilisation to the RTI campaign, strengthening democracy and holding the state accountable.

## Key features
- **Pluralism**: a diversity of religious, cultural, caste-based and professional associations.
- **Advocacy role**: a pressure group shaping policy (the **MKSS** and the RTI movement).
- **Watchdog function**: monitoring corruption and rights violations (the India Against Corruption/Lokpal movement).
- **Service delivery**: supplementing the state in education, health and disaster relief.
- **Democratic participation**: fostering debate, mobilisation and grassroots engagement.

## Limitations in a democratic system
- **Fragmentation**: social divisions (caste, religion, region) weaken collective action.
- **Funding issues**: dependence on foreign or state funds (and **FCRA** restrictions) can compromise autonomy.
- **Accountability concerns**: opacity and misuse of some NGO platforms.
- **Political co-option**: reducing neutrality.
- **Urban-centric** reach, leaving rural areas underserved.

## Conclusion
Civil society is a **pillar of Indian democracy** — amplifying citizen voices, empowering the weak and enhancing accountability. To function effectively it needs **greater transparency, internal democracy and independence** from political and financial pressures. A strengthened civil society ensures democracy is not merely electoral but **participatory and inclusive**.
P3-Q8b:
## Introduction
Women's empowerment is a pillar of inclusive development and social justice. Alongside the State's constitutional provisions and welfare schemes, **NGOs** have become vital partners in bridging gaps, mobilising communities and empowering women at the grassroots.

## How NGOs advance women's empowerment
- **Education and literacy**: Pratham and SEWA Bharat run literacy and skill-training for rural and urban women.
- **Economic empowerment**: promoting **Self-Help Groups, microfinance and entrepreneurship** — the SHG movement in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana turned women into economic agents.
- **Health and nutrition**: supplementing government schemes on maternal health, sanitation and nutrition.
- **Legal and social awareness**: workshops on rights, domestic violence, dowry and workplace harassment.
- **Leadership and participation**: nurturing women leaders in Panchayats and community forums.

## How their role can be enhanced
- **Transparent, stable funding** and rationalised FCRA norms; **capacity building** of grassroots NGOs; **partnership with government** (convergence with schemes); and **accountability mechanisms** to build public trust.

## Key challenges
- **Funding constraints** and FCRA restrictions; **capacity limitations**; **political/bureaucratic hurdles** and fund-release delays; **fragmentation** and weak coordination; and **credibility issues** from occasional misuse.

## Conclusion
NGOs complement state efforts by reaching the most vulnerable, innovating at the grassroots and amplifying women's voices. Strengthening their role — through transparent funding, capacity, partnership and accountability — can ensure that women achieve not just welfare but **genuine empowerment and equality**.
P3-Q9a:
## Introduction
The **National Commission for Women (NCW)** was established under the **National Commission for Women Act, 1990** as a **statutory body** to safeguard women's rights and address discrimination, violence and inequality — deriving its powers from statute rather than directly from the Constitution.

## Main features
- **Statutory basis and composition**: a **Chairperson, five Members and a Member-Secretary**, appointed by the Central Government.
- **Advisory and investigative role**: reviews constitutional/legal safeguards and recommends amendments; investigates complaints of deprivation of women's rights and gender-based violence; can take *suo motu* notice.
- **Quasi-judicial powers**: while inquiring, it has the **powers of a civil court** (summoning witnesses, examining evidence, requisitioning records); recommends action including FIRs.
- **Awareness and outreach**: research, gender-sensitisation programmes, public hearings (Mahila Jansunwai) and initiatives on emerging issues (AI/cyber-safety, deepfakes).

## Limitations
- **Advisory nature**: its recommendations are **not binding**.
- **No enforcement powers**: it relies on the police/state agencies, causing delays.
- **Resource constraints**: limited budget and staff weaken rural/tribal outreach despite rising complaints (over 30,000 a year).
- **Overlapping jurisdiction** with State Women's Commissions and the NHRC; and **dependence on political will** (e.g., limited progress on marital-rape recognition).

## Conclusion
The NCW is a **vital institution for amplifying women's voices** and redressing grievances, but its **advisory character and dependence on state action** limit its effectiveness. Empowering it with **greater autonomy, binding authority in specific cases and adequate resources** would transform it from an advisory body into a robust guardian of gender justice — advancing the constitutional vision of equality.
P3-Q9b:
## Introduction
Quasi-judicial authorities perform court-like functions in specialised areas; certain constitutional provisions empower their creation.

## Constitutional provisions
- **Articles 323A and 323B**: empower Parliament and legislatures to establish **administrative tribunals** and tribunals for other matters (tax, industrial disputes, land reforms, elections).
- These provisions (added by the 42nd Amendment) enable specialised adjudicatory bodies.
- Broadly, the legislative power to create statutory bodies with adjudicatory functions.

## Examples
- **Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)** — service matters.
- **National Green Tribunal (NGT)** — environmental disputes.
- Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, and regulatory bodies like SEBI and TRAI with quasi-judicial powers.

## Significance
- Provide speedy, specialised justice and reduce the burden on courts.

## Conclusion
Articles 323A and 323B empower the creation of quasi-judicial tribunals like CAT and NGT—specialised bodies that deliver expert, speedy adjudication while remaining subject to judicial review.
P3-Q10a:
## Introduction
**Social audit** is a participatory tool by which citizens evaluate the implementation of policies and programmes against their stated objectives — bridging the gap between the **vision** of welfare schemes and their **ground reality**. India pioneered it (statutorily under MGNREGA), but its **institutionalisation** faces real impediments.

## How social audit narrows the vision–reality gap
- **Accountability**: exposing misuse of funds and poor implementation (irregularities like ghost beneficiaries and inflated bills in MGNREGA works).
- **Citizen empowerment**: enabling direct, bottom-up monitoring through the **Gram Sabha**.
- **Better service delivery**: providing feedback for course correction — aligning schemes (MGNREGA, PMAY, NFSA) with their inclusive-growth vision.

## Impediments to institutionalisation
- **Weak legal backing**: except MGNREGA (2005), most schemes lack a statutory audit mandate.
- **Bureaucratic and political resistance**: officials often see audits as exposing corruption.
- **Lack of awareness**: low beneficiary knowledge of entitlements (rural awareness often below 40%).
- **Resource constraints**: shortage of trained auditors and funds.
- **Fear of reprisal**: intimidation of whistle-blowers and community auditors.

## The way forward
- **Legal mandate** across all major schemes; **independent social-audit units** with citizen participation; **technology** (GIS, online dashboards) for credibility; and **capacity building and awareness** through civil society (the AP–Telangana **SSAAT** model being a national template).

## Conclusion
Social audits are crucial for turning **paper promises into lived realities** through accountability and participation. Institutionalising them — with **stronger legal frameworks, awareness and administrative will** — will make governance more transparent, inclusive and people-centric.
P3-Q10b:
## Introduction
**Good governance** is the transparent, accountable and participatory exercise of authority in managing a nation's political, social and economic affairs. Per **UNESCAP**, it rests on participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, equity, effectiveness, accountability and inclusiveness. The **RTI Act, 2005** operationalises several of these, deepening democracy.

## Good governance — meaning and principles
- Beyond mere government functioning, it concerns **how power is exercised** to manage resources and ensure inclusive growth — its principles being **transparency, accountability, rule of law, participation, effectiveness/efficiency, and equity/inclusiveness**.

## How the RTI Act promotes good governance
- **Transparency**: citizens can demand records on spending, recruitment and decisions — RTI exposed the **2G spectrum and CWG** irregularities.
- **Accountability**: officials must justify decisions, curbing corruption and improving compliance in service delivery (ration shops, MGNREGA wages).
- **Participation**: citizens monitor PDS, school funds and Panchayat expenditure, engaging actively in governance.
- **Rule of law**: empowering citizens against arbitrary State action (*CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay*, 2011 — access to evaluated answer sheets).
- **Equity and inclusiveness**: marginalised groups, women and SC/STs use RTI to claim welfare entitlements.
- Reinforced by **proactive disclosure (Section 4)** and digital RTI portals.

## Concerns
- **Pendency** in Information Commissions, threats to RTI activists, low rural awareness, and dilution via the **2019 amendment** and the **DPDP Act, 2023**.

## Conclusion
The RTI Act has strengthened **transparency, accountability and participation** — the core of good governance. Despite challenges of pendency and dilution, it remains indispensable to responsive governance; strengthening it through digitisation, activist protection and proactive disclosure can align India with global standards of good governance.
P3-Q11a:
## Introduction
Public servants frequently face situations where **personal values conflict with public responsibilities** — empathy versus rule enforcement, personal morality versus official policy, or private loyalty versus public duty. A strong **ethical foundation** equips officers with the moral clarity to resolve such dilemmas while preserving accountability.

## The nature of value conflicts
- Officers balance **impartiality against political pressure, compassion against the law, and personal belief against policy** — e.g., empathy toward encroachers versus the duty to protect public land.

## How an ethical foundation resolves dilemmas
- **Objectivity and impartiality**: decisions guided by **fairness, not bias** (election officials' neutrality safeguarding democracy).
- **Integrity and honesty**: resisting bribery and nepotism even at personal cost (officers who cancel tainted deals despite transfers).
- **Commitment to the public good**: a moral compass prioritising citizens over personal or political gain, enhancing the **legitimacy** of governance.

## Maintaining accountability through ethical conduct
- **Legal accountability**: adherence to laws, service rules and constitutional mandates.
- **Administrative accountability**: proactive transparency (RTI disclosure, Citizen's Charters).
- **Moral accountability**: going beyond duty in the Gandhian spirit (officers building public infrastructure through community effort; whistle-blowers like Satyendra Dubey exposing corruption at personal risk).

## Conclusion
A strong ethical foundation acts as a **compass** for public servants navigating value conflicts. By aligning **personal morality with constitutional responsibility** — supported by codes of conduct, whistle-blower protection and ethics training (Mission Karmayogi) — officers can ensure both effective governance and accountability, transforming dilemmas into opportunities to build public trust.
P3-Q11b:
## Introduction
Whistleblowers, who expose wrongdoing, are guardians of ethical accountability; their protection is vital for integrity in governance.

## Ethical importance
- Uphold **honesty, transparency and public interest**.
- Expose corruption, fraud and abuse of power.
- Reinforce a culture of accountability and moral courage.

## Institutional importance of whistleblower protection
- Encourages reporting by shielding whistleblowers from **retaliation** (victimisation, dismissal, threats).
- The **Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014** provides a framework.
- Strengthens oversight mechanisms (CVC, Lokpal).
- Deters wrongdoing and builds public trust.

## Challenges
- Weak implementation and risk to whistleblowers' safety.

## Conclusion
Whistleblower protection is essential to safeguard those who expose wrongdoing—reinforcing ethical accountability and integrity in public service; robust, well-implemented protection encourages honest disclosure without fear.
P3-Q12a:
## Introduction
A diverse society like India requires certain ethical values to ensure peaceful coexistence.

## Essential ethical values
- **Tolerance and respect** for diversity of religion, language and culture.
- **Empathy and compassion** for others.
- **Justice and equality**—non-discrimination.
- **Non-violence and harmony** (Gandhian ideals).
- **Fraternity and mutual understanding**.
- **Secularism** and inclusiveness.

## Illustrations
- India's tradition of **'unity in diversity'** and religious tolerance.
- Constitutional values of fraternity and equality (Preamble).
- Communal harmony initiatives and Ek Bharat Shrestha Bharat.

## Significance
- These values prevent conflict and build social cohesion.

## Conclusion
Tolerance, empathy, justice, non-violence and fraternity are essential for peaceful coexistence in a diverse society—values embodied in India's ethos of unity in diversity and its constitutional principles.
P3-Q12b:
## Introduction
Early value education in the family profoundly shapes ethical decision-making in adulthood.

## Influence of family value education
- **Foundation of character**: the family is the first school where honesty, empathy, respect and responsibility are instilled.
- **Role modelling**: children imitate parents' ethical (or unethical) behaviour.
- **Moral reasoning**: early guidance shapes conscience and the ability to distinguish right from wrong.
- **Emotional intelligence and empathy** developed in childhood.
- **Habits and values** internalised early persist into adulthood.

## Impact in adulthood
- Guides ethical choices, integrity and social conduct in personal and professional life.

## Conclusion
Values nurtured early in the family form the moral foundation of an individual—shaping conscience, empathy and integrity that guide ethical decision-making throughout adult life.
P3-Q13a:
## Introduction
**Attitude** is a psychological tendency expressed by evaluating a person, object or situation favourably or unfavourably. Formed through beliefs, values, experience and socialisation, it profoundly shapes a public servant's **decision-making, citizen interaction and commitment to public welfare**.

## Definition
- A **learned predisposition** to respond consistently favourably or unfavourably toward an object, with three components — **cognitive (beliefs), affective (feelings) and behavioural (action tendency)**.

## How attitude affects the behaviour of public servants
- **Citizen-centric service delivery**: a **positive, pro-poor attitude** brings empathy, patience and efficiency in handling grievances and implementing welfare (PMAY, MGNREGA).
- **Ethical and responsive governance**: attitudes of **integrity and honesty** prevent corruption and misuse of authority (the 'steel frame' ideal of neutrality).
- **Inclusiveness**: a **gender- and diversity-sensitive** attitude improves the delivery of schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and reduces caste/regional bias.
- **Resistance and bias**: **negative attitudes** — apathy, arrogance, prejudice — hinder governance and erode public trust.

## Shaping the right attitude
- Through **training, value inculcation, ethics codes and exposure to citizen realities** (village immersion) — and drawing on role models of integrity and persistence (e.g., electoral reform driven by an official's steadfastness).

## Conclusion
Attitude significantly determines the conduct of public servants. A **positive, citizen-centric and ethical attitude** ensures transparency, accountability and people-friendly governance — making the cultivation of the right attitude, through training and value education, essential to a responsive civil service in a democracy.
P3-Q13b:
## Introduction
**Attitude** is a learned predisposition to respond positively or negatively toward a person, issue or situation. It is not a single trait but a combination of **three interrelated components — cognitive, affective and behavioural** — which together shape how administrators perceive issues, feel about them and act.

## The three components (with public-service examples)
- **Cognitive component (beliefs and knowledge)**: what a person knows or believes about an issue. *Example*: an officer's belief that 'corruption undermines democracy' shapes a firm anti-corruption stand; cognitive awareness of poverty or climate change motivates **evidence-based policymaking**.
- **Affective component (feelings and emotions)**: the emotional response to an issue. *Example*: **empathy** for marginalised groups leads an officer to prioritise welfare schemes (PM POSHAN, MGNREGA); compassion during disasters drives officials to work beyond office hours for relief.
- **Behavioural component (action and conduct)**: the actual or intended action flowing from beliefs and feelings. *Example*: an officer who believes in equality (cognitive) and feels empathy (affective) actively promotes **gender budgeting** or ensures fair PDS distribution.

## Their interrelation and change
- The three are **consistent and reinforcing**; inconsistency creates **cognitive dissonance**. Attitudes can be shaped through conditioning, rewards, social observation and role-modelling.

## Conclusion
The cognitive, affective and behavioural components together determine how a public servant functions. A **balanced, positive attitude** ensures integrity, empathy and responsiveness in governance — making **ethics training, value orientation and exposure to citizen issues** essential to develop such attitudes and strengthen democratic administration.
P3-Q14a:
## Introduction
A **Code of Ethics** is a set of principles guiding the moral conduct of public servants in their professional duties. In a democracy where officials wield authority and discretion, a well-defined ethical framework helps **resolve conflicts of interest** and promote **ethical, citizen-centric decision-making**.

## How a code resolves conflicts of interest
- **Clarity in decision-making**: separating personal interests from official duty — **asset disclosure and post-retirement job restrictions** prevent misuse of office.
- **Promoting impartiality**: mandating neutrality regardless of caste, religion or political pressure (fair recruitment and welfare distribution).
- **Preventing corruption**: emphasising **integrity and accountability**, drawing on the **Nolan Principles (UK)** and the **2nd ARC's** stress on transparency and selflessness.

## How a code promotes ethical decision-making
- **Citizen-centric governance**: prioritising public interest over personal or political gain (equitable vaccine distribution during COVID-19).
- **Strengthening public trust**: ethical conduct builds credibility (Lal Bahadur Shastri's resignation over a rail accident as a model of accountability).
- **Guidance in dilemmas**: balancing competing values (development versus tribal rights) with principled reasoning.

## The Nolan framework
- **Selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership** — the seven principles of public life that an Indian code of ethics can institutionalise.

## Conclusion
A Code of Ethics acts as a **moral compass** for civil servants — helping them avoid conflicts of interest, resist undue influence and uphold fairness. Institutionalising ethical standards (as the 2nd ARC urged, alongside the Conduct Rules) makes public administration **transparent, accountable and citizen-centric**, strengthening democratic governance.
P3-Q14b:
## Introduction
Leadership in public life is not merely about authority but about **ethical responsibility toward citizens**. **Integrity, transparency and accountability** form the triad of good governance, ensuring that decisions serve the public interest and that leaders enjoy trust and legitimacy.

## Significance of the triad
- **Integrity**: consistency between words and actions, preventing misuse of power (E. Sreedharan delivering the Delhi Metro on time and corruption-free).
- **Transparency**: making decision-making open to scrutiny, minimising arbitrariness and secrecy — the **RTI Act (2005)** institutionalised it.
- **Accountability**: leaders answerable for their actions and outcomes, strengthening democratic legitimacy (the **CAG's 2G and coal** reports holding leadership to account).

## How public leaders can demonstrate these values
- **Integrity**: avoiding conflicts of interest and upholding impartiality (mobilising resources for public projects without personal gain).
- **Transparency**: using **digital dashboards, open-data portals and public consultation** before policy rollout.
- **Accountability**: setting clear **performance targets, publishing outcomes, and submitting to audits and citizen feedback** — reinforced by **whistle-blower protection** (the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014), the **CVC and CAG**, and grievance systems (CPGRAMS).
- Global and Indian parallels — New Zealand's transparent COVID-19 communication; Kiran Bedi's integrity-driven Tihar reforms.

## Conclusion
Integrity, transparency and accountability are **indispensable to ethical leadership and good governance**. Leaders demonstrate them by aligning personal conduct with **constitutional morality** and institutional safeguards — creating a governance culture rooted in trust, justice and service to citizens, in which whistle-blowers serve as the ethical conscience of public service.
P3-Q15a:
## Introduction
**Cybercrime** refers to offences committed using computers, networks or digital devices to harass, cheat, threaten or defraud. Among the most serious is **cyberstalking**, a growing concern in India, especially for women and youth, addressed through the IT Act and criminal law.

## What is cyberstalking?
- The use of the internet or electronic means to **persistently follow, harass or intimidate** an individual — a 'course of conduct' of repeated acts causing alarm or distress. Its forms include:
  - **Unsolicited persistent contact** despite the victim's disinterest;
  - **Monitoring online activity** (spyware, GPS tracking);
  - **Doxxing** — publishing private information/images without consent;
  - **Threats and false accusations**.
- India has **no single dedicated section**; cyberstalking is tackled through the **IT Act, 2000** and **Section 354D of the IPC/BNS** (which criminalises stalking, including its digital form, against women).

## Other cyber offences under the IT Act, 2000
- **Hacking/unauthorised access (Section 66)**; **identity theft (66C)** and **cheating by personation (66D)**; **violation of privacy (66E)**; **cyber-terrorism (66F)**; **publishing/transmitting obscene or sexually explicit material (67, 67A, 67B — child sexual abuse material)**; and tampering with computer source documents (65).
- Related frauds — **phishing, smishing, vishing, ransomware** — and interception powers under **Section 69**; enforcement via **CERT-In** and the **I4C/1930 helpline**.

## Conclusion
Cyberstalking and other cyber offences are serious threats to **privacy, safety and freedom** in the digital age. The IT Act, 2000, with the criminal law, provides a framework to deter and punish them — but **stronger enforcement, digital awareness and responsible online behaviour** (and the proposed **Digital India Act**) are crucial to a safe cyberspace for all.
P3-Q15b:
## Introduction
The **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** is a comprehensive, **destination-based indirect tax** implemented on **1 July 2017**, subsuming multiple indirect taxes (excise, service tax, VAT, octroi) to realise the idea of **'One Nation, One Tax, One Market'** — a landmark in fiscal federalism.

## Key characteristics
- **Destination-based**: revenue accrues to the State of **consumption**, not production.
- **Elimination of cascading**: seamless **Input Tax Credit** removes the 'tax on tax' effect.
- **Dual model**: both the Centre and States levy tax on the same supply.

## The regulatory framework
- **Types**: **CGST and SGST/UTGST** on intra-State supplies; **IGST** (levied by the Centre) on inter-State supplies and imports.
- **Governing body — the GST Council (a constitutional body, Article 279A)**: chaired by the Union Finance Minister with State Finance Ministers; decisions by a **three-fourths weighted majority** — an embodiment of cooperative federalism (*Mohit Minerals*, 2022, held its recommendations persuasive, not binding).

## Constitutional provisions
- Enabled by the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016**:
  - **Article 246A** — concurrent power of Parliament and States to legislate on GST (Parliament exclusive on IGST);
  - **Article 269A** — levy and apportionment of IGST;
  - **Article 279A** — the GST Council;
  - **Article 366(12A)** — defines GST (excluding alcoholic liquor for human consumption);
  - amendments to the **Seventh Schedule**.

## Conclusion
GST is a major milestone in India's fiscal history, strengthening **cooperative federalism** through a common, transparent, simplified regime. Despite challenges of compliance and rate rationalisation — addressed by ongoing reforms such as the move toward a **simplified two-slab structure** — it continues to evolve into a more efficient, growth-oriented taxation framework.
P4-Q1a:
## Introduction

The Balance of Payments records all economic transactions between residents and the rest of the world; the Current Account captures trade in goods and services, primary income and transfers. India’s structural pattern is a large merchandise deficit financed by a surplus in invisibles. Reassuringly, CAD narrowed to USD 15 billion (0.8% of GDP) in H1 FY26, from USD 25.3 billion (1.3%) in H1 FY25 — placing India among economies with modest and sustainable deficits, well ahead of New Zealand (−7.7%), Brazil (−3.8%) and Australia (−3.6%).

## Factors contributing to CAD / adverse BoP
- Structural merchandise trade deficit

Import basket dominated by crude oil (~88–90% import dependence), gold and silver, electronics, edible oils and fertilisers.

Precious-metal imports surged in 2025–26 on safe-haven demand — gold in RBI reserves alone rose from USD 78.2 bn (Mar 2025) to USD 117.5 bn (Jan 2026) on price effects.

Merchandise imports grew 5.9% (Apr–Dec 2025) against export growth of 2.4%.

## Narrow export basket and protectionism

US reciprocal tariffs and the 2026 “forced-labour” duties hit labour-intensive exports (textiles, gems & jewellery, seafood).

ES 2025–26 notes India’s exports are “high-beta” to global trade — they amplify global slowdowns.

- Cyclical commodity price shocks — Brent crossing USD 100/bbl in 2026 (Red Sea attacks, Strait of Hormuz disruption) directly widens the oil import bill.

## Capital-flow volatility (the financing side)

FPI flows are episodic — outflows during US yield spikes and “flight-to-safety” episodes; only three months of net inflows in FY26.

Rising external commercial borrowing costs when global rates harden.

## The stabilising counterweights (analytical balance)
- **Cushion** — Latest data
- **Services surplus** — Record total exports USD 825.3 bn (FY25); USD 418.5 bn in H1 FY26; services exports +6.5%; driven by IT, business services and Global Capability Centres
- **Remittances** — USD 73 bn in H1 FY26 (against USD 64.7 bn); USD 135.4 bn in FY25 ≈ 3.5% of GDP — world’s largest recipient; in most years exceed gross FDI
- **Remittance geography (RBI 6th Survey)** — US 27.7%, UAE 19.2%, UK 10.8%, Singapore 6.6% → shift from Gulf blue-collar to advanced-economy white-collar
- **FDI** — Gross FDI inflows +16.1% YoY (Apr–Nov 2025)
- **Reserves** — USD 701.4 bn (16 Jan 2026); peak USD 728.5 bn (Feb 2026); USD 676.2 bn (17 July 2026) — about 11 months import cover, ~94% of external debt

## Implications for the Indian economy
- **Channel** — Consequence
- **Currency pressure** — A wide CAD raises dollar demand → the rupee slid to a record ₹96.84 (20 May 2026); INR depreciated about 5.4% (Apr 2025–Jan 2026)
- **Imported inflation** — Weaker rupee plus costly crude feed into CPI (June 2026: 4.38%), raising the fertiliser and LPG subsidy bill and squeezing fiscal space
- **Reserve drawdown** — RBI net dollar sales of USD 8.9 bn (April) and USD 6.1 bn (May 2026); sustained depletion erodes shock-absorbing capacity
- **Debt servicing** — External debt about 19% of GDP — moderate, but depreciation raises the rupee cost of repayment for corporates with unhedged exposure
- **Investor confidence** — Deterioration raises risk premia and borrowing costs — though offset in FY26 by three sovereign rating upgrades and a halving of the 10-year spread over US Treasuries
- **Positive side** — A moderate CAD in a fast-growing economy signals investment exceeding domestic savings — capital imported for capacity creation, not consumption

## Way forward
- Export diversification: operationalise the Export Promotion Mission; leverage India–UK CETA and India–EFTA TEPA, and conclude the India–US trade agreement to reduce tariff uncertainty.
- Energy security: raise ethanol blending, renewables and nuclear capacity; expand Strategic Petroleum Reserves; scale the National Green Hydrogen Mission; new incentives for critical mineral recycling.
- Value addition over volume: deepen electronics, pharma and semiconductor exports (ISM 2.0), replacing low-value shipments.
- Stable financing: prefer FDI over FPI; internationalise the rupee through Special Rupee Vostro Accounts and rupee invoicing; the expanded Fully Accessible Route (2026) for long-tenor G-secs deepens stable debt inflows.
- Gold demand management: revive gold monetisation and promote sovereign / financial gold substitutes.

P4-Q1b:
## Introduction

Manufacturing is more infrastructure-dependent than any other sector: it needs reliable power, cheap transport, assured water, serviced land and fast digital connectivity — simultaneously and continuously. A shortfall in any one nullifies investment in the others. This is a principal reason India’s manufacturing remains at about 12.8% of nominal GDP, far short of the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011.

- How each bottleneck hinders manufacturing
- Power — cost and reliability

How it hinders: Industrial tariffs in India are raised by cross-subsidy — industry pays more so that agriculture and domestic consumers pay less. Andhra Pradesh alone budgets about ₹11,000 crore in agricultural power subsidy and ₹890 crore for aquaculture. Unreliable supply forces firms to install captive diesel generation, which is several times costlier. For an energy-intensive manufacturer, power cost alone can determine whether an Indian location is viable against a Vietnamese or Bangladeshi one.

- Logistics cost

How it hinders: At about 7.97% of GDP (NCAER, 2023-24), India’s logistics cost exceeds that of competitor economies. Since a manufacturer’s product must reach a port or a market, this is a direct tax on competitiveness applied to every unit sold. It particularly penalises firms located inland — which is precisely where employment is most needed.

- Modal imbalance

How it hinders: Roads carry a disproportionate share of freight, though rail is cheaper for bulk over long distances. Steel, cement, coal and fertiliser producers therefore pay more to move heavy inputs than they would with an optimal modal mix.

- Last-mile connectivity

How it hinders: A port with adequate capacity but congested approach roads delivers the delay it was built to remove. Industrial parks without functional connecting roads cannot attract tenants regardless of the incentives offered.

- Land

How it hinders: Acquisition cost, litigation and delay under the LARR Act, 2013 raise project cost and, more damagingly, create uncertainty about timelines, which investors price heavily. Unclear titles — India’s system remains presumptive rather than conclusive, and the AP Land Titling Act, 2022 was repealed in 2024 — add legal risk to every transaction.

- Water

How it hinders: Textiles, paper, chemicals, food processing and semiconductors are water-intensive. Groundwater depletion and competing agricultural demand make assured industrial supply uncertain, and effluent treatment

obligations add cost.

- Digital and telecom

How it hinders: Industry 4.0 — predictive maintenance, quality inspection, supply-chain traceability — requires industrial-grade connectivity. Where it is absent, firms cannot meet the digital traceability requirements that global buyers now impose as a condition of purchase.

- Warehousing and cold chain

How it hinders: Inadequate storage forces immediate sale and raises wastage. The World Bank has estimated that grain and perishables lost to inadequate storage in India could feed a third of the country’s poor — for food processors, that loss is a direct input cost.

- Port and customs efficiency

How it hinders: Dwell time at ports and customs delays raise working capital requirements, since goods sitting in a container are capital not earning a return.

- Urban infrastructure and housing

How it hinders: Workers must live near factories. Where housing, transport, schools and health facilities are absent, firms cannot retain labour — a constraint that particularly affects greenfield industrial nodes.

- Institutional fragmentation

How it hinders: When road, rail, power and utility agencies plan independently, a factory may be connected to a road but not to a transmission line, or to power but not to a water main. The bottleneck is coordination, not any single asset.

- Steps to address the bottlenecks
- Integrated planning — the foundational step PM GatiShakti places 16-plus ministries on a common GIS platform so that road, rail, power, water and telecom are sequenced together. The National Logistics Policy (2022) and its Unified Logistics Interface Platform extend this to freight movement. Institutionalising these is worth more than any additional project.
- Reduce logistics cost through modal rebalancing Shift bulk freight to Dedicated Freight Corridors and coastal shipping; rationalise rail freight tariffs, which currently cross-subsidise passenger fares; develop multimodal logistics parks.
- Power sector reform Reduce cross-subsidy so that industrial tariffs reflect cost; strengthen distribution finances. The 16th Finance Commission recommends DISCOM privatisation with a special purpose vehicle to warehouse legacy debt, linked to release of capital investment assistance — the structural answer.
- Serviced industrial land Maintain land banks with plots pre-cleared for environment, power, water and road access, so an investor buys readiness rather than potential. Land pooling, as at Amaravati (about 33,000 acres from over 24,000 farmers), avoids the conflict acquisition generates. Complete land records digitisation under DILRMP and move toward conclusive titling.
- Node and cluster development Concentrate infrastructure in nodes rather than spreading it thinly — the logic of the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor with ADB support of US$631 million, and of AP’s 175 MSME parks. Agglomeration is what makes manufacturing competitive.
- Deepen infrastructure finance NaBFID (2021); develop the corporate bond market beyond its current 15-16% of GDP; use InvITs, REITs and NMP 2.0 (₹10 lakh crore, 2025-30) to recycle capital.
- Reform PPP Allocate risk by capability, extend the Hybrid Annuity Model, permit renegotiation on transparent triggers, and establish the IPRC and IPAT recommended by the Kelkar Committee (2015).
- Fund maintenance Ring-fence maintenance budgets and adopt performance-based asset management contracts.
- Digital and utility connectivity for industry Industrial-grade broadband, common effluent treatment, and assured water allocation as part of the standard industrial-park offering rather than as an afterthought.
- Skills alongside infrastructure Infrastructure without a workforce is idle capacity. The Employment Linked Incentive Scheme (₹99,446 crore) and industry-linked ITI models — Andhra Pradesh’s with 167 industry partners and 98% placement — are the complement to physical investment.
- Procedural certainty Statutory single-window clearance with deemed approval, as in AP’s Single Desk; Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 decriminalisation extended to State laws.

## Conclusion

Infrastructure bottlenecks hinder Indian manufacturing not by any single deficiency but by their simultaneity — a firm needs power, transport, water, land and connectivity together, and the absence of one negates the rest. The most valuable interventions are therefore the integrating ones: PM GatiShakti for planning, the National Logistics Policy for freight, node-based development for concentration, and DISCOM reform for power cost. India’s capital expenditure now exceeds its fiscal deficit — the resources are being committed; the returns depend on coordination, maintenance and the skills to use what is built.

- The cost benchmark: logistics at about 7.97% of GDP (NCAER, 2023-24); India 38th on the World Bank LPI (2023), improved from 44th in 2018.
- The integrating instruments: PM GatiShakti (GIS-based, 16-plus ministries), National Logistics Policy (2022)

and the Unified Logistics Interface Platform, and the LEADS State ranking.

## Introduction

Monetary policy — framed by the RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee under a statutory mandate — targets price stability; fiscal policy, framed by the government under Article 112, mobilises resources and allocates them. In March 2026 the Centre retained the 4% ±2% CPI inflation target for 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031 under Section 45ZA of the RBI Act, 1934, giving both arms a stable anchor.

## Instruments of monetary policy (position as of mid-2026)
- **Repo rate** — 5.25% · Single policy rate; signals stance
- **SDF (floor)** — 5.00% · Absorbs liquidity without collateral
- **MSF / Bank Rate (ceiling)** — 5.50% · Safety valve; 50 bps corridor
- **CRR** — 3.00% · Durable liquidity
- **SLR** — 18.00% · Prudential + captive G-Sec demand
- **OMOs, VRR/VRRR, FX swaps** — Active · Fine-tuning frictional and durable liquidity

- Taxation: gross tax receipts ₹44.04 lakh crore; GST 2.0’s two-slab structure (5%/18%); nil income tax up to ₹12.75 lakh for salaried taxpayers.
- Expenditure: total ₹53.47 lakh crore; capex ₹12.22 lakh crore; effective capex ₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of

## GDP).
- Borrowing and deficit management: fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP; debt anchor 50±1% by FY31.
- Transfers and subsidies: DBT, Just-in-Time releases, ₹1.85 lakh crore capex loans to States.

## Evaluation — the FY26 episode
- Inflation management worked, and worked jointly. Headline CPI fell to 1.7% (April-December 2025) — the lowest average in the current series, with 0.3% in October 2025 — driven by food disinflation. Core inflation appeared sticky at 4.62%, but excluding gold and silver it had fallen to about 2.3%, showing no demand overheating. Fiscal measures (GST rate cuts, duty rationalisation, buffer stock releases) attacked prices directly, while monetary policy delivered 125 bps of easing since February 2025.
- Transmission improved: with system liquidity in surplus of about ₹1.89 lakh crore in FY26, the weighted average call rate stayed on average 8 bps below the repo rate, and lending rates on fresh rupee loans fell 64 bps to 8.71% (November 2025) — the strongest pass-through in years.
- Resource mobilisation: revenue receipts strengthened from 8.5% of GDP (FY16-20) to about 9.1% (FY22-25), enabling higher capex without wider deficits.
- Limits are visible in 2026. In June 2026 the MPC held the repo rate at 5.25% with a neutral stance, cutting the FY27 growth forecast to 6.6% and raising the inflation forecast to 5.1% amid West Asian conflict, higher fuel prices and monsoon uncertainty. Monetary policy cannot offset supply shocks; fiscal instruments (duties, buffer stocks) must carry that load.

## Conclusion

Monetary policy delivers speed and price stability; fiscal policy delivers scale and structural capacity. India’s recent record shows their complementarity at its best — fiscal consolidation created room for rate cuts, and rate cuts lowered the government’s own borrowing cost. With supply shocks resurfacing, coordinated, data-driven calibration — not competition between the two arms — remains the key to sustaining growth with stability.

## Introduction

Public debt is the accumulated borrowing of government to bridge the gap between expenditure and non-debt receipts. Article 292 empowers Union borrowing on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India; Article 293(3) requires States indebted to the Centre to obtain its consent. Debt is classified as internal (domestic sources) or external (foreign sources).

- **Source** — Households, banks, insurance, provident funds, RBI · Multilateral (World Bank, ADB, IMF), bilateral (JICA), global markets
- **Currency** — Domestic (₹) · Foreign (USD, Yen, Euro, SDR)
- **Instruments** — G-Secs, T-bills, small savings/NSSF, State Development Loans · Concessional loans, ECBs, sovereign/masala bonds
- **Repayment effect** — Transfer within the economy; no forex outgo · Genuine resource outflow in foreign exchange
- **Key risk** — Crowding out; inflation if monetised · Currency depreciation, rollover and BoP risk
- **India (2026)** — ~95%+ of Centre’s liabilities; outstanding liabilities 55.6% of GDP (BE 2026-27) · Total external debt US$762.8 bn = 20.8% of GDP (end-March 2026); sovereign share small and largely concessional

## Internal debt
- Advantages: no exchange-rate risk; interest recirculates as domestic income; a deep captive investor base (SLR, insurance, pension funds); long maturities cut rollover risk — weighted average maturity of central market borrowings rose from 10.4 years (FY19) to about 13 years (FY25).
- Risks: absorbs private savings and can crowd out investment; monetisation is inflationary; a large interest bill (about

20 paise of every rupee the Centre spends) compresses capital outlay.

## External debt
- Advantages: supplements domestic savings; brings concessional finance, technology and project expertise (e.g., JICA-assisted metro and industrial corridor projects); inclusion of Indian G-Secs in global bond indices has widened the investor base and lowered yields.
- Risks: forex outflow and valuation shocks — of the US$26.3 billion rise in FY26, US$24.6 billion was pure valuation effect from dollar appreciation; short-term debt rose to 19.6% of the total; the 1991 BoP crisis remains the cautionary precedent.
- Cushions: debt service ratio a comfortable 5.8% of current receipts (down from 6.6%); 29.4% of external debt is rupee-denominated; large forex reserves cover short-term obligations.

## Conclusion

For India, the predominance of long-dated, rupee-denominated internal debt has insulated the economy from external debt crises, while calibrated external borrowing supplies scarce capital and technology. The real test is not the source but the use: borrowing that finances capital assets is self-liquidating; borrowing for consumption is not. A prudent mix, transparent accounting of off-budget liabilities, and productive deployment remain the anchors of sustainability.

## Value addition
- Constitutional/legal: Art. 292 (Union borrowing), Art. 293 (State borrowing, Centre’s consent); RBI Act, 1934 (Sec. 20, 21A) — RBI as debt manager; Government Securities Act, 2006; FRBM Act, 2003.
- RBI (end-March 2026): external debt US$762.8 bn; external debt/GDP 20.8% (19.8% a year earlier); long-term debt US$613.5 bn; currency mix — USD 55.5%, INR 29.4%, Yen 6.4%, SDR 4.3%, Euro 3.7%.
- 16th FC (2026-31): all off-budget borrowings of States to be brought on-budget; definitions of debt and fiscal deficit uniformly expanded — a major transparency reform.
- AP illustration: off-budget borrowings of ₹1.28 lakh crore (9.7% of GSDP) as of March 2023 (CAG) — the classic case for the 16th FC’s disclosure mandate.

## Introduction

The Government Budget is the Annual Financial Statement of estimated receipts and expenditure for a financial year, laid before Parliament under Article 112 (and before a State legislature under Article 202). Beyond accounting, it is the principal instrument of resource allocation, redistribution and stabilisation — Musgrave’s three functions of public finance.

## Types of budget
- Balanced: receipts equal expenditure — theoretically neat, practically rare in a developing economy.
- Surplus: receipts exceed expenditure — appropriate for cooling an overheated economy.
- Deficit: expenditure exceeds receipts — India’s norm, justified when borrowing finances asset creation. Union Budget 2026-27 projects a fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP.

## Types of public expenditure
- **Revenue expenditure** — Recurring — salaries, pensions, subsidies, interest, grants; creates no asset · Bulk of the ₹53.47 lakh crore total; interest payments alone about ₹14.04 lakh crore (20 paise of every rupee)
- **Capital expenditure** — Creates assets or reduces liabilities — infrastructure, defence equipment, loans to States · ₹12.22 lakh crore; effective capex ₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP), over 32% of total spending

A telling indicator of quality: effective capital expenditure (₹17.15 lakh crore) now exceeds the fiscal deficit (about ₹16.9 lakh crore) — borrowing is financing assets, not consumption.

## How expenditure is classified
- **Economic** — Revenue vs capital · Salaries (revenue) vs highways (capital)
- **Functional** — Purpose of spending · General services (defence ₹7.85 lakh crore, interest, administration); social services (education, health); economic services (agriculture, infrastructure); grants-in-aid to States
- **Accounting** — Major/minor head codes · Major heads 2000-3999 for revenue, 4000- 5999 for capital
- **Institutional** — Central Sector Schemes (17% of spending) vs Centrally Sponsored Schemes (8%) · CSS are shared with States; CS are fully Union-funded
- **Special statements** — Gender Budget, Child Budget, SC/ST welfare allocations, Outcome Budget · Gender Budget outlay rose from ₹0.98 lakh crore (2014-15) to ₹4.49 lakh crore (2025-26)

## Budget documents that give effect to this

The Annual Financial Statement (Art. 112), Demands for Grants (Art. 113), the Appropriation Bill (Art. 114) authorising withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund, the Finance Bill (Art. 110) for taxation, and the FRBM statements — Medium-Term Fiscal Policy, Fiscal Policy Strategy and Macroeconomic Framework.

## Conclusion

The budget is a statement of national priorities in the language of money. Its classification into revenue and capital, and by function, is what allows citizens and legislators to judge not merely how much is spent but how well. India’s recent shift — revenue expenditure falling from 13.6% of GDP (FY22) to 10.9% (FY25) while capital spending rose to about 3% — shows classification working as a discipline, not just a convention.

## Value addition
- Constitutional provisions: Art. 112 (AFS), 113 (Demands for Grants), 114 (Appropriation Bill), 110 (Money Bill), 266 (Consolidated Fund), 267 (Contingency Fund), 202 (State budget), 266(2) (Public Account).
- Union Budget 2026-27 at a glance: total expenditure ₹53.47 lakh crore; gross tax receipts ₹44.04 lakh crore; receipts excluding borrowings ₹36.51 lakh crore; nominal GDP ₹393 lakh crore; disinvestment target ₹80,000 crore; capex loans to States ₹1.85 lakh crore.

## Introduction

A deficit is the excess of government expenditure over its receipts in a financial year. It is a flow concept — the annual gap — whereas debt is the stock that accumulates from successive deficits. Different deficit measures answer different questions about fiscal health, which is why India’s budget reports four of them.

## Types of deficit — formula, meaning and current position
- **Revenue deficit** — Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts · Borrowing to meet consumption — the most worrying deficit · 1.5% of GDP
- **Effective revenue deficit** — Revenue deficit − Grants for capital asset creation · The true consumption gap, netting out grants that build assets in States · 0.3% of GDP
- **Fiscal deficit** — Total expenditure − Total receipts excluding borrowings · The government’s total borrowing requirement · 4.3% of GDP (≈ ₹16.9 lakh crore)
- **Primary deficit** — Fiscal deficit − Interest payments · The current fiscal stance, stripped of past debt burdens · 0.7% of GDP
- **Budgetary deficit** — Total receipts (including borrowings) − Total expenditure · Discontinued from 1997-98 with the end of ad-hoc treasury bills; conceptually important

## Economic implications

Where deficits help:

- Counter-cyclical stabilisation: during shocks — 2008 and COVID-19 — deficit spending sustained demand and prevented a deeper contraction.
- Growth-enhancing when productive: in Budget 2026-27, effective capital expenditure of ₹17.15 lakh crore exceeds the fiscal deficit of about ₹16.9 lakh crore, meaning borrowing is financing assets, not consumption.
- Crowding-in: public infrastructure lowers logistics and energy costs, raising private returns.

Where deficits harm:

- Debt accumulation and interest burden: interest payments absorb about 20 paise of every rupee the Centre spends — ₹14.04 lakh crore in FY27.
- Crowding out: heavy government borrowing absorbs domestic savings and can raise interest rates for private borrowers.
- Inflation risk: if financed by monetisation — which is why the FRBM Act barred RBI subscription to primary issues from April 2006.
- Intergenerational inequity: future taxpayers service debt incurred for present consumption.
- Macro credibility: persistent slippage raises risk premia and threatens ratings.

## The decisive distinction

A revenue deficit is always a warning sign — it means borrowing for salaries and subsidies. A fiscal deficit financed by capital expenditure is potentially self-liquidating, provided nominal growth exceeds the cost of borrowing (g > r). India’s nominal growth of about 10% against a lower average borrowing cost gives it that cushion.

## Conclusion

Deficits are neither inherently virtuous nor inherently dangerous — their composition determines their consequence.

India’s record since FY21 — the fiscal deficit falling from 9.2% to 4.3% while capital spending rose — shows consolidation and investment can proceed together. The anchor is now a debt-to-GDP target of 50±1% by March 2031, which shifts the discipline from an annual number to a medium-term path.

## Value addition
- FRBM Act, 2003 objectives: transparency in fiscal operations, inter-generational equity, debt smoothing, and giving the RBI flexibility to manage inflation free of fiscal dominance.
- Deficit trajectory: 9.2% (FY21) → 6.4% (FY23) → 5.6% (FY24) → 4.8% (FY25 PA) → 4.4% (FY26) → 4.3% (BE 2026-

27).

- 16th FC roadmap: Centre to reach 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31; States capped at 3% of GSDP; off-budget borrowings to be brought on-budget.
- State comparison: combined State fiscal deficit at 3.2% of GDP (FY25 PA) — 2.8% excluding SASCI loans; Andhra Pradesh at 3.84% of GSDP (BE 2026-27), down from 5.11% in FY25.

## Introduction

The State Finance Commission is to a State what the Union Finance Commission is to the Union — the constitutional mechanism for sharing resources with the tier below. Mandated by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, it is constituted by the Governor every five years under Article 243-I for panchayats, with Article 243-Y extending its review to municipalities.

## Role and functions of the SFC in Andhra Pradesh
- **Vertical and horizontal distribution** — Recommend the share of the net proceeds of State taxes, duties, tolls and fees to be assigned to local bodies, and the distribution among Gram Panchayats, Mandal Praja Parishads, Zilla Praja Parishads and municipalities
- **Grants-in-aid** — Recommend principles governing grants to local bodies from the Consolidated Fund of the State
- **Own Source Revenue** — Suggest measures to strengthen local revenue — property tax reform, user charges, advertisement and trade licence fees
- **Fiscal management** — Guide budgeting, accounting standards, audit and transparency at the local level
- **Review** — Assess the financial position and functioning of local bodies and recommend reforms

## Significance — strengthening local finances
- Bridging the resource gap: the SFC estimates local bodies’ revenue and expenditure on a normative basis, identifying the gap and recommending how to close it. AP’s Fifth State Finance Commission projected a resource gap of ₹7,033 crore for Panchayati Raj institutions and ₹2,016 crore for Urban Local Bodies over 2025-26 to 2029-30.
- Diagnosing the underlying problem: the same Commission found that in 2023-24, salaries, pensions and interest payments exceeded the State’s own revenues by 111% — meaning the State itself lacked the fiscal space to fund local bodies adequately. It also flagged a large gap between property tax demand and actual collection, locating the remedy in local revenue effort rather than only in transfers.
- Unlocking Union Finance Commission grants: timely constitution of the SFC and publication of audited accounts are entry conditions for Central Finance Commission local body grants. AP receives ₹13,302 crore in rural and

₹9,727 crore in urban basic grants for 2026-31 under the 16th FC, and released ₹3,797 crore to panchayats and municipalities in 2025-26.

## Significance — promoting fiscal decentralisation
- Fulfils the constitutional design: the 73rd and 74th Amendments devolved functions, functionaries and finances; without an effective SFC, only the first two are transferred, leaving local bodies responsible but resourceless.
- Reduces dependence on ad-hoc grants: by strengthening own-source revenue, the SFC increases genuine local autonomy rather than merely local spending.
- Improves allocative efficiency: financially empowered panchayats and municipalities can address community-specific needs — drinking water, sanitation, drainage, street lighting — more responsively than State departments.
- Incentivises performance through performance-linked grant recommendations.

## Challenges in implementation
- Delay in constitution and in acting on reports, so that award periods lapse before recommendations are implemented — the single most common criticism nationally.
- Weak local tax administration, evident in AP’s property tax demand-collection gap.
- Political override, where State-level priorities displace SFC recommendations.
- Data deficiency — reliable, comparable local body accounts remain scarce, weakening normative estimation.
- Non-uniform methodology across successive SFCs, preventing longitudinal comparison.

## Conclusion

The State Finance Commission is the weakest link and the greatest opportunity in Indian fiscal federalism: constitutionally mandated but institutionally under-powered. For Andhra Pradesh, whose local bodies serve about 13,300 gram panchayats across 26 districts, strengthening the SFC means timely constitution, an Action Taken Report placed before the Assembly, standardised methodology, and serious investment in local revenue administration. Only then will the third tier become a genuine level of government rather than an implementing agency.

## Value addition
- Constitutional provisions: Art. 243-I (SFC for panchayats, constituted every five years by the Governor), Art. 243-Y (extension to municipalities), Art. 243-H and 243-X (power of State legislatures to authorise local bodies to levy taxes), Art. 280(3)(bb) and (c) (Union FC to recommend measures to augment State Consolidated Funds for local bodies).
- 16th FC on local bodies: total grants of ₹7.91 lakh crore for 2026-31 — the largest ever — with Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada eligible for the Special Infrastructure (wastewater) component; entry conditions include timely SFC constitution, online publication of audited accounts, and notification of property tax floor rates.
- Devolution index context: successive Union Finance Commissions have repeatedly flagged that delays in constituting SFCs are the principal obstacle to effective third-tier finance.
- One-line revision point: The 73rd and 74th Amendments created local governments; only the State Finance Commission can make them solvent.
