## Introduction

India’s gender record is a study in contrasts. In the WEF Global Gender Gap Report 2025, India ranked 131 of 148 with a parity score of 64.1% — having achieved 97.1% parity in educational attainment, its strongest dimension, while remaining weakest in political empowerment. The challenge is therefore not primarily access to education, but converting that access into economic and political power.

Challenges faced by women

- Economic - Low workforce participation: FLFPR at 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24) — though a striking improvement from 23.3% in 2017-18, still far below male participation of 79.1%. - Wage gap: women earn about 73% of male wages on average, and less in sectors such as technology. - Invisible work: the Economic Survey 2022-23 valued women’s unpaid care work at ₹22.7 lakh crore — about 7.5% of GDP — entirely excluded from labour statistics. - Leadership deficit: only about 17% of C-suite roles and 20% of board positions in corporate India are held by women. - Informality: most working women are in agriculture, construction and domestic work without contracts or social security.
- Educational - Near parity in enrolment, with female GER in higher education above 46% — but nearly 40% of girls aged 15-18 remain out of school, constrained by early marriage, sanitation and safety. - Streaming into lower-return disciplines despite India having one of the world’s highest shares of women STEM graduates.
- Health - 57% of women aged 15-49 are anaemic (NFHS-5) — the single most damaging health statistic for female productivity. - Maternal mortality has improved substantially, from 174 (2013-15) to 97 (2018-20) per lakh live births, but remains above the SDG target of 70 by 2030. - Sex ratio at birth still reflects son preference; Andhra Pradesh’s child sex ratio stood at 939 in Census 2011.
- Political - India’s weakest dimension: women’s representation in Parliament fell from 14.7% to 13.8%, and ministerial representation to 5.6%. - The 106th Constitutional Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023) reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies — but is contingent on delimitation and a Census, so it is not yet operational.
- Social and safety - Early marriage, dowry, restricted mobility, and limited asset and land ownership. - Domestic violence, workplace harassment and cybercrime against women. - Care burden falling almost entirely on women, which is the proximate reason for low workforce participation.

Recent programmes — by function

- **Function** — Programmes
- **Survival and child sex ratio** — Beti Bachao Beti Padhao; PCPNDT enforcement; Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana
- **Health and nutrition** — PM Matru Vandana Yojana (maternity benefit); POSHAN 2.0; Anaemia Mukt Bharat; free sanitary napkins under Suvidha
- **Safety and protection** — Mission Shakti with its two sub-schemes — Sambal (safety, including One Stop Centres, Women Helpline 181, Nari Adalat) and Samarthya (empowerment, including Shakti Sadan, Sakhi Niwas, Palna crèches)
- **Economic participation** — DAY-NRLM SHGs; Lakhpati Didi initiative to raise SHG household incomes above ₹1 lakh a year; Namo Drone Didi providing drones to women’s SHGs for agricultural services
- **Entrepreneurship and credit** — Stand-Up India, PMMY (MUDRA), Mahila e-Haat, Mahila Coir Yojana
- **Workplace rights** — Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 — paid leave raised to 26 weeks with mandatory crèches; POSH Act, 2013; the four Labour Codes (effective 21 November 2025) permitting women in all establishments and night shifts with consent and safeguards, and mandating equal remuneration
- **Financial inclusion** — PMJDY — over 28 crore women hold Jan Dhan accounts; microfinance with 95% women borrowers
- **Political** — 33% reservation in Panchayati Raj Institutions; 106th Amendment (2023) for legislatures
- **Budgeting** — Gender Budget of ₹4.49 lakh crore (2025-26) — 8.86% of the Union Budget, up from ₹0.98 lakh crore and 5.46% in 2014-15

Assessment

What is working: the near-doubling of FLFPR, the fall in maternal mortality, near-parity in education, and financial inclusion at scale are genuine structural gains — not merely programme outputs.

What is not: political representation has regressed; the wage gap and care burden persist; schemes suffer from weak last-mile delivery and gender-blind monitoring; and India ranks behind Nepal (125) and Sri Lanka (130) in South Asia, with Bangladesh at 24th leading the region.

## Conclusion

India’s gender challenge has shifted: the access problem is largely solved, the conversion problem is not. Girls are in school; women are not in the workforce, boardroom or legislature in proportionate numbers. Closing that gap requires the unglamorous work of childcare infrastructure, safe transport, enforcement of equal pay, recognition of unpaid work, and operationalising the 106th Amendment — supported by the Labour Codes’ new protections. As the WEF notes, at the current global pace full parity will take 123 years; India’s demographic and economic ambitions cannot wait that long.

## Value addition
- WEF Global Gender Gap Report 2025 (19th edition, 12 June 2025): India 131/148, score 64.1% against a global average of 68.8%; Iceland first for the 16th consecutive year; Bangladesh 24th leads South Asia; Nepal 125, Sri Lanka 130, Pakistan 148. Sub-index scores — Educational Attainment 97.1%, Economic Participation 40.7%, Political Empowerment weakest.
- Constitutional provisions: Art. 14, 15(3), 16, 39(a) and (d), 42, 51A(e); 73rd and 74th Amendments (one-third reservation in local bodies); 106th Amendment, 2023.
- Landmark judgments: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), codified as the POSH Act, 2013; Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018); Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya (2020) on permanent commission for women officers.
- Andhra Pradesh: 33% reservation for women in government jobs and educational institutions; Adabidda Nidhi (₹1,500 a month, ages 19-59); Deepam 2.0 — three free LPG cylinders a year to 1.08 crore women, ₹2,897 crore credited; Stree Shakti free bus travel; Shakti App with a seven-minute response target and 164 Shakti teams.

## Introduction

Inclusive growth is growth that both generates opportunity broadly and ensures that its benefits reach all sections of society. It differs from redistribution: redistribution divides an existing output more equally; inclusive growth expands productive participation so that more people contribute to and share in output. The Eleventh Plan made it India’s official development philosophy; it remains the organising idea of Viksit Bharat @2047.

## Dimensions of inclusion
- Social: SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities, persons with disabilities.
- Gender: women’s participation in work, credit and decision-making.
- Regional: aspirational districts, the North-East, backward blocks.
- Sectoral: agriculture and the informal sector, which employ the majority but generate far less value added.
- Financial: access to savings, credit, insurance and pensions.

## Key strategies and instruments
- **Agriculture and rural development** — PM-KISAN, PMGSY, PMAY-G, micro- irrigation, e-NAM · PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000 a year in three instalments through DBT; now linked with the Kisan Credit Card to ease formal credit access
- **Employment and skilling** — MGNREGA, Skill India, PMKVY, MUDRA, PLI in labour-intensive sectors · 56.2 crore persons employed in Q2 FY26, with 8.7 lakh net jobs added over Q1; unemployment at 3.1%
- **Formalisation and worker protection** — Four Labour Codes, effective 21 November 2025; ELI Scheme (₹99,446 crore) · ELI targets over 3.5 crore jobs including 1.92 crore first-timers between August 2025 and July 2027; Codes extend social security to gig and platform workers
- **Social sector investment** — Samagra Shiksha, NEP 2020, Ayushman Bharat, POSHAN 2.0 · Government health expenditure rose from 1.13% of GDP (2014-15) to 1.84% (2021-22)
- **Financial inclusion** — PMJDY (over 56 crore accounts, about 55% held by women), UPI, Account Aggregator, PMJJBY/PMSBY/APY · UPI processed about 241.6 billion transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore in FY26; the Survey finds UPI’s transaction trail expanded credit to new-to-credit borrowers without raising default rates
- **Food and social security** — NFSA 2013 covering about 80.67 crore persons; PMGKAY; DBT · DBT has generated cumulative savings exceeding ₹3.5 lakh crore by eliminating duplicate beneficiaries
- **Regional balance** — Aspirational Districts (112) and Aspirational Blocks (500) Programmes; North-East and border-area development · Measurable gains in health and education indicators through real-time dashboards

## Evidence of progress
- About 24.8 crore people exited multidimensional poverty over nine years (NITI Aayog MPI).
- The World Bank’s 2025 assessment places India’s extreme poverty rate at 2.3% in 2022-23, down from 16.2% in 2011-12, with a Gini index of about 25.5 — among the lower inequality readings globally on consumption.
- Female LFPR (UPSS) rose from 23.3% (2017-18) to 41.7% (2023-24) — the single most striking inclusion gain of the decade.
- SDG India Index composite score reached 71 in 2023-24, with 32 States and UTs in the front-runner category.

## Where inclusion remains incomplete
- Informality persists: the unincorporated sector alone employs 12.9 crore persons, and 42% of formal manufacturing workers are contractual.
- Wealth inequality remains high even where consumption inequality is low.
- The agriculture-employment overhang: roughly 45% of workers remain in a sector producing a far smaller share of output — the core productivity gap.
- Learning and health outcomes lag spending; agriculture’s GNPA of 6.0% shows that credit access without capacity creates stress.

## Conclusion

Inclusive growth in India has moved decisively from access to participation — accounts opened, roads built, insurance extended, poverty reduced. The next stage must move from participation to productivity: formal jobs rather than transfers, learning outcomes rather than enrolment, and credit that builds enterprise rather than consumption. That is the substance of Viksit Bharat @2047 — and, at the State level, of Andhra Pradesh’s Swarna Andhra @2047, whose first sutra is Zero Poverty through the P4 (Public-Private-People Partnership) model.

## Value addition
- PM-KISAN features: ₹6,000 a year in three instalments of ₹2,000, transferred directly to bank accounts; all landholding farmer families eligible; a “family” means husband, wife and minor children; States and UTs identify beneficiaries; implemented by the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare; now integrated with the Kisan Credit Card to speed formal credit.
- Constitutional foundation: Preamble (justice — social, economic, political); Art. 38(2) (minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities); Art. 39(b) and (c); Art. 41, 45, 46, 47.
- SDG linkage: inclusive growth maps to SDG 1, 4, 5, 8 and 10; the World Bank identifies financial inclusion as an enabler for 7 of the 17 SDGs.
- Andhra Pradesh instruments: Talliki Vandanam, Adabidda Nidhi, Deepam 2.0, Annadata Sukhibhava, Stree Shakti, NTR Bharosa pensions (₹4,000-₹15,000 by DBT, over ₹58,000 crore in 19 months), and the P4 model for zero poverty.

## Introduction

India’s poverty reduction has come from two engines working together — sustained growth that created incomes, and targeted programmes that protected the vulnerable and built assets. The results are striking: the World Bank’s 2025 assessment places extreme poverty at 2.3% in 2022-23, down from 16.2% in 2011-12, while NITI Aayog reports that about 24.8 crore people exited multidimensional poverty in nine years.

Rural programmes

- **MGNREGA (2005)** — Legal guarantee of 100 days of wage employment per rural household · Demand-driven, self-selecting through the wage rate, creates durable assets, one-third of work for women; a wage floor for rural labour markets. Recently restructured under the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika Mission (Rural) Act, 2025, a change several States have contested
- **DAY-NRLM / Aajeevika** — Build institutions of the poor for sustainable livelihoods · SHG federation model with credit linkage; the basis of AP’s SERP network of about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women
- **PMAY-Gramin** — Housing for all rural households · Grant-based construction with assets typically registered in women’s names
- **PMGSY** — All-weather rural connectivity · Market access, school and health access — an indirect but powerful poverty lever
- **NSAP** — Social security for the destitute · Old-age, widow and disability pensions
- **PM-KISAN** — Income support to farmers · ₹6,000 a year in three instalments by DBT; now linked to the Kisan Credit Card

Urban programmes

- **DAY-NULM** — Urban livelihoods and skills · Self-employment support, SHG formation, shelters for the urban homeless, vendor support
- **PM SVANidhi** — Working capital for street vendors · Collateral-free micro-loans in escalating tranches, with interest subvention and digital-transaction cashback — designed to build credit history
- **PMAY-Urban** — Affordable housing · Credit-linked subsidy, in-situ slum redevelopment, affordable housing partnership
- **AMRUT / Swachh Bharat (Urban)** — Basic services · Water, sewerage and sanitation, which reduce health-related impoverishment

Critical examination — where they have worked

- Consumption floor and shock absorption: MGNREGA proved its counter-cyclical value during COVID-19, absorbing

returning migrants; it remains the most effective automatic stabiliser in rural India.

- Asset creation for women: the SHG model has produced repayment rates above 97% in Andhra Pradesh and became the delivery channel for microfinance, pensions and DBT.
- Delivery has been transformed: DBT savings exceed ₹3.5 lakh crore cumulatively; PFMS and Just-in-Time releases cut float and leakage; One Nation One Ration Card enabled portability for migrants.
- Multidimensional deprivation has fallen sharply — the MPI decline is broad-based across health, education and living standards, not driven by income alone.
- Female participation rose: FLFPR (UPSS) climbed from 23.3% (2017-18) to 41.7% (2023-24). Critical examination — where they fall short
- **Targeting errors** — Beneficiary lists still rest substantially on the 2011 Census — a 15-year-old base; both inclusion and exclusion errors persist
- **Urban poverty is under-served** — India has no urban equivalent of MGNREGA’s legal guarantee; urban poverty is more about informality, housing and services than about employment days
- **Wage and payment delays** — MGNREGA’s effectiveness depends on timely wage payment; delays convert a guarantee into a gamble
- **Asset quality** — Durability and productivity of assets created vary widely across States and depend on local administrative capacity
- **Quality of employment** — Programmes provide work, not jobs — 42% of formal manufacturing workers are contractual, and the unincorporated sector employs 12.9 crore persons
- **Fiscal rigidity** — State-level unconditional cash transfers reached about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26, crowding out capital spending; the 16th Finance Commission has urged conditional, time-bound transfers instead
- **Migrant invisibility** — Circular migrants fall between State jurisdictions despite portability reforms

The verdict

Programmes have been highly effective at reducing destitution and absorbing shocks, and only partly effective at creating durable livelihoods. They put a floor under poverty; growth and formal job creation must lift the ceiling. The clearest evidence is that poverty fell fastest where programmes and growth reinforced each other — where roads, electricity and connectivity from public spending made private employment viable.

## Conclusion

India’s poverty alleviation architecture has delivered a historic reduction in deprivation, and its delivery systems are now among the most sophisticated in the developing world. The next phase must shift from protection to productivity — a stronger urban livelihoods mission, conditional and time-bound transfers, updated beneficiary databases, and formal job creation through the four Labour Codes (effective 21 November 2025) and the Employment Linked Incentive Scheme (₹99,446 crore). Poverty alleviation succeeds finally not when transfers reach everyone, but when fewer people need them.

## Value addition
- Constitutional basis: Art. 41 (right to work and public assistance), Art. 39(a) and (b), Art. 43 (living wage), Art. 47 (nutrition and public health) — DPSPs given programmatic form.
- Poverty estimation lineage: Dandekar and Rath (1971); Alagh Committee (1979) calorie norms; Lakdawala Committee (1993); Tendulkar Committee (2009); Rangarajan Committee (2014) — India has had no official poverty line since, with the National MPI and consumption surveys (HCES 2023-24) filling the gap.
- Current data: extreme poverty 2.3% (2022-23) and a Gini of about 25.5 on consumption (World Bank, 2025); 56.2 crore persons employed in Q2 FY26; unemployment 3.1%.
- Andhra Pradesh: SERP and Stree Nidhi as the institutional backbone; the P4 (Public-Private-People Partnership) model for Zero Poverty — the first of the ten “Padhi Sutralu” under Swarna Andhra @2047.

## Introduction

Inclusive growth requires that the poor participate in growth as producers, not only as recipients. In an economy where the unincorporated sector alone employs 12.9 crore persons and roughly 45% of workers remain in agriculture, social welfare schemes are the bridge that converts aggregate growth into household capability — protecting against shocks while building the health, nutrition and skills that make participation possible.

Why welfare schemes matter for inclusive growth

- Consumption floor: they prevent distress sales of assets and distress migration during shocks.
- Human capital formation: nutrition, health and schooling raise future productivity — welfare as investment, not merely transfer.
- Demand support: transfers to low-income households have a high marginal propensity to consume, sustaining rural demand.
- Equity and social justice: they give programmatic content to the Directive Principles — Art. 41 (right to work and assistance), Art. 47 (nutrition and public health), Art. 21A (education).

Major schemes — objectives and features

- **PM-KISAN** — Income support to farmers · ₹6,000 a year in three instalments of ₹2,000 by DBT to landholding farmer families; now linked to the Kisan Credit Card to ease formal credit
- **MGNREGA** — Legal guarantee of wage employment · 100 days per rural household; demand-driven; creates durable assets; a wage floor for rural labour
- **Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY** — Protection from catastrophic health expenditure · ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care; extended in 2024 to all citizens aged 70 and above through the Ayushman Vay Vandana Card, irrespective of income
- **National Food Security Act, 2013** — Legal entitlement to subsidised foodgrain · Covers about 80.67 crore persons; up to 75% rural and 50% urban population
- **PMAY (Urban and Gramin)** — Housing for all · Interest subsidy and grant-based construction; assets registered in women’s names
- **POSHAN 2.0 / ICDS** — Combat malnutrition · Supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, pre-school education for children under six and pregnant and lactating mothers
- **NSAP** — Social security for the destitute · Old-age, widow and disability pensions
- **PMJJBY / PMSBY / APY** — Micro-insurance and pension · Low-premium life and accident cover; guaranteed pension for the unorganised sector

Evaluation — what has worked

- Poverty has fallen sharply. About 24.8 crore people exited multidimensional poverty over nine years (NITI Aayog MPI). The World Bank’s 2025 assessment places extreme poverty at 2.3% in 2022-23, down from 16.2% in 2011-12, with a Gini index of about 25.5 on consumption.
- Delivery has been transformed. DBT has generated cumulative savings exceeding ₹3.5 lakh crore by eliminating duplicate and ghost beneficiaries; over 4 crore duplicate LPG connections were deactivated under PAHAL. Just-in-Time releases and PFMS cut float and leakage.
- Women’s participation improved: female LFPR (UPSS) rose from 23.3% (2017-18) to 41.7% (2023-24) — the single largest inclusion gain of the decade, aided by SHG credit, housing titles and safety-net certainty.
- Formalisation has begun: the four Labour Codes (effective 21 November 2025) extend social security to gig and platform workers for the first time.

Evaluation — what has not

- Exclusion errors persist: Aadhaar-based authentication failures, outdated beneficiary lists based on the 2011 Census, and migrant workers falling between State jurisdictions despite One Nation One Ration Card.
- Quality lags coverage: enrolment in schools and enrolment in PM-JAY are near-universal, but learning outcomes and empanelled hospital availability vary sharply across States.
- Fiscal rigidity is rising: the Economic Survey 2025-26 warns that unconditional cash transfers across States reached about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26, with the number of States running such schemes rising more than fivefold between FY23 and FY26 — nearly half of them already in revenue deficit. Committed expenditure absorbed 51.76% of States’ revenue expenditure in FY24.
- Transfers can substitute for, rather than build, capability: the 16th Finance Commission has accordingly urged States to set exclusion criteria for subsidies and shift from unconditional to conditional, time-bound transfers, citing Mexico’s Progresa/Oportunidades model where payments were tied to school attendance and health check-ups.
- Institutional churn: the restructuring of MGNREGA under the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika Mission (Rural) Act, 2025 has itself become contested, with some States passing resolutions to preserve the original guarantee — a reminder that predictability is part of a scheme’s value to the poor.

## Conclusion

Social welfare schemes have moved India decisively from access to participation — accounts opened, food secured, health protected, poverty reduced. The next stage must move from participation to productivity: conditional and time-bound transfers, outcome-linked financing, and welfare spending that builds capability rather than only providing relief. That is the substance of Viksit Bharat @2047 — and, at the State level, of Andhra Pradesh’s Swarna Andhra @2047, whose first sutra is Zero Poverty through the P4 (Public-Private-People Partnership) model.

## Value addition
- Constitutional foundation: Preamble (social, economic and political justice); Art. 38(2) (minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities); Art. 39(b) and (c); Art. 41, 45, 46, 47.
- Delivery architecture: JAM trinity, PFMS, DBT, Aadhaar-enabled Payment System, One Nation One Ration Card for portability.
- Andhra Pradesh instruments: Talliki Vandanam (₹15,000 a year per child from Class 1 to Intermediate), Adabidda Nidhi (₹1,500 a month to women aged 19-59), Deepam 2.0 (three free LPG cylinders a year to 1.08 crore women, ₹2,897 crore credited), Annadata Sukhibhava (₹20,000 a year for small, marginal and tenant farmers), NTR Bharosa pensions (₹4,000–₹15,000 by DBT, over ₹58,000 crore in 19 months), Stree Shakti free bus travel.
- SDG linkage: SDG 1 (No Poverty), 2 (Zero Hunger), 3 (Good Health), 5 (Gender Equality), 10 (Reduced Inequalities). India’s SDG India Index score reached 71 in 2023-24, with 32 States and UTs in the front-runner category.

## Introduction

Financial inclusion is the delivery of affordable, appropriate financial services — savings, credit, payments, insurance and pension — to all sections of society, particularly the excluded. The RBI’s Financial Inclusion Index measures it on three dimensions — Access, Usage and Quality — and stood at 67.0 in March 2025, up from 53.9 in March 2021.

Why it is critical for inclusive growth

- Breaks the dependence on informal credit at usurious rates — the single largest drain on poor households’ incomes.
- Enables consumption smoothing against illness, crop failure and job loss, so that shocks do not become permanent poverty.
- Raises productivity by allowing investment in tools, seeds, education and micro-enterprise.
- Makes DBT possible — without universal accounts, targeted transfers cannot be delivered without leakage.
- Formalises the economy, widening the tax base and improving the quality of credit information.
- The 2030 Agenda identifies financial inclusion as an enabler for 7 of the 17 SDGs. Key initiatives — a layered architecture
- **Identity** — Aadhaar, e-KYC, video-KYC · Removed the documentation barrier that had excluded the poor
- **Accounts** — PMJDY (2014) · Over 56 crore accounts, roughly 55% held by women; zero-balance, RuPay card, overdraft facility
- **Payments** — UPI, AePS, UPI Lite, UPI 123Pay · FY26: about 241.6 billion transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore; India accounts for roughly 49% of global real-time payment volume
- **Institutions** — Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, RRBs, Business Correspondents, Digital Banking Units · SFBs must lend 75% of ANBC to the priority sector; RRBs’ credit-deposit ratio reached 73.8% (March 2025), the highest in 35 years
- **Credit** — PMMY (MUDRA), Stand-Up India, PM SVANidhi, PM Vishwakarma, KCC · Collateral-free micro-credit to first-time and small borrowers
- **Insurance and pension** — PMJJBY, PMSBY, Atal Pension Yojana · Low-premium life and accident cover; guaranteed pension for the unorganised sector
- **Data infrastructure** — Account Aggregator, Open Credit Enablement Network · Consent-based data sharing enabling cash-flow-based lending

Evaluation — the real impact

Where it has succeeded:

- The access gap is largely closed. Account ownership has reached roughly 89% (Global Findex 2025), against about 35% in 2011 — one of the fastest financial-inclusion transitions ever recorded.
- The leap from payments to credit is the decisive gain. The Economic Survey 2025-26 cites evidence that UPI’s verifiable transaction trail lets lenders serve new-to-credit borrowers who lacked collateral or credit history — without a rise in default rates. Digital public infrastructure is therefore deepening finance, not merely digitising it.
- Microfinance reaches the intended population: active borrowers rose from 330 lakh (FY14) to 627 lakh (FY25), with a gross loan portfolio of ₹2.38 lakh crore; 95% of borrowers are women and 80% rural.
- Formal credit is displacing informal sources: among unincorporated manufacturing units, the share using formal credit rose from 48% (2021-22) to 51% (2023-24), with commercial bank borrowing up 6 percentage points.

Where it falls short:

- Usage and quality lag access — dormant accounts, low insurance and pension penetration, and limited productive credit for the informal sector.
- Cash has not disappeared: the Survey records that over 90% of UPI users continue to use cash regularly — India runs a hybrid, not a cashless, economy.
- New risks: UPI fraud reached about 10.64 lakh cases worth ₹805 crore in FY26 up to November, prompting NPCI to cap limits and deploy AI-based mule-account detection.
- Over-indebtedness: the FY25 microfinance stress, when MFI loans outstanding fell 14% on over-lending, prompted the RBI to cut NBFC-MFI qualifying assets from 75% to 60% (June 2025) so lenders could diversify risk.
- Viability: zero-MDR on UPI leaves the rails unmonetised, straining the business case for last-mile agents.

## Conclusion

India has built, in roughly a decade, the world’s largest financial-inclusion infrastructure — and has crossed the harder threshold from payments to credit. The remaining agenda is quality: converting dormant accounts into active savings, extending insurance and pension coverage, protecting consumers from fraud and over-indebtedness, and ensuring credit builds enterprise rather than consumption. Inclusion is complete not when everyone has an account, but when everyone can borrow productively and insure against risk.

## Value addition
- RBI Financial Inclusion Index: 67.0 (March 2025) against 53.9 (March 2021) — sub-indices Access, Usage and Quality. RBI Digital Payments Index: 493.22 (March 2025) against 153.47 (March 2019).

PSB GNPA 1.93%, CRAR 16.6% (March 2026).

## Introduction

Sustainable agriculture is farming that meets present food and income needs without degrading the natural resource base on which future production depends. It rests on three simultaneous requirements — ecologically sound, economically viable and socially equitable — and a system failing any one of them is not sustainable, however good it looks on the others.

Why it became necessary in India

The Green Revolution delivered food security but at a measurable ecological cost: groundwater depletion in the north-west, soil organic carbon decline, an N:P:K consumption ratio far more skewed toward nitrogen than the recommended 4:2:1 because of the urea subsidy, salinisation, biodiversity loss and rising input costs that squeezed farm incomes.

Key objectives

- **Soil health** — Restore organic carbon, biological activity and structure
- **Water security** — Raise water-use efficiency and arrest groundwater depletion
- **Reduced chemical dependence** — Cut synthetic fertiliser and pesticide use, and their health and cost burdens
- **Biodiversity** — Preserve indigenous seed varieties, pollinators and soil organisms
- **Climate resilience and mitigation** — Adapt to erratic monsoons; reduce emissions and sequester carbon
- **Farmer income** — Lower input costs and secure price premiums — sustainability must pay, or it will not last
- **Food and nutrition security** — Diversify beyond cereals into pulses, millets and horticulture
- **Intergenerational equity** — Leave the resource base intact for the next generation

Common practices in India

- Soil management - Organic manures — farmyard manure, compost, vermicompost, green manuring. - Biofertilisers

— Rhizobium, Azotobacter, mycorrhiza. - Zero and minimum tillage, and residue retention instead of stubble burning. - Soil Health Cards guiding balanced nutrient application.

- Water management - Micro-irrigation — drip and sprinkler — under the “Per Drop More Crop” component of PMKSY. - Watershed development, rainwater harvesting, farm ponds and check dams. - System of Rice Intensification (SRI) and alternate wetting and drying, which cut water use substantially in paddy.
- Crop and cropping-system practices - Crop rotation, intercropping and mixed cropping to break pest cycles and restore fertility. - Millets (Shree Anna) — drought-tolerant, nutritious and low-input; promoted since the International Year of Millets, 2023. - Agroforestry and integrated farming systems combining crops, livestock, fish and trees.
- Pest and nutrient management - Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and Integrated Nutrient Management (INM). - Non-Pesticide Management (NPM), pioneered at scale in Andhra Pradesh. - Neem-coated urea to reduce diversion and improve nitrogen-use efficiency.
- Organic and natural farming - Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) for cluster-based organic farming. - Mission Organic Value Chain Development for the North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER). - National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF), launched November 2024 with an outlay of about ₹2,481 crore, targeting 1 crore farmers

across 7.5 lakh hectares. - Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming (APCNF) — the world’s largest agroecology programme (detailed in Q.161).

- Institutional and policy framework - National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA) — one of the eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008). - PM-PRANAM to incentivise States that reduce chemical fertiliser use. - Agriculture Infrastructure Fund for storage and cold chains, reducing post-harvest loss — itself a sustainability gain.

## Conclusion

Sustainable agriculture is not a rejection of productivity but a redefinition of it — output per unit of water, soil carbon and energy, rather than output per hectare alone. India’s decadal agricultural growth of 4.45% (FY16-FY25), driven by livestock, fisheries and horticulture rather than cereals, shows that diversification and sustainability can move together. The task now is to ensure that sustainable practice is also profitable practice, through price premiums, certification and market access — because a farmer will not adopt what does not pay.

## Introduction

The Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) Acts, enacted by States from the 1960s, were a protective intervention. Before them, farmers sold at the farm gate to traders and moneylenders who controlled weighing, grading and payment. APMC regulation required the first sale to occur in a notified market yard under open auction, with licensed traders and recorded transactions. Agricultural marketing is a State subject (Entry 28, List II), so each State has its own Act.

Role of the APMC Act in market regulation and price policy

- **Ending farm-gate exploitation** — Compels the first sale in a regulated market yard rather than at the farm gate
- **Transparent price discovery** — Open auction among licensed traders replaces private, one-sided bargaining
- **Standardised weights and grading** — Regulated weighment and quality assessment prevent under-measurement
- **Payment security** — Licensing of traders and market committee oversight secure timely payment
- **Market infrastructure** — Market fees fund yards, auction platforms, storage, drying and grading facilities
- **Link to MSP operations** — Regulated mandis are the physical points at which government procurement at MSP takes place — without them, price support could not be operationalised
- **Price data** — Mandi arrivals and prices feed AGMARKNET and national price monitoring, informing MSP fixation by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
- **Curbing speculation** — Restrictions on hoarding by traders within the yard

The connection to agricultural price policy is direct: MSP is a floor price, but a floor requires a place to stand. Procurement agencies operate in notified mandis; the APMC network is therefore the delivery infrastructure of price support, which is why proposals to dismantle it raise fears about MSP itself.

Issues observed by policy makers

- Monopoly replaced, not removed By restricting the first sale to a notified yard, the Act created a legal monopoly for licensed traders within it. Limited licences, high entry barriers and long-standing relationships enable cartelisation and collusive bidding, so auctions are often not genuinely competitive.
- High and cascading market charges Market fees, commission agent (arhtiya) charges, cess and levies vary by State and can amount to a significant share of the sale value, all ultimately borne by the farmer.
- Persistence of the commission agent The arhtiya often functions simultaneously as buyer, lender and commission agent — creating an interlocked credit-and-marketing relationship in which an indebted farmer cannot sell elsewhere.
- Inadequate market density India has far fewer regulated markets than the recommended norm of one market within a 5-km radius; average area served per market is many times that, so most farmers still sell outside the regulated system.
- Fragmented markets Each mandi is a separate market, and inter-State movement historically attracted repeated fees

— preventing the emergence of a single national market and causing large price differences between adjoining States.

- Poor infrastructure Many yards lack grading, storage, cold chain, drying platforms and electronic weighing, so market fees are collected without commensurate service.
- Governance capture Market committees are frequently dominated by traders and political interests rather than farmers, and elections to them are often delayed.
- Exclusion of high-value produce Perishables — fruit, vegetables, milk, poultry, fish — do not suit an auction-and-storage model; forcing them through mandis raises loss and delays, which is why several States have de-listed them.

The reform trajectory

- **Model APMC Act, 2003** — Permitted direct marketing, contract farming and private markets — but adoption by States was partial
- **Model APLM Act, 2017** — Agricultural Produce and Livestock Marketing Act — a single licence valid State-wide, single-point levy, and e-trading
- **Model Contract Farming Act, 2018** — Contract farming outside APMC jurisdiction, with dispute resolution
- **e-NAM (April 2016)** — Electronic national market overlaying existing mandis — now 1,656 mandis (March 2026), up from 1,389 in 2024, with 1.80 crore farmers, 2.73 lakh traders and 4,724 FPOs, and cumulative trade of 13.25 crore metric tonnes worth ₹4.84 lakh crore
- **e-NWR integration** — Farmers store in WDRA-accredited warehouses, obtain electronic Negotiable Warehouse Receipts and sell on e-NAM — separating the sale decision from the harvest date, which is what ends distress sales
- **The 2020 farm laws** — Sought to permit trade outside APMC yards entirely; repealed in 2021 after sustained protest — a reminder that marketing reform is politically constrained

## Conclusion

The APMC Act was a genuine reform in its time — it ended farm-gate exploitation and created the infrastructure through which price support operates. Its failure was that it replaced one monopoly with another, this time legally sanctioned. The workable path forward is neither to preserve nor to abolish it but to make it compete: expand e-NAM and inter-State trade, allow direct sale and contract farming alongside mandis, permit FPOs to trade without intermediaries, invest market fee revenue in actual infrastructure, and use warehouse receipt finance so that the farmer chooses when to sell. Since agricultural marketing is a State subject, this can only be achieved through State-level adoption of the model laws — which remains the reform’s binding constraint.

## Value addition
- Constitutional position: agricultural marketing falls under Entry 28, List II (State List) — the reason reform proceeds through model laws requiring State adoption, and the reason the 2020 central farm laws were constitutionally contested.
- MSP framework: recommended by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) for 22 mandated crops plus toria and de-husked coconut; since 2018-19 fixed at a minimum of 1.5 times the A2+FL cost; the Swaminathan Commission had recommended C2+50%.
- e-NAM architecture: implemented by the Small Farmers Agribusiness Consortium (SFAC); 12-language interface, live price dashboard, AI-enabled quality assessment, Platform of Platforms, and inter-State trade facility.
- Andhra Pradesh instruments: Rythu Bharosa Kendras as village-level procurement and input points with digital farmer registration and direct e-payment — an attempt to bring the mandi function to the village.

## Introduction

Agriculture supports about 46.1% of India’s population while contributing roughly 16-18% of GDP — the productivity gap that defines Indian development. Finance, production and marketing form a single chain: credit funds the inputs that raise production, and marketing determines whether that production converts into income. A break at any point makes the other two ineffective.

Significance of the three pillars

- Finance — enabling investment - Institutional credit to agriculture rose from ₹8.5 lakh crore (2014-15) to ₹25.48 lakh crore (2023-24); short-term credit from ₹6.4 to ₹15.07 lakh crore. - The share of small and marginal farmers accessing agricultural loans rose from 57% to 76% over the same period. - Instruments: KCC (limit ₹5 lakh, effective interest 4%), PSL mandating 18% of ANBC to agriculture, the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (₹1 lakh crore, with

₹52,738 crore sanctioned by December 2024), and PM-KISAN (₹6,000 a year) easing dependence on informal

borrowing.

- Production — the supply base - Foodgrain production reached a record 3,577.3 lakh metric tonnes in 2024-25, an increase of 254.3 LMT over the previous year, led by rice, wheat, maize and Shree Anna (coarse cereals). - Horticulture production of 362.08 MT actually exceeded foodgrain output — evidence of diversification toward high-value crops; horticulture now contributes about 33% of agricultural GVA. - Allied sectors are the real growth engines: decadal agricultural growth of 4.45% (FY16-FY25) — the highest of any decade — was driven by livestock (7.1%) and fishing and aquaculture (8.8%) against crops at 3.5%. Livestock GVA rose about 195% between FY15 and FY24.
- Marketing — converting output into income - e-NAM, launched April 2016, now connects 1,656 mandis (March 2026), up from 1,389 in 2024, with 1.80 crore registered farmers, 2.73 lakh traders and 4,724 FPOs; cumulative trade of 13.25 crore metric tonnes worth ₹4.84 lakh crore. - FPOs: the 10,000 FPO programme has registered about

56.32 lakh farmers, roughly 39% of them women. - Integration with electronic Negotiable Warehouse Receipts (e-NWR) allows farmers to store produce in WDRA-accredited warehouses and sell on the platform — separating the sale decision from the harvest date, which is what ends distress sales. - Agricultural exports reached about ₹4.4 lakh crore in FY25; processed food’s share of agri-exports rose from 13.7% (2014-15) to 20.4% (2024-25).

Challenges

- **Finance** — Tenant farmers without title excluded, since credit follows land records; small-ticket lending is administratively unattractive; agriculture’s GNPA stands at 6.0% — the highest of any sector and over a third of all bad loans; credit skewed to short-term crop loans rather than term credit for irrigation and mechanisation
- **Production** — Fragmented holdings; groundwater depletion; skewed fertiliser use — India’s N:P:K ratio far exceeds the recommended 4:2:1 because of the urea subsidy; climate volatility; low mechanisation on small farms
- **Marketing** — APMC monopolies and intermediary layers; e-NAM covers only 1,656 of India’s mandis; inadequate cold chain and storage — the World Bank has estimated that grain and perishables lost to poor storage could feed a third of India’s poor; price volatility
- **Structural** — India imports 56% of its edible oil (15.66 MMT in 2023-24); pulses import dependence; storage concentrated in Punjab and Haryana while eastern States lack facilities

Opportunities

- Allied sector diversification — livestock, fisheries and horticulture already outperform crops and are less land-intensive, making them the natural route to higher incomes on small holdings.
- Import substitution missions — the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (₹11,440 crore, 2025-26 to 2030-31, targeting self-sufficiency by December 2027) and the National Mission on Edible Oils.
- Food processing — the sector grew 7.3% annually (2015-2022) and contributes 10.54% of manufacturing GVA; every unit of processing adds value at the farm gate.
- Digital infrastructure — the Kisan Rin Portal, Agristack, DILRMP land records digitisation and e-KYC of KCC accounts can finally bring tenant farmers into formal credit.
- Warehouse receipt financing through e-NWR, and FPO aggregation to give small farmers scale in both input purchase and output sale.
- Storage expansion through the AIF and the World’s Largest Grain Storage Plan in the Cooperative Sector at PACS level.

## Conclusion

Finance, production and marketing succeed or fail together. India has demonstrably improved finance (credit tripled, small-farmer access up to 76%) and production (record foodgrain and horticulture output, best decadal growth in fifty years); the weakest link remains marketing, where price realisation, storage and value addition still leak most of the farmer’s potential income. The route to sustainable growth therefore runs through allied sectors, food processing, FPO aggregation and warehouse-receipt finance — so that the farmer captures value rather than merely producing volume.

## Introduction

Fisheries is the fastest-growing sub-sector of Indian agriculture, expanding at 8.8% a decade (FY16-FY25) against crops at 3.5%, with fish production rising over 140% between 2014 and 2025. It is the core of the Blue Economy — high in employment intensity, export value and protein contribution — and Andhra Pradesh is India’s leading producer.

- Key drivers of growth
- Resource endowment - A long coastline, a wide continental shelf, and an Exclusive Economic Zone extending 200 nautical miles. - Extensive inland resources — rivers, reservoirs, tanks, brackish-water areas and floodplain wetlands. Andhra Pradesh’s 974-km coastline, second only to Gujarat’s, plus the Krishna-Godavari delta’s brackish water, make it the country’s aquaculture leader.
- The shift from capture to culture — the single most important driver Marine capture is limited by the sustainable yield of the sea; aquaculture is limited only by land, water, seed and feed. India’s growth has come overwhelmingly from inland aquaculture, which is why a landlocked pond in West Godavari now contributes more growth than a trawler.
- Returns per hectare Aquaculture yields several times the return of paddy on the same land, which is why large areas of delta paddy were converted to fish and shrimp ponds. This economic pull, not policy, drove the initial expansion.
- Export demand Shrimp is among India’s largest agricultural export earners; processed marine products command high unit values. Agricultural exports reached about ₹4.4 lakh crore in FY25, with marine products a leading component.
- Domestic protein demand Rising incomes and urbanisation have raised demand for animal protein; fish is the cheapest and most widely acceptable source.
- Technology Hatcheries and quality seed, formulated feed, Recirculatory Aquaculture Systems (RAS) and biofloc, disease diagnostics, aerators, and cage culture in reservoirs.
- Employment and inclusion Fisheries is labour-intensive across the value chain — capture, culture, processing, ice, transport and marketing — and employs a high proportion of women in processing and marketing.
- Institutional and credit support KCC extended to fisheries and animal husbandry in 2018-19; a separate Department of Fisheries created at the Centre in 2019, giving the sector its own administrative focus for the first time.
- Policy priority Fisheries was designated a sunrise sector, with the largest-ever investment programme in its history.
- Schemes for the growth of the sector National schemes
- **Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY), 2020** — Outlay of about ₹20,050 crore — the largest-ever investment in Indian fisheries; targets production, productivity, post-harvest infrastructure, exports and doubling fishers’ incomes
- **PM Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana (PM-MKSSY)** — A sub-scheme for formalisation of the sector — registration of fishers and enterprises on the National Fisheries Digital Platform, working capital and insurance
- **Fisheries and Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund (FIDF)** — About ₹7,522 crore for fishing harbours, landing centres, cold chains and hatcheries, at concessional interest
- **Blue Revolution (2015-16)** — The predecessor umbrella scheme for integrated development of fisheries
- **Kisan Credit Card for fisheries** — Extended in 2018-19, giving fish farmers working capital at the KCC’s effective 4%
- **National Fisheries Development Board (NFDB)** — Hyderabad-based, providing technical and financial support
- **Aquaculture and marine institutions** — ICAR institutes — CIFA, CIBA, CMFRI, CIFT, CIFE — for research, seed and disease management

Andhra Pradesh’s departmental schemes

- **Fishing harbours and landing centres** — A major State programme — new and upgraded harbours at Juvvaladinne, Nizampatnam, Machilipatnam, Uppada, Budagatlapalem, Mulapeta and others — to reduce landing losses and enable deep-sea fishing
- **Support during the fishing ban** — Financial assistance to marine fishing families during the annual 61-day ban (mid-April to mid-June) on the east coast, when fishing is prohibited to protect the breeding season
- **Diesel subsidy** — For mechanised and motorised craft, reducing the largest operating cost
- **Aqua zoning and regulation** — Under the AP Aquaculture Development Authority, to control unregulated pond conversion and the salinisation it causes
- **Subsidised power for aquaculture** — About ₹890 crore in aqua tariff subsidy in the State budget, alongside ₹11,000 crore in agricultural power subsidy
- **Seed and feed quality regulation** — Hatchery certification and feed quality control, since seed and feed are the two determinants of pond productivity
- **Fisheries university and extension** — Specialised education, training and disease advisory
- **Insurance and welfare** — Accident insurance for fishers, housing, and support for fisherwomen in processing and marketing
- **Post-harvest infrastructure** — Cold chains, ice plants, processing units and market linkage, financed through FIDF and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

Challenges the schemes must address

- Ecological limits — salinisation of adjoining paddy land and groundwater from unregulated pond conversion in the delta.
- Disease risk — shrimp disease can destroy an entire cycle; the sector is capital-intensive, so failure produces debt rather than a poor season.
- Price and export volatility, including sanitary and phytosanitary barriers and anti-dumping measures in destination markets.
- Over-fishing in near-shore waters, and the need to move to deep-sea and mariculture.
- Feed cost dependence on imported fishmeal and soya.

## Conclusion

Fisheries growth is driven by a favourable combination of resource endowment, the shift from capture to culture, superior returns per hectare, and export and protein demand — with policy, through PMMSY’s ₹20,050 crore, accelerating rather than initiating it. For Andhra Pradesh, the sector is already a national leader and the State’s most profitable use of delta land. Sustaining it requires shifting emphasis from expansion to regulation and value addition

— aqua zoning to prevent salinisation, disease management, deep-sea capacity, and processing that captures export value within the State.

- Growth benchmark: fisheries and aquaculture grew 8.8% a decade (FY16-FY25) — the fastest agricultural sub-sector; fish production rose over 140% between 2014 and 2025.

- Institutional milestone: a separate Department of Fisheries was created at the Centre in 2019, and fisheries was brought within the Kisan Credit Card framework in 2018-19.

## Introduction

Industry occupies a paradoxical position in India’s development. It contributes about 24.3% of GDP (FY26 nominal) — with manufacturing at 12.8% — and grew 6.2% in FY26. Yet its share has remained broadly stagnant at a quarter of output for three decades, well below the 35-40% peak that East Asian economies reached. India’s structural transformation therefore skipped the industrial stage, moving from agriculture directly to services — which is why examining industry’s role means examining both what it has delivered and what it has failed to.

- Income generation
- Higher value added per worker Industry generates far more value per worker than agriculture. ASI FY24 records net value added per person engaged in factories at ₹10.7 lakh — a multiple of what a farm worker produces. Every worker moved from agriculture to industry therefore raises national income.
- Backward and forward linkages A steel plant creates demand for ore, coal, transport and power, and supplies construction, machinery and automobiles. These multiplier effects are far stronger than in agriculture or most services.
- Export earnings and the current account Manufactured exports finance imports of capital goods and energy. India’s total exports reached a record US$825.3 billion in FY25, with the current account deficit contained at 0.8% of GDP in H1 FY26 — manageability that rests on the export base.
- Fiscal contribution Industry is the most taxable sector: GST, corporate tax and customs flow disproportionately from it. Gross GST reached ₹22.27 lakh crore in FY26, and gross tax receipts are budgeted at ₹44.04 lakh crore in 2026-27.
- Investment and capital formation Gross fixed capital formation stood at 30.0% of GDP in FY26, and private corporate investment announcements reached about ₹14.6 lakh crore in H1 FY26 — industry being both the destination and the driver.
- Employment
- Direct employment and formalisation Industry creates formal, contract-based, socially secured employment of a kind agriculture cannot. ASI FY24 recorded over 10 lakh new factory jobs, and 57 lakh added over FY15-FY24 (4% CAGR).
- Absorbing surplus farm labour — the unfinished task This is industry’s central developmental function, and where India has under-performed. Roughly 45% of the workforce remains in agriculture producing about 15-16% of GDP; the unincorporated sector alone employs 12.9 crore persons. Industry has not absorbed labour at the rate the Lewis model predicts.
- Quality of employment remains a concern 42% of formal manufacturing workers are contractual (ASI 2023-24) — so formalisation has been partial. The four Labour Codes, effective 21 November 2025, extend social security to gig and platform workers and mandate written appointment letters; the Employment Linked Incentive Scheme (₹99,446 crore) subsidises first-time formal hiring, targeting over 3.5 crore jobs including 1.92 crore first-timers.
- Indirect employment Construction, logistics, retail and services around industrial clusters typically generate more jobs than the factory itself.
- Women’s participation Labour-intensive industry — textiles, electronics assembly, food processing — is a principal route for women into paid work; female LFPR (UPSS) rose from 23.3% (2017-18) to 41.7% (2023-24).
- Modernisation of the economy
- Technology and productivity diffusion Industry is where new technology is absorbed and then spreads. Automation,

robotics, AI and Industry 4.0 processes entering manufacturing raise productivity across the supply chain.

- Urbanisation and infrastructure Industrial location drives city growth, and city growth drives roads, power, water and housing. Industry is therefore the engine of urbanisation, which India needs — it is only about 36% urbanised against roughly 50% typical at its income level.
- Skill formation Industry demands and finances vocational skills. Andhra Pradesh’s government ITIs, with MoUs with

167 industry partners and 98% placement or apprenticeship, illustrate industry pulling the training system into relevance.

- Entrepreneurship and innovation India is now the world’s third-largest startup ecosystem, with over 2.40 lakh DPIIT-recognised startups and nearly 24 lakh direct jobs created — innovation increasingly emerging from industry rather than from laboratories alone.
- Structural transformation Industry is the bridge from a subsistence to a modern economy — the stage India partially skipped, and is now attempting to recover through PLI and mission-mode manufacturing.
- Policy references — the framework
- **1948, 1956** — Industrial Policy Resolutions — public sector dominance, the “commanding heights”, licensing
- **1977, 1980** — Emphasis on small-scale and village industry; district industry centres
- **1991** — New Industrial Policy — delicensing (retaining only a handful of reserved industries), MRTP relaxation, FDI liberalisation, disinvestment, dereservation
- **2011** — National Manufacturing Policy — target of raising manufacturing to 25% of GDP and creating 100 million jobs; National Investment and Manufacturing Zones
- **2014 onwards** — Make in India, Startup India, Skill India, Ease of Doing Business reform
- **Recent** — PLI schemes across 14+ sectors; National Logistics Policy and PM GatiShakti; National Single Window System; National Industrial Corridor Development Programme; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016; GST (2017) and GST 2.0 (September 2025); India Semiconductor Mission, with Mission 2.0 launched alongside Union Budget 2026-27 and ₹40,000 crore for the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme

- Examining the record — an honest assessment

Achievements: industry grew 6.2% in FY26; India became a major exporter of pharmaceuticals, automobiles, engineering goods and increasingly electronics; FDI reached a record US$94.52 billion in FY26; three sovereign rating upgrades in FY26 reflected macro credibility.

Failures: - Manufacturing’s share has not risen to the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy — nominal manufacturing GVA is about 12.8%, though its real share has held steady at 17-18% and its gross output share at about 38%, so the “decline” is substantially a relative-price and intermediate-consumption effect rather than a collapse in activity. - Employment generation lagged output growth — capital-intensive industrialisation and size-linked regulatory disincentives favoured fewer, larger, machine-intensive firms. - The “missing middle” — India has many micro firms and a few large ones, but too few mid-sized firms, which is where employment growth usually comes from. - Logistics and infrastructure remain a cost handicap; India ranks 38th on the World Bank LPI (2023), up from 44th in 2018 but behind competitors.

Industry has been indispensable to India’s development — it generates the highest value added per worker, funds the exchequer, absorbs technology and drives urbanisation. But India industrialised too little to absorb its workforce, which is why nearly half of all workers remain in a sector producing a sixth of output. The current policy architecture — PLI, the Labour Codes, the ELI Scheme, GST 2.0, PM GatiShakti and the Semiconductor Mission — is correctly aimed at that gap. Whether Viksit Bharat @2047 is achieved will depend on whether industry finally becomes labour-absorbing as well as productive.

## Introduction

Start-up India was launched on 16 January 2016 — now observed annually as National Startup Day — to shift India from being a nation of job-seekers to one of job-creators. Its premise was that Indian entrepreneurship was constrained not by talent or ideas but by regulatory friction, absence of early-stage capital and lack of market access. The programme completed its tenth anniversary in January 2026.

- The definition — who qualifies

An entity is recognised as a startup by DPIIT if it is: - Up to 10 years from incorporation; - With annual turnover not exceeding ₹100 crore in any financial year; - Working toward innovation, development or improvement of products, processes or services, or having a scalable business model with potential for employment generation or wealth creation; - Not formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business.

- Major features of the programme
- Simplification and regulatory relief - Self-certification for compliance under nine labour and three environment laws, with no inspections for a specified period. - Faster exit — insolvency resolution within 90 days for startups under the IBC, 2016. - Startup India Hub and a single online portal for recognition, learning and networking. - Revised Startup Recognition Framework, 2026, which addresses a specific structural problem: deep tech ventures typically need 10 to 15 years to translate research into a commercial product, so losing recognition at the ten-year mark was a funding obstacle.
- Funding support - Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS) — ₹10,000 crore operated through SIDBI, investing in SEBI-registered alternative investment funds which in turn invest in startups. A Fund of Funds 2.0 of ₹10,000 crore has since been launched to improve access to growth capital. - Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS), 2021 — ₹945 crore for proof of concept, prototype development, product trials and market entry; now fully committed. - Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups (CGSS) — collateral-free loan guarantees; ₹555.24 crore guaranteed to 235 startups, including ₹24.60 crore to 18 women-led startups (as of October 2024).
- Tax incentives - Section 80-IAC — income tax exemption for three consecutive years out of the first ten. - Angel tax abolished in Budget 2024-25 for all classes of investors — removing a long-standing deterrent to early-stage funding.

- Exemption on long-term capital gains on specified investments.

- Intellectual property support - Fast-track patent examination, an 80% rebate on patent filing fees and 50% on trademarks, with facilitators’ costs borne by the government.
- Market access - Public procurement relaxations — exemption from prior turnover and experience requirements in government tenders, and access to the Government e-Marketplace (GeM). - International bridges and participation in global startup events.
- Ecosystem and mentoring - Atal Innovation Mission with Atal Tinkering Labs in schools and Atal Incubation Centres. - National Startup Awards and the States’ Startup Ranking Framework, which introduced competitive federalism into startup policy. - BHASKAR (Bharat Startup Knowledge Access Registry) as a unified digital platform connecting founders, investors and mentors.
- Deep tech focus - The National Deep Tech Startup Policy, with an ambitious target of 500 deep tech unicorns by

2030. - India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, launched alongside Union Budget 2026-27 with ₹40,000 crore for the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme — pivoting support from assembly-led incentives to IP-centric, fabless models. - ISRO’s NewSpace India Limited opening space-tech opportunities to private deep tech startups.

- Contribution to industrial and economic growth
- **Indicator** — Achievement
- **Recognised startups** — Over 2.40 lakh DPIIT-recognised startups by mid-2026, from about 350 in 2014
- **Annual additions** — Over 55,200 startups recognised in FY26 — the highest annual addition since 2016, up 51.6% year-on-year
- **Employment** — Nearly 24 lakh direct jobs created, across more than 55 industries
- **Global position** — The world’s third-largest startup ecosystem, after the United States and China
- **Unicorns** — India had 8 unicorns in 2015; more than 100 companies have since reached unicorn valuation (counts vary by valuation methodology), with 45 minted in 2021 alone
- **Geographic decentralisation** — Startups now span 669 districts, with over 51% from Tier-II and Tier-III cities — arguably the programme’s most important structural achievement
- **Women’s participation** — Over 73,000 startups have at least one woman director
- **Funding** — Indian startups raised about $7.62 billion across 760 equity rounds between January and May 2026; roughly ₹94,500 crore in 2025; the wider ecosystem has cumulatively raised about $620 billion across more than 50,800 funding rounds from over 1,21,000 investors
- **Sectoral spread** — AI, fintech, quick commerce, SaaS, healthtech, EV mobility, spacetech, semiconductors and climate tech

How this contributes to growth

- Employment creation at scale — nearly 24 lakh direct jobs, in formal and skilled roles.
- Decentralised industrialisation — with over half of startups outside the metros, the programme disperses economic opportunity in a way traditional industrial policy did not.
- Innovation and productivity — startups commercialise technology faster than incumbents, and force incumbents to modernise.
- Formalisation — DPIIT recognition brings enterprises into the tax, credit and regulatory system.
- Digital public infrastructure spillovers — UPI, ONDC and Account Aggregator created the rails on which fintech and commerce startups built.
- Import substitution and exports — SaaS, pharma, electronics and space startups earn foreign exchange.
- Women’s entrepreneurship — over 73,000 startups with a woman director.
- Limitations — a balanced examination
- Funding concentration: capital clusters in a few sectors and cities; Bengaluru alone hosts about 52 unicorns, with Delhi-NCR and Mumbai each above 20.
- Funding volatility — the 2022-24 “funding winter” showed dependence on global capital and investor sentiment.
- Survival rate — a high proportion of startups fail; recognition numbers measure entry, not endurance.
- Consumption over deep tech — the ecosystem has been weighted toward e-commerce, delivery and fintech rather than research-intensive sectors; the Deep Tech Policy and the revised recognition framework are the correction.
- Job quality — gig and platform work generated by startups is often insecure; the Labour Codes now extend social security to such workers.
- Regulatory friction persists despite self-certification, particularly at State and municipal level.
- Profitability — the post-2024 shift toward unit economics reflects that many valuations had outrun earnings.

## Conclusion

Start-up India has been among the most successful of India’s recent policy interventions, judged by its own objective: it converted an ecosystem of about 350 startups into the world’s third-largest, with over 2.40 lakh recognised ventures and nearly 24 lakh jobs, and — critically — pushed over half of that activity into Tier-II and Tier-III cities. Its next phase must shift from quantity to depth: from consumer-internet ventures toward deep tech, semiconductors, space and climate technology, supported by the Deep Tech Policy, the revised recognition framework and patient domestic capital through Fund of Funds 2.0. Recognition numbers measure entry; the test now is survival, scale and intellectual property.

- Eligibility to state precisely: up to 10 years from incorporation, turnover up to ₹100 crore, working on innovation or a scalable model — DPIIT recognition unlocks the benefits.

## Introduction

Bifurcation in 2014 left Andhra Pradesh without Hyderabad — its industrial headquarters, services engine and largest urban labour market. Industrial policy in the residuary State has therefore not been about incremental promotion but about building an industrial base from a coastal and agrarian foundation. That context explains both the ambition of the policy and the difficulty of executing it.

- Major initiatives
- **Initiative** — Content
- **The “4.0” policy suite (2024-29)** — Industrial Development Policy 4.0 — targeting ₹30 lakh crore investment, US$10 billion FDI, 5 lakh jobs and 175 industrial parks; alongside MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0, Food Processing Policy 4.0, IT & GCC Policy 4.0, the Electronics Policy and the Integrated Clean Energy Policy
- **Single Desk Policy** — Statutory single-window clearance with defined timelines and deemed approval — AP was among the first States to give this statutory backing
- **Port-led development** — Six ports; new ones at Ramayapatnam (75%), Mulapeta (65%) and Machilipatnam (50%), complementing Visakhapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada and Krishnapatnam
- **Industrial corridors** — Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC) — ADB-supported, Phase 1 of the East Coast Economic Corridor; and the Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor
- **Deliberate inland dispersal** — Industrial nodes at Orvakal (Kurnool) and Kopparthy (Kadapa) in Rayalaseema, alongside coastal Krishnapatnam; 175 MSME parks — one in every assembly constituency
- **Clean energy** — 55 projects worth ₹2.88 lakh crore cleared since June 2024 — solar, wind, pumped storage and green hydrogen
- **Marquee projects** — Google’s US$15 billion AI data centre at Visakhapatnam — the largest single FDI commitment in the country; Integrated Steel Plant (Anakapalli); Bulk Drug Park (Nakkapalli); semiconductor facility (Orvakal); Green Aluminium (Kakinada); Amaravati Quantum Valley; Drone City, Orvakal
- **Investment mobilisation** — Global Partnership Summit 2025 — commitments exceeding ₹13.25 lakh crore across 610 MoUs, with employment potential of 16.13 lakh; since June 2024, 1.19 lakh proposals worth ₹9.68 lakh crore with 5.41 lakh jobs potential

- Support measures

Fiscal Capital investment subsidy graded by unit size and category, with higher rates for women, SC, ST, OBC and minority entrepreneurs; power tariff subsidy and electricity duty reimbursement; SGST reimbursement; stamp duty and land conversion charge reimbursement; interest subvention; and reimbursement of quality certification and patent costs. In food processing, the subsidy reaches 45% for primary processing with ₹1.50 per unit power subsidy.

Infrastructure APIIC land banks and industrial parks; the Alluri Sitaramaraju International Airport at Bhogapuram (97% complete); the AP Logistics Corporation; ₹4,000 crore under UIDF over two years; and capital expenditure of ₹53,915 crore in Budget 2026-27.

Governance and digital AP State Data Lake integrating 36-plus departments and 139 databases; Mana Mitra

WhatsApp governance scaled from 150 to over 900 citizen services in under a year; land records through Meebhoomi; labour reform aligned to the four Labour Codes (effective 21 November 2025).

Skilling Government ITIs with MoUs with 167 industry partners, 9,188 trainees in in-plant training and 98% placement or apprenticeship; Skill Development allocation of ₹1,232 crore.

- Critical examination — the bottlenecks
- **Conversion of MoUs into plants** — The pipeline is very large — ₹13.25 lakh crore in commitments — but memoranda are not payrolls. Historically, a significant share of investment commitments at such summits does not reach financial closure. Execution, not attraction, is the binding constraint
- **Human capital — the deepest constraint** — AP’s literacy at 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States; female literacy stood at 59.96% in Census 2011. No State can move up the industrial value chain faster than its education allows
- **Land** — Acquisition costs and timelines under the LARR Act, 2013; litigation over assigned and tribal land; the Koneru Ranga Rao Committee found about 48% of tribal land had passed to non-tribals in violation of Regulation 1 of 70
- **Power cost and reliability** — Large agricultural and aqua power subsidies — about ₹11,000 crore and ₹890 crore respectively — strain discom finances, and cross-subsidy raises industrial tariffs. The 16th Finance Commission recommends DISCOM privatisation with an SPV to warehouse legacy debt
- **Fiscal space** — Incentives compete with a fiscal deficit budgeted at 3.84% of GSDP and public debt at 36% of GSDP (₹7.11 lakh crore); delayed incentive disbursement erodes investor confidence
- **Regional concentration** — Despite Orvakal and Kopparthy, investment still clusters on the coast; Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra remain thinly industrialised
- **Loss of the metropolitan anchor** — Bifurcation removed Hyderabad; AP is only about 29.5% urbanised, so it lacks the agglomeration economies that draw investment without incentives
- **Policy discontinuity** — Successive governments have renamed and restructured policies and flagship projects — the AP Land Titling Act, 2022 was repealed in 2024, and Amaravati’s status changed with the three-capital proposal. Investors price political risk, and discontinuity is expensive
- **Logistics** — Improving, but India ranks 38th on the World Bank LPI (2023); last-mile connectivity to inland nodes remains weak
- **MSME weakness** — Most units are micro and own-account; the “missing middle” limits supplier depth for large anchor investments

- The balanced verdict

The policy framework is credible. The “4.0” suite is comprehensive, the incentives are competitive with any State’s, port-led development plays to a genuine comparative advantage, and the 175 MSME parks represent a serious attempt at spatial balance rather than a slogan.

The delivery record is unproven. Investment commitments have consistently exceeded commissioned capacity. And the constraint is increasingly not policy at all: land, power reliability, logistics and above all literacy are what determine whether an MoU becomes a factory.

The deepest criticism is that AP has treated industrial development primarily as an investment-attraction problem when it is substantially a human-capital problem. A State with India’s lowest literacy cannot supply the workforce that a US$15 billion data centre, a semiconductor fab and a bulk drug park will collectively require.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s industrial policy is well designed, generously incentivised and correctly aimed at ports, clean energy, deep tech and spatial dispersal. Its bottlenecks are executional and structural rather than conceptual — land, power, logistics, fiscal space and, decisively, education and skills. Converting the current pipeline into employment therefore depends less on new policy than on completing infrastructure, ensuring policy continuity across political cycles, and closing the literacy gap that caps everything else.

## Value addition
