- Institutional agencies: APIIC (industrial infrastructure), APEDB (investment promotion), APFPS (food processing), the Single Desk portal, and the AP Logistics Corporation.
- The structural advantage: a 974-km coastline — India’s second longest — with six ports, and proximity to the Chennai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad markets.
- The comparison that frames the critique: AP’s per capita GSDP of ₹2,70,295 (2023-24) exceeds India’s

₹2,15,935, yet its literacy is the country’s lowest — income without human capital is not a sustainable industrial base.
P4-Q12b:
## Introduction

Correction: the DIPP was renamed the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) in January 2019, when internal trade, e-commerce, retail and startups were brought within its remit. Noting the change and explaining its significance earns credit; writing only “DIPP” dates the answer.

Industry contributes about 24.3% of India’s GDP and grew 6.2% in FY26, but its developmental significance lies less in its share than in its function — it generates the highest value added per worker, absorbs technology, and is the bridge from a subsistence to a modern economy. Coordinating that function across ministries, States and investors is the work of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT).

- Role of the industrial sector — in brief
- **Income generation** — ASI FY24: net value added per person engaged in factories ₹10.7 lakh — a multiple of agricultural productivity
- **Employment and formalisation** — Over 10 lakh new factory jobs in FY24, 57 lakh over FY15-FY24; formal, contract-based work with social security
- **Absorbing surplus farm labour** — The unfinished task — roughly 45% of workers remain in agriculture producing about 15-16% of GDP
- **Export earnings** — Total exports a record US$825.3 billion in FY25; manufactured exports finance capital goods and energy imports
- **Fiscal contribution** — Gross GST ₹22.27 lakh crore in FY26; industry is the most taxable sector
- **Capital formation** — GFCF at 30.0% of GDP in FY26; private corporate investment announcements about ₹14.6 lakh crore in H1 FY26
- **Modernisation and urbanisation** — Technology diffusion, skill formation, city growth and infrastructure demand
- **Linkages** — Backward and forward multipliers far stronger than in agriculture or most services

- DPIIT — evolution and status
- **Origin** — Established in 1995 as the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, formed by merging the Department of Industrial Development with the earlier industrial administration apparatus
- **Renaming — January 2019** — Became the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, with internal trade, welfare of traders and their employees, e-commerce and retail added to its remit; Startup India was also brought under it
- **Ministry** — Part of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry
- **Significance of the change** — The renaming marked a shift from regulating industrial licensing to promoting industry, internal trade and enterprise — from control to facilitation

- Role and functions of DPIIT
- Industrial policy formulation Frames and reviews India’s industrial policy, and coordinates industrial development across sectors not allotted to other specific ministries.
- FDI policy — its most consequential function - Formulates and issues the Consolidated FDI Policy and Press Notes amending it. - Recent examples: the insurance FDI cap raised from 74% to 100% under the automatic route through Press Note 1 (2026 Series) following the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, 2025; and the 2026 relaxation permitting foreign companies with up to 10% Chinese or Hong Kong shareholding under the automatic route. - Monitors FDI inflows — a record US$94.52 billion total FDI in FY26, with equity inflows of US$58.84 billion.
- Ease of doing business and regulatory reform - The Business Reform Action Plan and States’ Business Reform rankings, which introduced competitive federalism into regulatory reform. - National Single Window System for approvals. - Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023, decriminalising minor business offences. - Reduction of compliance burden across central and State rules.
- Startup India - DPIIT recognition of startups — over 2.40 lakh recognised by mid-2026, with over 55,200 in FY26 alone; administers tax exemption certification, the Seed Fund Scheme, Fund of Funds and CGSS.
- Make in India and manufacturing promotion - Coordinates Make in India, sectoral PLI schemes across 14+ sectors, and the National Industrial Corridor Development Programme (including the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor). - Administers the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order and local content requirements.
- Intellectual property Administers the Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM) and the National IPR Policy (2016) — patents, trademarks, designs, geographical indications and copyright.
- Internal trade and e-commerce - Policy for retail and internal trade, welfare of traders, and the National Retail Trade Policy framework. - Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules input, and support for ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce) as a democratised e-commerce alternative.
- Logistics and infrastructure - National Logistics Policy (2022) and coordination with PM GatiShakti; the Logistics Ease Across Different States (LEADS) index. India’s LPI rank improved from 44th (2018) to 38th (2023).
- Data, indices and monitoring - The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) in coordination with MoSPI; Wholesale Price Index; FDI statistics; and the Project Monitoring Group for large project clearances.
- Specific industries Direct administrative responsibility for a set of industries including cement, paper, light engineering, rubber, leather and explosives, plus the salt sector.
- Bilateral and multilateral engagement Investment promotion through Invest India, and the investment chapters of trade agreements such as India-EFTA TEPA (with its binding US$100 billion investment commitment) and India-UK CETA.
- Assessment of DPIIT’s performance

Achievements - FDI liberalisation delivered a record US$94.52 billion in FY26 and cumulative inflows of about US$1.16 trillion since April 2000. - Startup India built the world’s third-largest ecosystem, with over 51% of startups from Tier-II and Tier-III cities. - Ease of doing business reform and State rankings produced genuine regulatory competition among States. - PLI schemes shifted electronics and pharmaceutical manufacturing measurably toward India.

Limitations - Manufacturing’s share of GDP has not risen to the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy (2011). - Net FDI remains modest relative to gross, because of repatriation and rising outward investment (US$22.1 billion in April-November 2025). - Policy predictability — the Economic Survey 2025-26 has urged that every policy change pass a “necessity test”, implying that frequent amendment has itself been a deterrent. - State-level implementation of central reform remains uneven, since land, labour and utilities are largely State subjects.

## Conclusion

The industrial sector’s role in India’s development is structurally central and quantitatively under-realised — it delivers the highest productivity per worker but has not absorbed the workforce. DPIIT is the institution charged with closing that gap, and its renaming in 2019 to include internal trade and startups captured the shift from licensing industry to promoting enterprise. Its record on FDI, startups and regulatory reform is strong; its unfinished task is the one that has defeated Indian industrial policy for three decades — raising manufacturing’s share and making it labour-absorbing, which requires State-level action on land, labour and logistics that no central department can deliver alone.

## Value addition
- The name change to state precisely: Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP) → Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), January 2019, with internal trade, e-commerce, retail and startups added.
- Key instruments administered: Consolidated FDI Policy and Press Notes; Invest India; National Single Window System; CGPDTM; National Logistics Policy (2022); LEADS index; Business Reform Action Plan; Jan Vishwas Act, 2023.
- FDI record: US$94.52 billion total and US$58.84 billion equity in FY26; cumulative US$1.16 trillion since April 2000; India rose to 11th globally in UNCTAD’s ranking.
- The policy target still unmet: the National Manufacturing Policy (2011) target of manufacturing at 25% of GDP and 100 million jobs.

## Introduction

Transport infrastructure determines the cost of distance — and therefore what a country can produce, where it can produce it, and at what price it can sell. India has undertaken infrastructure expansion at unprecedented scale in the past decade, with the Centre’s effective capital expenditure reaching ₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP) in Budget 2026-27 — now exceeding the fiscal deficit itself.

- The current state — mode by mode
- **Roads** — The second-largest road network in the world, carrying the bulk of freight and passenger traffic. Bharatmala Pariyojana has completed over 18,900 km of highways; national highway construction pace rose sharply over the decade
- **Railways** — Among the world’s largest networks; near-complete electrification of the broad-gauge network; Dedicated Freight Corridors operational on the Eastern and Western routes; Vande Bharat and Amrit Bharat trains; station redevelopment under PPP
- **High-speed rail** — Budget 2026-27 announced seven High-Speed Rail “Growth Connectors” — Mumbai-Pune, Pune-Hyderabad, Hyderabad-Bengaluru, Hyderabad-Chennai, Chennai-Bengaluru, Delhi-Varanasi and Varanasi-Siliguri — as environmentally sustainable passenger systems linking City Economic Regions
- **Ports and shipping** — Major and non-major ports under Sagarmala; capacity and turnaround times improved substantially; coastal shipping and inland waterways under development
- **Aviation** — Operational airports more than doubled over the decade; UDAN has operationalised 619 routes and 88 airports, connecting Tier-II and Tier-III towns
- **Urban transport** — Metro rail operational across a growing number of cities — the second-largest metro network in the world by some measures; BRTS and electric bus fleets
- **Rural connectivity** — PMGSY has connected the overwhelming majority of eligible habitations with all-weather roads
- **Logistics performance** — India ranks 38th on the World Bank Logistics Performance Index (2023), improved from 44th in 2018; logistics cost estimated at about 7.97% of GDP (NCAER, 2023-24)

- Contribution to economic development
- Reducing the cost of distance Transport determines whether a producer in Anantapur can compete in Mumbai or Rotterdam. Every reduction in freight cost widens the market a firm can serve, which is the precondition for scale.
- Enabling industrial location and agglomeration Industry follows transport. Corridors such as the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor, developed with ADB support of US$631 million, exist precisely to make industrial location viable outside established metropolitan areas.
- Integration into global value chains Between 1991 and 2011, parts and components were about 70% of East Asia’s manufacturing exports but only 22% of India’s — participation in such chains requires fast, reliable, low-cost logistics, which is why transport investment is an industrial policy instrument, not merely a public service.
- Agricultural marketing and rural incomes Rural roads under PMGSY improved farm-gate prices by widening the set of buyers a farmer can reach, and reduced post-harvest loss. The Economic Survey notes this improved rural livelihoods, farm-gate prices and women’s workforce participation.
- Employment Construction is among the most labour-intensive activities in the economy, and transport assets generate permanent employment in operations, maintenance and the activity they enable.
- Regional balance UDAN’s 619 routes and 88 airports and Bharatmala’s connectivity to backward regions integrate smaller towns into the national economy — reducing the isolation that perpetuates regional disparity.
- Fiscal multiplier Capital expenditure on infrastructure has among the highest multipliers in the economy; the Centre’s capex share of total expenditure rose from 12.5% (FY20) to 22.6% (FY25).
- Human development Access to schools, hospitals and markets depends on transport. This is a welfare contribution independent of its economic one.
- Key challenges
- **Modal imbalance** — Roads carry a disproportionate share of freight, though rail is  cheaper and less carbon-intensive for bulk over long distances. The optimal modal mix would shift substantial tonnage to rail and coastal shipping
- **Logistics cost** — At about 7.97% of GDP, higher than in competitor economies — a direct handicap on export competitiveness
- **Last-mile connectivity** — Ports, freight corridors and industrial nodes suffer from weak final-leg road and rail links, which nullify gains on the trunk network
- **Land acquisition** — The single largest cause of delay and cost overrun; the LARR Act, 2013 raised compensation and consent requirements
- **Maintenance deficit** — Assets are built and under-maintained; the plan/non-plan distinction historically starved maintenance, and the habit persists
- **Urban congestion** — Rapid motorisation without commensurate public transport; air quality and productivity losses
- **Financing** — Requirements far exceed budgetary capacity; PPP participation weakened after the twin-balance-sheet problem, and the corporate bond market at 15-16% of GDP (against Korea’s 79%) cannot yet supply long-tenure finance
- **Institutional fragmentation** — Multiple ministries and agencies planning independently — the problem PM GatiShakti was created to solve
- **Safety** — Road fatalities remain among the highest in the world
- **Climate vulnerability** — Coastal and riverine infrastructure exposed to cyclones and flooding, requiring resilience standards not yet universally applied

- Suggested policy measures
- Rebalance the modal mix Shift bulk freight to rail and coastal shipping through Dedicated Freight Corridors, port connectivity and rationalised freight tariffs — the largest available reduction in both logistics cost and emissions.
- Integrated planning Institutionalise PM GatiShakti, which brings 16-plus ministries onto a common GIS platform, and the National Logistics Policy (2022) with its Unified Logistics Interface Platform, so that road, rail, port and utility projects are sequenced rather than duplicated.
- Prioritise last-mile connectivity Fund final-leg links to ports, freight corridors and industrial nodes; a trunk route without last-mile access delivers a fraction of its benefit.
- Deepen long-term finance Expand NaBFID, develop the corporate bond market, and use InvITs and REITs and the National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP 2.0, ₹10 lakh crore for 2025-30) to recycle capital from completed assets into new ones.
- Reform PPP on the Kelkar principles Allocate risk by capability — government bearing land and clearance risk, the private party bearing construction and operation risk — extend the Hybrid Annuity Model, permit renegotiation on transparent triggers, and establish the IPRC and IPAT the Kelkar Committee (2015) recommended.
- Fund maintenance explicitly Ring-fence maintenance budgets and adopt asset management contracts, since a road not maintained is a road rebuilt.
- Urban public transport Prioritise metro, bus rapid transit and electric bus fleets over private-vehicle infrastructure; integrate land use with transit planning.
- Digitisation and efficiency FASTag, e-way bills, port community systems and the ULIP to cut dwell time — often the cheapest available efficiency gain.
- Green and resilient standards Electrification of rail, EV charging corridors, and climate-resilient design for coastal and flood-prone assets.
- Complete land and clearance before bidding This single procedural change would remove the largest source of delay and dispute in Indian infrastructure.

## Conclusion

India’s transport infrastructure has been transformed in a decade — 18,900 km under Bharatmala, 619 UDAN routes, dedicated freight corridors, and capital expenditure now exceeding the fiscal deficit. Its contribution to development runs through lower distance costs, industrial location, agricultural marketing and regional integration. The remaining agenda is less about building more and more about using better: rebalancing toward rail and coastal shipping, closing last-mile gaps, funding maintenance, and deepening the long-term finance on which the next phase depends.

## Value addition
- The integrating instruments: PM GatiShakti National Master Plan (GIS-based, 16-plus ministries), the National Logistics Policy (2022) with the Unified Logistics Interface Platform, and the LEADS index ranking States on logistics performance.
- The programmes to name: Bharatmala (highways), Sagarmala (ports), UDAN (regional aviation), PMGSY (rural roads), Dedicated Freight Corridors, and Setu Bharatam (level crossings).
- The financing architecture: NaBFID (2021), the National Infrastructure Pipeline, NMP 2.0 (₹10 lakh crore, 2025-30), InvITs and REITs, and VGF for socially necessary projects.
- AP illustration: six ports with Ramayapatnam (75%), Mulapeta (65%) and Machilipatnam (50%) under construction; Bhogapuram airport (97% complete); NH-16 on the Golden Quadrilateral; and a dedicated South Coast Railway zone.

## Introduction

Correction: the master text states solar capacity as “over 110 GW by mid-2025”. The Economic Survey 2025-26 records 135.81 GW by December 2025 — a 45-fold increase from 3 GW in 2014. Using the current figure is essential.

Solar is the cornerstone of India’s energy transition. India receives about 5,000 trillion kWh of solar radiation annually, tariffs have fallen to among the lowest in the world, and solar now constitutes 52% of India’s renewable

capacity. The country has surpassed its target of 50% installed capacity from non-fossil sources — reaching 51.93% by December 2025, five years ahead of its NDC commitment.

- Why solar is central to the strategy
- **Natural endowment** — About 5,000 trillion kWh of solar radiation annually; most of India receives 250-300 sunny days a year
- **Falling cost** — Solar tariffs have fallen to around ₹2-2.20 per unit, among the lowest globally — solar is now cheaper than new thermal capacity
- **Speed of deployment** — A solar park can be commissioned in months against years for thermal or nuclear
- **Scalability and modularity** — Works at every scale — from a rooftop panel to a 30 GW park
- **Energy security** — Reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels, which dominate India’s import bill
- **Climate commitments** — Central to the Paris Agreement NDCs and the net-zero by 2070 commitment
- **Decentralised access** — Rooftop and off-grid systems reach areas the grid serves poorly
- **Employment** — Manufacturing, installation and maintenance are labour-intensive

- Major initiatives
- **Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (2010)** — The foundational programme; target progressively revised upward to 100 GW
- **PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana** — Rooftop solar for households — 8 GW of rooftop capacity installed by December 2025
- **PM-KUSUM** — Solar for agriculture — Component B: over 9.75 lakh standalone pumps installed (December 2025); Component C: 11,781 grid-connected pumps solarised and 11,89,787 feeder-level solarisation pumps completed
- **Solar Parks and Ultra Mega Solar Power Projects** — 55 solar parks approved with a combined sanctioned capacity of 39,973 MW, of which 16,121 MW installed by December 2025 — plug-and-play infrastructure with land and evacuation pre-arranged
- **PLI Scheme for High-Efficiency Solar PV Modules** — ₹24,000 crore to build integrated domestic manufacturing — from polysilicon to modules
- **CPSU Scheme Phase II** — 8.2 GW sanctioned, 5.5 GW commissioned by December 2025 — public sector undertakings deploying domestically manufactured cells
- **Green Energy Corridor** — Inter-State transmission to evacuate large-scale renewable power from generation zones to demand centres
- **New Solar Power scheme under PM JANMAN and Dharti Aaba** — Solar for tribal households — 6,897 households benefited by December 2025
- **ALMM (Approved List of Models and Manufacturers)** — Domestic content requirement for government-supported projects
- **International Solar Alliance** — India-led, headquartered at Gurugram — the country’s principal climate diplomacy instrument
- **Budget 2026-27 support** — BCD exemption on sodium antimonate for solar glass manufacture; exemption on capital goods for lithium-ion cells used in battery energy storage; a ₹20,000 crore CCUS scheme

- Achievements
- **Solar capacity** — 3 GW (2014) → 135.81 GW (December 2025) — a 45-fold increase
- **Total renewable capacity** — 253.96 GW (November 2025), up from 76.38 GW in March 2014 — more than a threefold rise
- **Renewable share** — About 49.83% of total installed capacity (30 November 2025); non-fossil at 51.93% by December 2025 — the 50% target achieved five years ahead of the NDC commitment
- **Record annual addition** — 34.56 GW of non-fossil capacity in the first eight months of FY26 — the largest ever; solar contributed 27.20 GW of it. To 31 December 2025, 38.61 GW of renewables including 30.16 GW of solar
- **Global ranking** — Third in overall renewable capacity and in installed solar, fourth in wind; fourth globally in total installed renewable capacity (IRENA, 2025) after China, the USA and Brazil
- **Solar’s share of the renewable mix** — 52%, ahead of wind (21%), large hydro (20%), bio-energy (5%) and small hydro (2%)
- **Tariffs** — Around ₹2-2.20 per unit, among the lowest globally
- **Flagship asset** — The 30 GW hybrid solar-wind park in Kutch, Gujarat — the world’s largest renewable energy park

- Challenges
- **Intermittency and storage — the central technical challenge** — Solar generates only in daylight and peaks at midday while demand peaks in the evening. The Economic Survey identifies large-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Pumped Storage Projects (PSP) as essential to address variability, ensure grid stability and manage peak load
- **Grid integration and evacuation** — Renewable generation is concentrated in a few States while demand is dispersed; transmission has lagged generation, and curtailment results
- **Baseload adequacy** — The Survey explicitly cautions — citing the Dutch experience, where 14,000 companies await grid connection — that transitions must be grounded in baseload adequacy and system reliability
- **Import dependence** — A high share of solar modules and most cells and wafers are imported, chiefly from China; the PLI scheme (₹24,000 crore) and ALMM address this, but the supply chain from polysilicon upward is still being built
- **Land acquisition** — Utility-scale solar is land-intensive; acquisition delays are a recognised constraint
- **High capital cost** — Renewables are capital-intensive with long payback; the Survey calls for innovative financing mechanisms and optimised project execution
- **DISCOM financial stress** — Distribution companies delay payments to generators, raising the cost of capital for developers. The 16th Finance Commission recommends DISCOM privatisation with an SPV to warehouse legacy debt
- **Rooftop adoption lag** — Procedural hurdles, net-metering disputes and DISCOM reluctance have kept rooftop capacity at 8 GW against a 40 GW target
- **Policy uncertainty at State level** — Andhra Pradesh’s own experience illustrates this — PPA review controversies and payment delays to developers created a “flip-flop” in renewable policy that damaged investor confidence
- **PV waste and recycling** — An emerging challenge as first-generation panels approach end of life; India lacks a mature solar-waste recycling framework
- **Critical minerals** — Dependence on imported lithium, cobalt and rare earths for storage — addressed through the National Critical Mineral Mission and the MMDR Amendment Act, 2025 creating the NMEDT with ₹8,700 crore over five years

- The way forward
- Storage above all — scale BESS and pumped storage, since without storage further solar addition yields diminishing

system value.

- Transmission ahead of generation — expand the Green Energy Corridor so evacuation does not lag capacity.
- Complete the domestic manufacturing chain — polysilicon, ingots, wafers and cells, not only module assembly.
- DISCOM reform — the single largest determinant of the sector’s cost of capital.
- Simplify rooftop procedures and resolve net-metering disputes.
- Round-the-clock renewable tenders and hybrid solar-wind-storage bundling.
- Solar waste management and circular-economy standards.
- Policy stability — honour existing power purchase agreements, since retrospective review destroys investor confidence far beyond the projects affected.

## Conclusion

Solar has taken India from 3 GW to 135.81 GW in eleven years and carried the country past its 50% non-fossil capacity target five years early, making it the world’s third-largest solar producer. The achievement is genuine and internationally recognised. The next phase is harder and less visible: capacity addition alone no longer suffices, because the binding constraints have shifted to storage, transmission, distribution finance and domestic manufacturing depth. India’s clean energy leadership will now be measured not by gigawatts installed but by how reliably that power reaches consumers when they need it.

## Value addition
- The headline figures: solar 3 GW (2014) → 135.81 GW (December 2025); total RE 253.96 GW (November 2025) from 76.38 GW (March 2014); non-fossil 51.93% of installed capacity, achieved five years early.
- Installed capacity by source (31 December 2025): fossils 247 GW, renewables excluding hydro 207 GW, hydro including pumped storage 51 GW, nuclear 9 GW.
- Wind for comparison: 54.51 GW (December 2025), fourth highest in the world; 30.04 GW under implementation; wind generated 83.35 billion units in 2024-25.
- AP context: installed capacity of about 24,854 MW; 55 clean-energy projects worth ₹2.88 lakh crore cleared since June 2024 in solar, wind, pumped storage and green hydrogen; the Green Energy Corridor for evacuation.

## Introduction

The Smart Cities Mission, launched in June 2015, selected 100 cities through a competitive City Challenge to develop as models of urban transformation. Its premise was that Indian urbanisation — the country is only about 36% urbanised against roughly 50% typical at its income level — required not merely more infrastructure but better-governed, technology-enabled and liveable cities.

- Design of the Mission
- **Selection** — 100 cities chosen through a two-stage competitive City Challenge, in which cities submitted their own proposals — a significant departure from allocation by formula
- **Strategy** — Two components: area-based development (retrofitting, redevelopment, greenfield) covering a defined part of the city, and a pan-city solution applying technology across the whole city
- **Implementation vehicle** — A Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) for each city, incorporated under the Companies Act, with a full-time CEO and State-municipal equity
- **Funding** — Central and State assistance, with the remainder to be raised through convergence, PPP, municipal bonds and own resources
- **Signature output** — Integrated Command and Control Centres (ICCCs) — the Mission’s most visible and durable creation

- Achievements — the case for
- Integrated Command and Control Centres — the most valuable legacy ICCCs integrate CCTV surveillance, traffic management, solid waste tracking, emergency response and utility monitoring on a single platform. Their value was demonstrated unexpectedly during COVID-19, when many were repurposed overnight as war rooms for pandemic management — contact tracing, ambulance dispatch and supply coordination. An asset that proves useful for a purpose it was not designed for is a well-designed asset.
- Urban mobility Smart traffic signalling, intelligent transport systems, multi-level parking, bus fleet tracking and non-motorised transport corridors.
- Utilities and services SCADA-based water supply monitoring, smart metering, sewage treatment, and solid waste management with GPS-tracked collection.
- Renewable energy and sustainability Rooftop solar on public buildings, LED street lighting, green buildings and urban forests.
- Public spaces Riverfronts, lakefronts, heritage precincts, cycle tracks and pedestrianisation — improving liveability in ways residents actually notice.
- Digital governance E-governance portals, grievance redressal, digital payments for municipal services, and GIS-based property mapping — the last of which has improved property tax collection, a genuine fiscal gain for chronically under-resourced municipalities.
- Municipal capacity and finance The Mission compelled cities to prepare project proposals, form SPVs and pursue municipal bonds — several cities issued bonds for the first time, building the capital-market access that urban local bodies had always lacked.
- Competitive federalism The City Challenge introduced competition among cities, and the Ease of Living Index and Municipal Performance Index institutionalised comparative assessment.
- Criticisms — the case against
- **Area-based development served a fraction of the city** — The most serious structural criticism. Area-based development typically covered a small proportion of a city’s area and population, so investment concentrated in already-better-served zones while peripheral and slum areas were untouched. This risked making cities more unequal, not less
- **The SPV bypassed elected government** — SPVs were company-form entities with appointed CEOs, effectively bypassing municipal corporations and elected councillors — raising a genuine constitutional objection under the 74th Amendment, which was enacted precisely to devolve urban governance to elected bodies
- **Technology over basic services** — Command centres and smart signals were funded while water supply, sewerage, drainage and solid waste — the services that actually determine urban health — remained inadequate in many of the same cities. Critics argued the Mission chose the visible over the essential
- **Financing assumptions did not hold** — The Mission assumed substantial convergence, PPP and own-source revenue. PPP participation was far below projection, so cities depended more heavily on central and State funds than intended
- **Municipal finances remain weak** — Urban local bodies’ own revenues are a small fraction of their requirements; the 16th Finance Commission allocates ₹9,727 crore in ULB basic grants for Andhra Pradesh alone (2026-31), indicating continuing dependence on transfers
- **Capacity constraints** — Municipalities lacked staff with project management, procurement and contract skills; SPVs relied heavily on consultants
- **Definition never settled** — “Smart city” was never precisely defined, so cities interpreted it differently — producing incomparable outcomes
- **Timeline extensions** — Completion deadlines were extended repeatedly, and some projects remain incomplete
- **Climate and disaster resilience** — Urban flooding — Chennai, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru — exposed that drainage and resilience received less attention than surveillance and signage
- **Equity** — Slum populations, informal workers and street vendors were rarely central to smart city plans, though they constitute a large share of urban residents

- The balanced verdict

The Mission succeeded at what it could control. It created ICCCs of demonstrable value, improved public spaces, digitised municipal services, strengthened property tax collection, opened municipal bond markets and introduced competitive assessment among cities. These are real and durable gains.

It could not succeed at what it did not address. Indian urban problems are fundamentally about municipal finance, governance capacity and devolution under the 74th Amendment. A mission that bypassed elected municipal government through SPVs and funded area-based enclaves could improve parts of cities but not transform urban governance itself.

The most useful framing: the Smart Cities Mission was a demonstration programme rather than a transformation programme. It showed what is possible in a defined area with adequate funding and a capable SPV. Whether that demonstration scales depends on reforms it did not attempt — empowered municipal governments with own revenue sources and professional staff.

- The successor framework

Urban policy has since moved toward agglomeration and regional scale: - Budget 2026-27 introduced the concept of City Economic Regions, focused on Tier-II, Tier-III cities and temple towns, and announced seven High-Speed Rail “Growth Connectors” — Mumbai-Pune, Pune-Hyderabad, Hyderabad-Bengaluru, Hyderabad-Chennai, Chennai-Bengaluru, Delhi-Varanasi and Varanasi-Siliguri. - AMRUT 2.0 for universal water supply and sewerage; Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0; PMAY-Urban 2.0; the Urban Challenge Fund; and the Urban Infrastructure Development Fund (UIDF) — under which Andhra Pradesh is availing ₹4,000 crore over two years. - The 16th Finance Commission has introduced a dedicated Special Infrastructure (wastewater) component for million-plus cities, with Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada among the qualifying cities in Andhra Pradesh.

## Conclusion

The Smart Cities Mission improved parts of a hundred cities without transforming urban India — a fair summary of both its achievement and its limitation. Its Integrated Command and Control Centres, digitised services and improved public spaces are genuine legacies, and its competitive selection process was an institutional innovation. But by

concentrating on area-based enclaves and delivering through SPVs that bypassed elected municipal bodies, it addressed the symptoms of urban underdevelopment rather than its cause — which is the fiscal and functional weakness of Indian municipal government. The shift to City Economic Regions and agglomeration-scale planning in Budget 2026-

27 is the correct next step, but it too will succeed only if accompanied by genuine devolution under the 74th Amendment.

## Value addition
- The Mission’s design elements to name: the City Challenge competitive selection; area-based development (retrofitting, redevelopment, greenfield) and pan-city solutions; Special Purpose Vehicles under the Companies Act; and Integrated Command and Control Centres.
- The constitutional objection: the 74th Constitutional Amendment (1992) devolved urban governance to elected municipal bodies with the Twelfth Schedule listing 18 functions — SPV-led implementation sits uneasily with this.
- The companion missions: AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0, Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban, PMAY-Urban, HRIDAY

(heritage), the National Urban Digital Mission, and the Ease of Living and Municipal Performance Indices.

- The urbanisation context: India is about 36% urbanised against roughly 50% typical at its income level; Andhra Pradesh is only about 29.5% urbanised — the lowest among major southern States, and a direct constraint on its industrial and services growth.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh’s infrastructure effort since bifurcation has centred on replacing what Hyderabad provided — connectivity, power and digital services — with a coastal, corridor-based alternative. Transport, energy and ICT together form the backbone of the State’s competitiveness, and each shows genuine progress alongside persistent weaknesses.

- Transport infrastructure

Development

- **Roads** — A dense network with national highway density above the national average; NH-16, part of the Golden Quadrilateral, forms the backbone; four-lane district connectivity and port hinterland connectivity are stated goals
- **Railways** — A crucial part of the national network, with the major junction at Vijayawada and a dedicated South Coast Railway zone headquartered at Visakhapatnam
- **Ports** — Port-led development using India’s second-longest coastline at 974 km — Visakhapatnam (a major cargo hub), Gangavaram, Kakinada and Krishnapatnam, with new ports at Ramayapatnam (75%), Mulapeta (65%) and Machilipatnam (50%)
- **Aviation** — International airports at Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Tirupati; the greenfield Alluri Sitaramaraju International Airport at Bhogapuram is 97% complete
- **Corridors** — The Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor, with ADB support of US$631 million approved in September 2016 and State counterpart funding of US$215 million
- **Logistics** — The AP Logistics Corporation, formed after the Reimagining Public Finance Summit; ₹4,000 crore under UIDF over two years; capital expenditure of ₹53,915 crore in Budget 2026-27

Critical assessment - Land acquisition, implementation delays and inadequate maintenance persist — assets are built and under-maintained. - Last-mile connectivity to ports and inland industrial nodes remains weak, which nullifies

gains on the trunk network. - Regional imbalance — the coastal corridor is well served; Rayalaseema’s interior and the tribal agency areas of North Coastal Andhra are not. - Port capacity has grown faster than the hinterland connectivity needed to feed it.

- Energy infrastructure

Development

- **Installed capacity** — Approximately 24,854 MW, drawing on thermal, hydro and rapidly growing renewables
- **Renewables** — 55 clean-energy projects worth ₹2.88 lakh crore cleared since June 2024 — solar, wind, pumped storage and green hydrogen, under the Integrated Clean Energy Policy
- **Transmission** — New substations and the Green Energy Corridor to evacuate renewable power from generation zones
- **National context** — India’s renewables reached 253.96 GW (November 2025), with non-fossil at 51.93% of installed capacity by December 2025 — the 50% target met five years early

Critical assessment - Policy discontinuity is the principal criticism. The “flip-flop” in renewable energy policy between administrations produced Power Purchase Agreement review controversies, payment delays to developers and grid integration issues — damaging investor confidence well beyond the projects affected. Retrospective review of contracts is the most expensive signal a State can send. - Subsidy burden: about ₹11,000 crore in agricultural power subsidy for 22.5 lakh farmers and ₹890 crore in aquaculture tariff subsidy strain distribution finances, and cross-subsidy raises industrial tariffs. - DISCOM financial stress — the 16th Finance Commission recommends privatisation with a special purpose vehicle to warehouse legacy debt, linked to release of capital investment assistance. - Storage and grid integration — the national constraint applies here too: solar and wind addition outpaces the storage and transmission needed to use it reliably.

- ICT infrastructure

Development

- **Connectivity** — High tele-density; an initiative to provide high-speed broadband up to 100 Mbps to every village; APSFL (AP State FiberNet Limited) provides telephone, internet and television services
- **Digital governance** — AP State Data Lake integrating 36-plus departments and 139 databases; Mana Mitra WhatsApp governance scaled from 150 to over 900 citizen services in under a year
- **Service delivery** — Meebhoomi land records with digitally signed e-passbooks; Smart Ration Cards with QR codes from August 2026; RBK-based e-crop booking for insurance and procurement; Shakti App with a seven-minute response target
- **IT and data centres** — IT & GCC Policy 4.0 (2024-29); Google’s US$15 billion AI data centre at Visakhapatnam — the largest single FDI commitment in the country; Amaravati Quantum Valley; the Ratan Tata Innovation Hub

Critical assessment - APSFL’s financial and operational viability has been a recurring concern, with utilisation below capacity. - The digital divide within the State — connectivity in tribal agency areas and remote mandals lags the coastal districts. - Literacy is the binding constraint. AP’s rate of 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States; digital literacy cannot exceed basic literacy, so infrastructure alone will not produce usage. - Authentication and connectivity failures exclude the elderly and manual workers, a live issue in PDS and welfare delivery.

- The common thread — the critical point

Across all three sectors the same pattern appears: Andhra Pradesh has been strong at creating assets and weaker at three things that determine whether assets deliver —

- Maintenance — roads, canals and equipment are built and then under-funded;
- Policy continuity — PPA reviews, the repeal of the AP Land Titling Act, 2022 in 2024, and the reopening of the capital question all raise the political risk investors price into every project;
- Human capital — a State with India’s lowest literacy cannot fully use the digital and industrial infrastructure it is building.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s transport, energy and ICT development represents a serious and largely well-directed reconstruction effort after bifurcation — port-led connectivity, a large clean energy pipeline, village-level broadband and genuinely innovative digital governance. The criticisms are consistent across sectors: maintenance deficits, regional imbalance, subsidy-driven financial stress in power, and policy discontinuity that raises the cost of capital. Infrastructure creates the possibility of growth; maintenance, credible policy and an educated workforce determine whether it is realised.

## Value addition
- AP’s structural advantage: the 974-km coastline, second longest in India, with six ports; NH-16 on the Golden Quadrilateral; a dedicated South Coast Railway zone.
- The energy position: installed capacity about 24,854 MW; 55 clean-energy projects worth ₹2.88 lakh crore

cleared since June 2024; national non-fossil share at 51.93% (December 2025).

- The digital assets: APSFL village broadband; AP State Data Lake (36-plus departments, 139 databases); Mana Mitra with over 900 services; Google’s US$15 billion Visakhapatnam data centre.
- The reform the 16th FC urges: DISCOM privatisation with an SPV to warehouse legacy debt, with capital investment assistance released against progress — directly relevant to AP’s power finances.

## Introduction

Note: “the latest Finance Commission” is now the Sixteenth, whose award took effect on 1 April 2026. Answering on the 15th FC would cost marks.

The Finance Commission, constituted under Article 280, is the constitutional arbiter of India’s vertical and horizontal fiscal balance. The Sixteenth Finance Commission (Chairperson: Dr. Arvind Panagariya) — constituted on 31 December 2023, which submitted its report on 17 November 2025 and was tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2026 under Article 281 — governs Union-State fiscal relations for 2026-27 to 2030-31. Its award took effect on 1 April 2026.

## What the 16th Finance Commission recommended

## Vertical devolution — continuity over change
- States’ share in the divisible pool retained at 41%, despite 18 States demanding 50%. The Commission held that the Union needed fiscal space for defence, internal security and national commitments.
- In Union Budget 2026-27, this translates into tax devolution of ₹15.26 lakh crore and total transfers to States of about ₹26.2 lakh crore.

## Horizontal distribution — a significant formula change
- **Criterion** — Weight · Change from 15th FC
- **Income distance** — 42.5% · Reduced from 45%
- **Population (2011)** — 17.5% · Raised from 15%
- **Demographic performance** — 10% · Reduced from 12.5%
- **Area** — 10% · Unchanged
- **Forest and ecology** — 10% · Unchanged
- **Contribution to GDP** — 10% · New criterion, replacing tax effort (2.5%)

The introduction of “Contribution to GDP” is the Commission’s most consequential innovation — it rewards States that generate national output, partially answering the long-standing grievance of the higher-income, higher-contributing States.

## Grants — a decisive shift to untied transfers
- Total grants of about ₹9.47 lakh crore — local bodies ₹7.91 lakh crore and disaster management ₹1.56 lakh crore.
- Discontinued: post-devolution revenue-deficit grants, sector-specific grants and state-specific grants — a major simplification, but a real loss for structurally deficit States.

## Fiscal discipline framework
- Centre’s fiscal deficit to fall to 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31; States capped at 3% of GSDP.
- Combined Centre-State debt projected to decline from 77.3% of GDP (2026-27) to 73.1% (2030-31).
- All off-budget borrowings to be discontinued and brought within the definition of debt — the single most important transparency reform.
- Structural advice: privatise DISCOMs with an SPV for legacy debt (linked to capital investment assistance), set exclusion criteria for subsidies, review unconditional cash transfers, and close 308 inactive State PSEs.

## Significance for Union-State fiscal relations
- **Predictability** — A five-year, formula-based entitlement enables States to budget beyond the annual cycle for capital and social spending
- **Greater autonomy** — Ending sector-specific and state-specific grants shifts the mix decisively towards untied devolution — States gain discretion
- **Rewarding productivity** — The GDP-contribution criterion begins to balance equity with efficiency, easing North-South federal friction
- **Deeper decentralisation** — ₹7.91 lakh crore for panchayats and municipalities pushes fiscal responsibility to the third tier
- **Fiscal discipline** — Uniform debt definitions and the off-budget ban end a long-standing accounting evasion

## Emerging tensions
- The 41% is notional, not effective: rising cess and surcharge collections stay outside the divisible pool (Art. 271), so States’ realised share is materially lower — the sharpest continuing grievance.
- Revenue-deficit States are exposed by the withdrawal of RD grants — a direct concern for Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Punjab and West Bengal.
- Equity versus contribution remains contested: population-weight increases help the more populous northern States, while the GDP criterion favours the southern and western ones — the Commission’s balancing act satisfies neither camp fully.

## Impact on Andhra Pradesh

AP’s horizontal share rises from 4.05% to 4.22%, worth ₹64,362 crore in 2026-27 against ₹56,741 crore in RE 2025-26. It also receives ₹13,302 crore in rural local body basic grants, ₹9,727 crore for urban local bodies and ₹6,125 crore for disaster management, with Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada eligible for the Special Infrastructure (wastewater) component. Offsetting this, the loss of revenue-deficit and state-specific grants removes a cushion the State had relied on since bifurcation.

## Conclusion

The Sixteenth Finance Commission has chosen stability in the vertical share, innovation in the horizontal formula, and simplification in grants. By rewarding economic contribution, expanding untied transfers and mandating full disclosure of off-budget borrowings, it strengthens both State autonomy and fiscal accountability. Its unfinished agenda is the one it could not settle: bringing cess and surcharge within the divisible pool, without which the promise of 41% will remain larger than its delivery.

## Value addition
- Constitutional provisions: Art. 280 (constitution and duties of the Finance Commission), Art. 281 (report to be laid before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum on action taken), Art. 270 (divisible pool), Art. 271 (surcharges retained by the Union), Art. 275 (grants-in-aid), Art. 293 (State borrowing).
- State Finance Commissions: established under the 73rd and 74th Amendments — Art. 243-I requires the Governor to constitute an SFC every five years for panchayats, and Art. 243-Y extends its review to municipalities.
- Devolution history: 13th FC 32% → 14th FC 42% → 15th FC 41% → 16th FC 41%.
- AP’s share across Commissions: 14th FC 4.31% → 15th FC 4.05% → 16th FC 4.22%.

How do these recommendations influence government budgeting at the Centre and State levels? (APPSC, 2025)SECTION X — Finance Commissions, Fiscal Consolidation and Budgetary Reallocation (Q. 85–90)

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (Chairperson: N.K. Singh) framed India’s fiscal federalism for 2021-26 — a period defined by the COVID-19 shock, a collapse in tax revenue and record borrowing. Its central achievement was to deliver predictability during a crisis, and its award has now been succeeded by the 16th FC from 1 April 2026.

## Key recommendations
- **Vertical devolution** — States’ share fixed at 41% of the divisible pool — a 1 percentage point adjustment from the 14th FC’s 42% to fund the newly created UTs of J&K and Ladakh; implying about ₹42.2 lakh crore over 2021-26
- **Horizontal formula** — Income distance 45%, Area 15%, Population-2011 15%, Demographic performance 12.5%, Forest & ecology 10%, Tax and fiscal effort 2.5%
- **Grants-in-aid** — About ₹10.33 lakh crore — revenue-deficit grants ₹2.95 lakh crore to 17 States, sectoral grants ₹1.3 lakh crore, state-specific grants ₹49,600 crore
- **Local bodies** — ₹4.36 lakh crore — rural ₹2.37 lakh crore, urban ₹1.21 lakh crore, health through local bodies ₹70,051 crore
- **Performance incentives** — ₹45,000 crore reform-linked window for agriculture; ₹4,800 crore for educational outcomes; ₹6,143 crore for online learning
- **Defence** — A non-lapsable Modernisation Fund for Defence and Internal Security (MFDIS) of about ₹2.4 lakh crore, outside the divisible pool

## How the recommendations influence budgeting At the Centre
- Fiscal space compressed: aggregate transfers (devolution plus grants) worked out to about 50.9% of the divisible pool and roughly 34% of Union gross revenue receipts, narrowing discretionary headroom and pushing the Union towards genuinely national functions.
- Incentive to use cess and surcharge: because these fall outside the divisible pool under Article 271, the Centre’s budgeting shifted at the margin towards cess-financed schemes — a documented, and contested, consequence.
- Off-budget resources ring-fenced: MFDIS allowed defence modernisation to be financed without touching the formula.

## At the State level
- Multi-year planning became possible: a five-year entitlement of ₹42.2 lakh crore let States commit to capital projects and continuing programmes beyond the annual cycle.
- Revenue-deficit grants stabilised weak States through the pandemic, allowing consolidation without emergency expenditure cuts.
- Conditionality steered priorities: sectoral and performance grants of about ₹1.3 lakh crore obliged States to budget for health, education, agricultural reform, judiciary and statistics — sometimes at the cost of their own priorities.
- Decentralisation deepened: ₹4.36 lakh crore for the third tier forced States to constitute State Finance Commissions, maintain audited accounts and build local capacity as entry conditions for the grants.
- Revenue effort was rewarded: the tax-effort criterion (2.5% weight) gave States a direct budgetary reason to widen their own tax base.

## Criticisms
- The 41% share is notional, since rising cess and surcharge collections — nearly 18% of gross tax revenue in 2022-23

— sit outside the pool.

- Conditionalities dilute autonomy and impose compliance burdens that fiscally weaker States struggle to meet.
- The heavier weight on 2011 population was seen by southern States as penalising demographic success.
- Projections of tax buoyancy and GST revenue proved optimistic.

## Conclusion

The Fifteenth Finance Commission’s lasting contribution was stability under stress — it held the vertical share steady through a pandemic while expanding local-body and performance-linked transfers. Its unresolved problem, the growing share of cess and surcharge outside the divisible pool, was inherited rather than solved. The 16th FC (2026-31) has since retained the 41% share, introduced a “Contribution to GDP” criterion (10%), and moved decisively towards untied transfers by discontinuing revenue-deficit, sector-specific and state-specific grants.

- Article 280 mandate: the President constitutes a Finance Commission every fifth year or earlier, to recommend (a) the distribution of net proceeds of shareable taxes between the Union and States and their allocation among States; (b) the principles governing grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of India; (c) measures to augment a State’s Consolidated Fund to supplement the resources of panchayats and municipalities, based on the State Finance Commission’s recommendations; and (d) any other matter referred by the President in the interests of sound finance.
- Article 281: the report and an explanatory memorandum on action taken must be laid before Parliament.
- Composition: a Chairperson with experience in public affairs and four members drawn from those qualified to be High Court judges, or with knowledge of government finance and accounts, financial administration, or economics.

## Introduction

Keyword discipline: Q.225 asked for problems and recommendations. This question asks for flaws in the model itself and key points for restructuring — a diagnostic and design answer rather than a policy wish-list.

India operates one of the world’s largest PPP programmes, and it is a necessity rather than a preference — the National Infrastructure Pipeline requirement exceeds what any exchequer can fund. But the model as practised has produced stalled projects, protracted arbitration and reduced private appetite. The flaws are structural — in how contracts allocate risk and how the State performs its side — rather than incidental failures of particular projects.

- The flaws in the existing model
- Risk allocated by bargaining power rather than by capability — the foundational flaw The governing principle of PPP is that each risk should be borne by the party best able to manage it. Indian contracts frequently violated this: private parties were made to bear land acquisition, clearance, right-of-way and political risk — risks only government controls. A developer cannot acquire land or grant an environmental clearance, so assigning that risk guarantees failure rather than transferring it.
- Demand risk transferred wholesale to the private party Toll-based BOT contracts required developers to forecast traffic over twenty to thirty years. No one can do this reliably. Over-optimistic forecasts produced aggressive bidding, and when traffic disappointed, projects became unviable — the origin of much of the sector’s stress.
- Contracts written as if the future were foreseeable Concessions were rigid, with no mechanism for renegotiation. The Kelkar Committee (2015) made this point explicitly: a thirty-year contract cannot anticipate every contingency, and treating any renegotiation as evidence of corruption forces both parties into litigation instead of adjustment.
- Aggressive bidding and the winner’s curse Competitive bidding without qualification on financial capacity rewarded the most optimistic bidder rather than the most capable — and the winner then could not deliver at the bid price.
- Poor project preparation Projects were bid without completed land acquisition, clearances or reliable traffic studies.

The State sold a project it had not yet made buildable, and every subsequent dispute traced to that.

- Financing mismatch Banks lent short-tenure money to twenty-five-year assets, creating asset-liability mismatch. When projects stalled, this contributed to the twin-balance-sheet problem — over-leveraged developers facing stressed banks — which required the IBC (2016) and large-scale recapitalisation to resolve.
- Dispute resolution failure Arbitration ran for years while assets lay idle; public authorities routinely appealed awards, and even undisputed amounts were withheld during disputes, destroying contractor cash flow.
- Weak public sector capacity A PPP is managed for thirty years after it is signed, and government capacity is weakest precisely in that phase. Frequent transfer of officials destroys institutional memory; few authorities have trained contract managers.
- Regulatory gaps Where a PPP creates a natural monopoly — a port, an airport, a water utility — an independent regulator with tariff-setting powers is essential. Without one, a public monopoly simply becomes a private monopoly, which is worse for the consumer.
- Sectoral and social imbalance PPPs concentrated in roads, ports and airports — sectors with identifiable user charges — and remained thin in water, sewerage, urban services, health and education, where the need is greatest but users cannot pay.
- Equity concerns User-charge-based models ration access by ability to pay, which is unacceptable in essential services.
- Transparency Concession agreements, renegotiations and performance data were frequently not published, though PPPs commit public assets and create public obligations.
- Key points to focus on while restructuring the model
- Rebalance risk on the capability principle
- **Land acquisition, clearances, right-of-way** — Government
- **Political and regulatory change** — Government
- **Construction, technology, cost overrun** — Private party
- **Operation and maintenance** — Private party
- **Demand and traffic** — Shared or retained by government

The Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) — government funding 40% during construction and paying the balance as annuity — codifies this and demonstrably revived road-sector participation. Extending the HAM principle to other sectors is the single most important restructuring measure.

- Build flexibility into contracts - Permit renegotiation on defined, transparent triggers rather than treating it as failure. - Provide structured exit, allowing a developer to transfer the asset after construction and recycle capital. - Include clear, bankable termination payment clauses.
- Create the institutional architecture — the Kelkar recommendations The Committee on Revisiting and Revitalising the PPP Model (2015), chaired by Vijay Kelkar, recommended three institutions that remain the standard reform agenda: - Infrastructure PPP Project Review Committee (IPRC) — to review stressed projects and recommend resolution before they collapse; - Infrastructure PPP Adjudication Tribunal (IPAT) — for swift, specialised dispute resolution; - 3PI — an institute to build PPP capacity, develop model contracts and disseminate best practice.

The Committee also advised that PPPs not be used for small projects, and warned against pursuing PPPs as a source of revenue rather than of efficiency — a caution worth quoting.

- Prepare projects properly before bidding - Complete land acquisition and clearances before the bid, so the developer bids on a known risk. - Fund high-quality feasibility and demand studies through the India Infrastructure Project Development Fund. - Standardise appraisal through the PPP Appraisal Committee (PPPAC).
- Deepen long-term finance - NaBFID (2021) as the dedicated infrastructure development finance institution. - Deepen the corporate bond market — at 15-16% of GDP against Korea’s 79%, it cannot yet supply twenty-five-year money. - InvITs and REITs to recycle capital from operating assets; NMP 2.0 (₹10 lakh crore, 2025-30). - Channel pension, insurance and sovereign wealth funds into completed, de-risked assets, whose profile suits them. - Revamped Viability Gap Funding for socially necessary but commercially marginal projects.
- Reform dispute resolution - Institutional arbitration with fixed timelines in place of ad hoc arbitration. - Conciliation before arbitration. - Mandatory payment of undisputed amounts during a dispute — a simple change that would prevent many contractor insolvencies.
- Build public-sector capacity - Dedicated PPP cells with trained contract managers in ministries and States. - Continuity of officials on a project, since transfers destroy institutional memory. - Publish performance monitoring data.
- Establish independent regulators In every sector where a PPP creates a monopoly, an empowered regulator with tariff-setting authority must exist before the concession is awarded.
- Extend PPPs to social sectors with appropriate models Use availability-based or outcome-based payments rather than user charges in health, education and water — as PM-JAY and Dr NTR Vaidya Seva do, where government purchases treatment and the citizen pays nothing.
- Ensure the public partner pays on time The most under-stated restructuring point. Andhra Pradesh’s empanelled hospitals suspended services in April 2026 over pending dues, and legacy health liabilities of about ₹6,486 crore had accumulated. A PPP in which the public partner does not pay cannot function, however well the contract is drafted.
- Transparency Publish concession agreements, renegotiation decisions and performance data.

## Conclusion

The flaws in India’s PPP model are structural and largely attributable to the public side — risk allocated by bargaining power, projects bid before they were buildable, contracts that could not adapt, disputes that could not be resolved, and dues that were not paid. Restructuring must therefore begin with the State’s own conduct: allocate risk by capability through HAM-type structures, prepare projects before bidding, build the IPRC, IPAT and 3PI, deepen long-term finance, and pay on time. PPPs remain indispensable — the infrastructure requirement exceeds any exchequer’s capacity — but they succeed only where the government is a capable partner rather than merely a contracting

authority.

## Value addition
- The key committee: Committee on Revisiting and Revitalising the PPP Model (2015), chaired by Vijay Kelkar — IPRC, IPAT, 3PI; PPPs not for small projects; efficiency, not revenue, as the objective.
- The models to name: BOT-toll, BOT-annuity, HAM (40% construction support plus annuity), TOT, DBFOT, EPC, Swiss Challenge, landlord port model, management contract, and availability-based payment for social infrastructure.
- The institutional support: PPPAC (appraisal), IIPDF (project development), VGF, NaBFID (2021), InvITs/REITs, and NMP 2.0.
- AP illustrations: ports at Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram and Kakinada; Bhogapuram airport (97% complete); 10 new medical colleges under PPP; and Dr NTR Vaidya Seva, whose April 2026 disruption illustrates the payment-discipline point exactly.

## Introduction

The Internet of Things refers to networks of physical objects embedded with sensors and connectivity that sense their environment, exchange data and act on it without human instruction. Applied to the household, it converts the home from a passive shelter into a responsive system that anticipates rather than awaits its occupant. MeitY's IoT Policy framework and the rollout of 5G have made this shift technically feasible in India; whether it becomes widespread depends on cost, standards and trust.

- Connectivity (Wi-Fi, 5G, NB-IoT) > Processing (edge/cloud analytics) > Application

Evaluating the impact on household automation

- Energy management — the largest measurable gain. Smart meters shift billing from estimated to real-time, letting households see and shift consumption. Under the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), the Ministry of Power is rolling out smart prepaid metering nationally with an outlay of 73.03 lakh crore, targeting about 25 crore consumers — bringing IoT metering to ordinary homes rather than premium ones. Coupled with rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, households become both consumers and producers, with automated load scheduling deciding when to draw and when to store.
- Safety and security. Networked locks, cameras and motion sensors replace periodic physical checking with continuous monitoring and instant alerts. The significance is behavioural: security shifts from deterrence-after-the-fact to detection-in-real-time, which matters especially for households where all adults work.
- Health and eldercare. Wearables that detect falls, dispensers that log medication adherence and sensors that flag unusual inactivity allow elderly people to live independently rather than institutionally. In an ageing India — where the 60+ share is projected to roughly double by 2050 (UNFPA India Ageing Report) and children often migrate for work — this substitutes for a caregiver who is not physically present.
- Water and appliance efficiency. Leak-detection sensors and scheduled appliance cycles cut wastage in cities facing intermittent supply, aligning household behaviour with Mission LIFE's emphasis on demand-side conservation.

Illustrating how everyday tasks have evolved — draw this as a three-column before/after table, which shows evolution far more efficiently than prose:

Everyday task Pre-IoT Post-IoT

Paying for electricity Bi-monthly estimated bill | Real-time prepaid consumption on phone

Securing the home Physical lock, periodic Remote lock, motion alert, video check verification

Caring for an elder Continuous physical Remote vitals, fall alert, adherence log

presence

Cooling a room Manual switch on arrival Geofenced pre-cooling, occupancy-based cut-off

Irrigating a kitchen Fixed schedule Soil-moisture-triggered watering garden

AP instance: Andhra Pradesh's AWARE platform, run by the Real Time Governance Society, integrates satellite feeds, drones, IoT sensors, mobile inputs and CCTV to push real-time alerts to citizens via SMS and WhatsApp; it was strengthened by a five-year MoU with ISRO's SHAR, Sriharikota (June 2025). RTGS has since built a City Flood Alert system with APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar, giving 48-hour rainfall outlooks and six-hour flashflood warnings starting with Vijayawada (2026) — showing how household-level IoT alerts

extend into public safety.

Challenges and risks

- Affordability and the digital divide: Smart appliances carry a price premium that excludes most Indian households; without public programmes like RDSS smart metering, IoT risks becoming an urban-affluent technology.
- Interoperability: Competing protocols and proprietary apps fragment the home into non-communicating islands, forcing consumers into single-vendor lock-in.
- Cybersecurity: Cheap devices ship with default credentials and are rarely patched, making them entry points into home networks. The Telecommunication Engineering Centre (TEC, DoT) has issued a Code of Practice for Securing Consumer IoT, and CERT-In's directions require incident reporting — but enforcement at the low-cost import end remains weak.
- Privacy: Occupancy patterns, energy curves and voice recordings reveal intimate detail about a household. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with Rules notified in 2025, establishes consent and purpose-limitation obligations, though awareness among consumers is low.
- E-waste: Short device lifecycles add to a rapidly growing waste stream governed by the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 and their EPR regime.

## Conclusion

IoT has genuinely restructured household life, converting discrete manual chores into continuous, sensor-driven services — most visibly in energy, security and eldercare. Its evaluation, however, must be two-sided: the same connectivity that delivers convenience also creates an attack surface and a surveillance capacity inside the home. India's approach — mass diffusion through public programmes like RDSS smart metering, combined with TEC security codes and the DPDP Act — is the right sequencing. The measure of success will be whether the smart home reaches the ordinary household or remains a premium enclave.

## Introduction

The Raman effect is the inelastic scattering of light: when a beam passes through a transparent medium, a very small fraction of the scattered light emerges with a changed wavelength, having exchanged energy with the vibrational or rotational modes of the molecules it struck. Announced by C.V. Raman on 28 February 1928 and published in Nature as “A New Type of Secondary Radiation,” it won him the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics — the first Nobel in the sciences awarded to an Asian.

## The discovery
- The motivating question: Raman was dissatisfied with Lord Rayleigh’s explanation that the sea’s blue colour was merely reflected sky. Observing the Mediterranean on a voyage in 1921, he suspected the colour arose from scattering within the water itself — a question about light-matter interaction rather than optics of reflection.
- The work: at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS), Kolkata, Raman and his collaborators, notably K.S. Krishnan, studied light scattered by liquids and vapours using filtered sunlight, a telescope and complementary filters — modest apparatus by contemporary Western standards, which makes the result more remarkable.
- The observation: besides the expected Rayleigh-scattered light of unchanged wavelength, a faint component appeared at a shifted wavelength. The shift corresponded exactly to the energy of molecular vibrations, meaning the photon had given energy to, or taken energy from, the molecule.
- The theoretical significance: it demonstrated experimentally that light exchanges energy with matter in discrete quanta, supporting the emerging quantum theory of radiation, and established that scattering is not purely elastic.

## Impact on the global scientific community
- It created an entire analytical technique — Raman spectroscopy. Because every molecule has a characteristic set of vibrational modes, the shifted spectrum is a molecular “fingerprint.” Crucially, the method is non-destructive and requires no sample preparation, which is why it spread across disciplines rather than remaining a physics curiosity.
- Materials science and nanotechnology: Raman spectroscopy is the standard tool for characterising graphene and carbon nanotubes, where the position and shape of specific spectral bands reveal layer number and defect density.
- Medicine and biology: it enables label-free detection of biochemical changes in tissue, with research applications in cancer margin detection and biomarker analysis.
- Forensics and security: portable Raman devices identify explosives, narcotics and unknown powders through sealed containers — routinely used by security agencies worldwide.
- Environmental and atmospheric monitoring:Raman LIDAR systems profile water vapour and aerosols in the atmosphere; India operates such instrumentation at facilities including NARL, Gadanki, in Andhra Pradesh.
- Astronomy and planetary science: Raman spectrometers have flown on planetary missions to identify minerals in situ without returning samples.

## Impact on Indian science — arguably the deeper legacy
- It refuted the assumption that first-rate science required Western laboratories. A Nobel-winning discovery made in colonial Calcutta with improvised equipment gave a generation of Indian scientists the confidence to pursue original research at home.
- Institution building: Raman founded the Indian Academy of Sciences (1934) at Bengaluru, the journal Indian Journal of Physics (1926), and the Raman Research Institute (1948); he was also the first Indian Director of the Indian Institute of Science.
- Lineage of students: his doctoral students included Vikram Sarabhai, founder of India’s space programme, and S.K. Mitra; K.S. Krishnan became a leading figure at the National Physical Laboratory.
- AP connection worth stating: Raman’s family moved to Visakhapatnam in 1892, where his father joined the physics faculty at Mrs A.V.N. College. Raman was schooled at St Aloysius’ Anglo-Indian High School, Visakhapatnam, matriculated at eleven, and studied at A.V.N. College before moving to Presidency College, Madras — his formative scientific education took place in what is today Andhra Pradesh.

## Conclusion

Raman’s discovery is significant on three levels: it settled a fundamental question about how light interacts with matter, it created a versatile analytical technique still central to chemistry, medicine and materials science a century later, and it established that world-class science could originate in India. India observes 28 February as National Science Day in commemoration — a reminder that the country’s scientific self-confidence has an identifiable starting point.

## Value addition
- National Science Day: observed on 28 February each year, marking the day Raman announced his discovery in 1928; celebrated since 1987 with an annual theme announced by DST.
- Raman’s honours: Nobel Prize in Physics (1930); Matteucci Medal (1928); Hughes Medal (1930); Bharat Ratna (1954); Lenin Peace Prize (1958).
- Institutions founded or led by Raman: Indian Journal of Physics (1926); Indian Academy of Sciences, Bengaluru (1934); Raman Research Institute, Bengaluru (1948); first Indian Director of the Indian Institute of Science (1933).
- Other Indian scientists worth naming in any “achievements” question:S.N. Bose (Bose-Einstein statistics, bosons); Meghnad Saha (Saha ionisation equation); Homi Bhabha (Bhabha scattering, architect of India’s nuclear programme); Vikram Sarabhai (space programme); S. Chandrasekhar (Chandrasekhar limit, Nobel 1983); Har Gobind Khorana (Nobel 1968, genetic code); Venkatraman Ramakrishnan (Nobel 2009, ribosome structure); M.S. Swaminathan (Green Revolution).
- Technical precision that impresses: the longer-wavelength shifted lines are Stokes lines (the molecule gains energy) and the shorter-wavelength lines are anti-Stokes lines (the molecule loses energy); anti-Stokes lines are weaker because fewer molecules occupy excited states at ordinary temperatures.
- Why the effect is faint: only about one photon in a million is Raman-scattered, which is why the discovery required exceptional experimental care and why practical Raman spectroscopy had to await the invention of the laser in the 1960s.
- AP linkage: Mrs A.V.N. College and St Aloysius’ High School, Visakhapatnam; Raman LIDAR and atmospheric instrumentation at NARL, Gadanki.

## Introduction

E-governance in India has evolved through a clear logic: from computerising the office (internal efficiency), to connecting offices (integration), to delivering services to citizens (outreach), and now to building public digital infrastructure on which others can deliver (platforms). Each phase solved the previous phase’s limitation, and the current phase — Digital Public Infrastructure — is India’s most internationally recognised governance innovation.

## Phase 1 — Computerisation and networking (1970s-1990s)

The National Informatics Centre (1976) and NICNET (1987) created a national administrative network linking Centre, States and districts — the first time government data could move without paper. Early departmental computerisation targeted internal efficiency: railway reservations, land records, treasury accounting.

## Phase 2 — Legal and institutional foundation (late 1990s-2005)

The National Task Force on IT and Software Development (1998) and the creation of a dedicated Ministry of Information Technology (1999) gave the agenda political weight. The Information Technology Act, 2000 (amended 2008) was decisive: by granting legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, it made online transactions with government legally valid — without which e-governance would have remained an internal convenience. State experiments defined this period: e-Seva in Andhra Pradesh, Bhoomi in Karnataka (digitised land records), FRIENDS in Kerala (single-window payments) and Gyandoot in Madhya Pradesh.

## Phase 3 — The National e-Governance Plan (2006)

NeGP brought coherence to scattered initiatives through Mission Mode Projects — central (Income Tax, Passport, MCA21), state (land records, transport, e-District) and integrated (CSCs, e-Procurement) — supported by common infrastructure: State Data Centres, State Wide Area Networks (SWAN) and Common Service Centres. Its guiding commitment was to make services accessible “in the citizen’s own locality, at affordable cost”. NeGP was later recast as e-Kranti (NeGP 2.0) in 2015, adding mobile-first delivery and integration.

## Phase 4 — Digital India and Digital Public Infrastructure (2015 onwards)

Digital India rests on three pillars — digital infrastructure as a utility, governance and services on demand, and digital empowerment of citizens. Its distinctive contribution is platform thinking: Aadhaar (identity), UPI (payments), DigiLocker (documents) and ONDC (commerce) are open rails on which government and private actors both build. UMANG aggregates services across ministries on one application; e-Office digitised file movement; CPGRAMS handles grievances end-to-end.

## Analysis — how service delivery and citizen engagement changed
- Scale of digital service availability. The NeSDA Way Forward framework of DARPG — a biennial assessment modelled on the UN e-Government Survey’s Online Service Index — reported 23,934 e-services across States and UTs in its November 2025 report, with saturation of the 59 mandatory e-services exceeding 80% nationally and 21 States/UTs above 90%. Six States/UTs now deliver 100% of services through a single unified portal.
- From application to entitlement. The direction of travel is toward faceless and suo-motu delivery — the citizen no longer applies for what data already proves they are due. This is the conceptual leap from “e-governance” to “governance”.
- Leakage reduction. Aadhaar-linked DBT transferred a cumulative Rs. 43.95 lakh crore by May 2025 with savings of about Rs. 3.48 lakh crore from removed duplicates and ghosts (PIB, 2025).
- Citizen engagement. MyGov enables participation in policy consultation; CPGRAMS makes grievance status trackable; RTI filing online lowers the cost of demanding accountability.
- AP instance: the 28th National Conference on e-Governance was held at Visakhapatnam on 22-23 September 2025, co-hosted by DARPG, MeitY and the Government of Andhra Pradesh with IIM Visakhapatnam as knowledge partner, on the theme “Viksit Bharat: Civil Service and Digital Transformation”. It adopted the Visakhapatnam Declaration on e-Governance, which committed to extending digital governance to underserved and connectivity-challenged regions by expanding mandatory e-services under NeSDA, to scaling AI platforms such as Bhashini, DigiYatra and NADRES, and endorsed Andhra Pradesh’s plan to develop Visakhapatnam as a premier IT and innovation hub (PIB, September 2025).

## Conclusion

India’s e-governance journey is best read as a progressive redefinition of the problem: first the file, then the network, then the service, and now the platform. The measurable gains are real — nearly 24,000 e-services, DBT savings of about Rs. 3.48 lakh crore, and grievance systems that citizens can track. The unfinished agenda is what the Visakhapatnam Declaration itself identifies: reaching the connectivity-challenged, using AI ethically, and moving from services citizens must request to entitlements the state delivers on its own initiative.
