## Introduction

Cybercrime is any unlawful act in which a computer, network or digital data is the target of the offence (hacking, ransomware), the tool used to commit it (online fraud, phishing), or the medium in which it occurs (harassment, obscenity). India’s exposure is structural rather than incidental: with household internet access at 86.3% (NSO, CMS: Telecom, 2025) and among the world’s highest digital transaction volumes, the attack surface expands with every gain in digital inclusion.

identity theft) | as MEDIUM (stalking, bullying, obscenity, radicalisation) . This classification is the answer’s backbone.

## Scale — using government figures
- Through the Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS), launched in 2021, more than Rs. 7,130 crore has been saved across over 23.02 lakh complaints (MHA, reply in Lok Sabha, 2 December 2025) — a figure that indicates both the volume of fraud attempted and the value of immediate reporting.
- I4C’s Suspect Registry, launched in September 2024 with banks and financial institutions, has received over 18.43 lakh suspect identifiers and 24.67 lakh Layer-1 mule accounts, helping block fraudulent transactions worth about Rs. 8,031.56 crore (MHA, Lok Sabha, December 2025).
- Preventive action includes blocking over 9.42 lakh SIM cards and 2,63,348 IMEIs linked to cyber fraud, and 3,962 Skype IDs and 83,668 WhatsApp accounts used in fraud operations (PIB, 2025).
- Union Budget 2025-26 allocated Rs. 782 crore for cybersecurity projects (PIB, 2025).

## Major types of cybercrime in India
- Online financial fraud — the dominant category. Methods include phishing (email), smishing (SMS), vishing (voice calls), fake investment and trading platforms, fraudulent loan applications, and spoofed payment links. Investment-scam frauds account for a large share of reported losses. The enabling infrastructure is the mule account — an account rented or sold by its holder to receive and forward fraudulent proceeds — which is why the Suspect Registry targets these accounts specifically.
- “Digital arrest” and impersonation scams. Fraudsters posing as police, CBI, customs or telecom officials place victims under simulated custody by video call and extract payment through fear. The scale was significant enough for the Prime Minister to address it in Mann Ki Baat on 28 October 2024, and for I4C to run a dedicated national awareness campaign, including a caller-tune campaign with the Department of Telecommunications and a weekly Cyber-Alert programme with DD News.
- Ransomware and malware. Encryption of data with a demand for payment, increasingly targeting hospitals, universities, financial-services vendors and public utilities. The systemic risk is that ransomware against operational technology converts a cyber incident into a physical service failure.
- Identity theft and data breaches. Theft of credentials, Aadhaar-linked information and payment data, enabling downstream fraud — punishable under Section 66C of the IT Act.
- Cybercrimes against women and children. Sextortion, cyberstalking, cyberbullying, morphing and non-consensual intimate imagery — increasingly assisted by AI-generated synthetic content. This category is addressed by a dedicated reporting channel on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal that permits anonymous complaints.
- Cyber-espionage and attacks on critical infrastructure. State-linked actors targeting government networks, telecom, power and SCADA systems — the domain of the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC).
- Transnational scam operations. A substantial share of fraud targeting Indians is now run from organised “scam compounds” in South-East Asia, using trafficked workers — which converts cybercrime into simultaneously a law-enforcement, diplomatic and human-trafficking problem.

## Institutional and legal response
- I4C (Ministry of Home Affairs) — nodal coordination body, operating the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, helpline 1930, CFCFRMS, the Suspect Registry and the Cyber Fraud Mitigation Centre.
- CERT-In (MeitY) — national incident response agency issuing advisories and coordinating on vulnerabilities; NCIIPC protects critical information infrastructure.
- Legal framework: the IT Act, 2000 (Sections 43, 65, 66, 66C identity theft, 66D cheating by personation using a computer resource, 66E privacy violation, 67 series obscenity, 70 protected systems); the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (in force 1 July 2024), which replaced the IPC and covers cheating, forgery, stalking and organised crime including in electronic form; the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 for electronic evidence; and the DPDP Act, 2023 for personal data.
- Capacity building: Cyber Surakshit Bharat, CyTrain for police and judicial officers, cyber forensic laboratories, and State cyber cells.

## Persisting challenges
- Under-reporting, particularly in sextortion and fraud, owing to stigma and the belief that recovery is impossible.
- Attribution and jurisdiction, since perpetrators, servers and proceeds routinely sit in three different countries.
- Speed mismatch: funds move in seconds while investigation moves in days — which is why the “golden hour” of reporting to 1930 matters more than any subsequent step.
- Legal lag behind AI-enabled offences, partly addressed by the IT Amendment Rules, 2026 on synthetically generated information.

## Conclusion

Cybercrime in India has shifted from opportunistic individual offences to organised, transnational and increasingly AI-assisted operations, with financial fraud as the dominant form and mule accounts as its circulatory system. India’s institutional response — I4C, the 1930 helpline, CFCFRMS and the Suspect Registry — has demonstrably recovered value, with over Rs. 7,130 crore saved across 23 lakh complaints. The remaining gap is behavioural and jurisdictional: citizens must report within the golden hour, and cross-border enforcement must catch up with cross-border crime.

## Value addition
- I4C (MHA, an attached office): objectives include acting as the nodal point against cybercrime; strengthening the fight against cybercrime against women and children; facilitating complaint filing and identifying trends; acting as an early-warning system for law enforcement; public awareness; and capacity building of police, prosecutors and judicial officers in cyber forensics and cyber-criminology.
- The key verifiable numbers (MHA/PIB, 2025): CFCFRMS savings of over Rs. 7,130 crore across 23.02 lakh complaints; Suspect Registry with 18.43 lakh suspect identifiers and 24.67 lakh mule accounts, blocking about Rs. 8,031.56 crore; 9.42 lakh SIM cards and 2,63,348 IMEIs blocked; 3,962 Skype IDs and 83,668 WhatsApp accounts blocked; Rs. 782 crore for cybersecurity in Budget 2025-26.
- Helpline 1930 and the “golden hour”: immediate reporting allows the transaction chain to be frozen before funds are layered away — the single most effective victim intervention available.
- Terminology to use precisely:phishing (email), smishing (SMS), vishing (voice), mule account, layering, ransomware, APT (advanced persistent threat), SCADA, zero-day.
- Policy instruments: National Cyber Security Policy 2013; CERT-In Directions of 2022 on incident reporting and log retention; Cyber Surakshit Bharat; CyTrain (MOOC platform for law enforcement); the National Cyber Coordination Centre.
- The legal transition to note: IPC –> Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; CrPC –> Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; Indian Evidence Act –> Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, all in force from 1 July 2024. Citing IPC sections in a 2026 answer dates it immediately.
- AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s cyber cells and the RTGS data infrastructure; Visakhapatnam hosted the 28th National Conference on e-Governance (2025), where secure and trusted digital service delivery was a declared priority.

The National Policy on Information Technology, 2012, approved by the Union Cabinet, marked a conceptual shift: IT was no longer to be seen merely as an export-earning services industry, but as a horizontal enabler of governance, health, education and agriculture. Its stated vision was to strengthen and enhance India's position as a global IT hub while using IT as an engine for rapid, inclusive and sustainable growth — the policy foundation on which Digital India (2015) was later built.

"FEATURES (the how)", with an arrow leading to a lower box "DIGITAL EMPOWERMENT (the so what)". This mirrors the three demands of the question.

Key objectives of NPIT 2012

- Scale the industry: raise IT-ITeS revenues from about USD 100 billion to USD 300 billion by 2020 and exports to USD 200 billion — the headline quantitative goal.
- Employment: create 1 crore additional skilled jobs by 2020, recognising IT as one of the few sectors capable of absorbing educated youth at scale.
- Digital inclusion: make IT affordable and accessible to citizens, especially in rural and marginalised areas, and enable delivery in Indian languages.
- Governance: use ICT to make service delivery transparent, accountable and citizencentric.
- Domestic capability: promote innovation, R&D and indigenous product development, so that India would design and not only service.

Salient features

- IT for All, in all sectors: mandated integration of IT into health, education, agriculture and financial inclusion rather than confining it to a services vertical.
- e-Infrastructure: broadband highways, data centres and cloud — later operationalised as BharatNet, which extends optical fibre to Gram Panchayats.
- Hardware and electronics manufacturing: supported through the Modified Special Incentive Package Scheme (M-SIPS), the policy's answer to India's software-strong, hardware-weak imbalance.
- Cyber security and open standards: a secure cyber ecosystem, use of open standards and open-source, and promotion of open data — the lineage of NDSAP 2012 and CERT-In's strengthening.
- Skills and language: digital literacy and localisation, so that access was not restricted to English-literate users.

Evaluating the outcome — did it deliver? A short, honest scorecard earns marks:

Target (by 2020) Outcome

USD 300 bn IT-ITeS Approached but not met; sector estimated near USD 283 bn in FY 2024-25 revenue (NASSCOM)

1crore additionaljobs Partially met; industry employs roughly 5.8 million (NASSCOM)

Hardware Slow under M-SIPS (closed to new applicants, 2018); succeeded only later manufacturing through PLI and the India Semiconductor Mission

Digital inclusion Substantially achieved through BharatNet, Aadhaar, UPI

How it aims at a digitally empowered society

- Bridging the divide through infrastructure: BharatNet and the National Broadband Mission convert connectivity from a private good into public infrastructure, which is the precondition for every other digital right.
- Citizen-centric governance: e-District, MyGov and UMANG made services available without physical presence; NPIT's insistence on proactive electronic delivery is the ancestor of today's WhatsApp governance models.
- The DPI dividend: NPIT laid the policy groundwork for the JAM trinity, Aadhaarenabled services and UPI — India's most successful digital exports as a governance model.

This is precisely the "e-infrastructure and global hub" outcome NPIT envisaged, arriving a decade later.

## Conclusion

NPIT 2012 is best judged not by its unmet revenue targets but by its framing: it was the first Indian policy to treat information technology as public infrastructure rather than a private

industry. That framing produced BharatNet, digital literacy missions and eventually the

Digital Public Infrastructure that now defines India's global technology identity. Its unfinished agenda — hardware manufacturing and indigenous product development — is being addressed today through PLI, the India Semiconductor Mission and IndiaAI.

## Introduction

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), established in 1958 under the Ministry of Defence, is India’s premier agency for indigenous defence research. Formed by merging the Technical Development Establishment, the Directorate of Technical Development and Production, and the Defence Science Organisation, it today runs a network of over 50 laboratories across disciplines. Its motto, “Balasya Mūlam Vigyānam” — science is the source of strength — captures a premise central to national development: strategic autonomy rests on technological capability, not on procurement budgets.

Human capital & institutions . This structure prevents the answer from collapsing into a weapons list.

## Vision and mission
- Vision: to make India prosperous by establishing a world-class science and technology base, and to provide the Armed Forces with decisive superiority through competitive indigenous systems.
- Mission:

design, develop and lead to production state-of-the-art sensors, weapon systems, platforms and allied equipment for the Armed Forces;

provide technological solutions to optimise combat effectiveness and promote the well-being of troops;

develop infrastructure, quality manpower and a strong indigenous technology base.

## Role in national development

## Strategic autonomy — the core function
- Missile capability through the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme and its successors: the Agni series (including Agni-Prime with canisterised launch), Prithvi, Akash surface-to-air, Nag anti-tank, and BrahMos through joint development. Hypersonic and directed-energy work is at various stages of testing.
- Air defence and sensors: the indigenous Surya VHF radar with 360deg coverage and anti-stealth capability, developed with BEL, and the Integrated Air Defence Weapon System (IADWS) — a three-layered system combining QRSAM (30 km), VSHORADS (up to 6 km) and a laser-based directed energy weapon (2-4 km), flight-tested off the Odisha coast.
- Platforms: the Tejas Light Combat Aircraft, developed with ADA and HAL, and a range of naval systems.
- Why this is development, not merely defence: import dependence in defence transfers both money and leverage abroad. At least 65% of defence equipment is now manufactured domestically, against import dependence of 65-70% a decade ago (Ministry of Defence).

## Building the defence industrial base
- Technology transfer to industry. DRDO transfers developed technologies to DPSUs, private firms and MSMEs — mounted artillery gun systems, CBRN reconnaissance vehicles, minefield marking equipment. The testing infrastructure of 24 DRDO laboratories has been opened to private industry through the Defence Testing Portal, removing a capital barrier that previously excluded smaller firms.
- Measurable outcome: indigenous defence production rose from Rs. 46,429 crore in 2014-15 to Rs. 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, and defence exports from Rs. 686 crore in 2013-14 to a record Rs. 38,424 crore in 2025-26 — a 62.66% jump over the previous year, with DPSUs contributing 54.84% and the private sector 45.16%, reaching over 80 countries (Ministry of Defence, April 2026). The target is Rs. 3 lakh crore in production and Rs. 50,000 crore in exports by 2029.
- Start-up and MSME engagement through iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) and the Technology Development Fund, with defence industrial corridors in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu providing manufacturing clusters.

## Civilian spin-off — the underrated contribution

DRDO technologies routinely cross into civilian use: composite materials and light-weight prosthetics, extreme-cold-weather clothing and specialised nutrition, water purification and food preservation technologies, and avalanche and landslide warning systems for Himalayan regions. During COVID-19, DRDO laboratories developed sanitisers, PPE, ventilators and rapidly built hospital facilities — demonstrating that a defence R&D base is also a national emergency reserve.

## Human capital and institutions

DRDO supports doctoral and postgraduate research, runs DRDO Young Scientist Laboratories (DYSL) in AI, quantum technologies, cognitive technologies, asymmetric technologies and smart materials, and partners with IITs and universities — building the researcher pool on which any indigenous technology base depends.

AP linkage: the Naval Science and Technological Laboratory (NSTL), Visakhapatnam, established in 1969, is DRDO’s lead laboratory for underwater weapons — torpedoes, mines, decoys and fire-control systems, including the Varunastra heavyweight torpedo. Together with Hindustan Shipyard and Bharat Heavy Plate and Vessels, it makes Visakhapatnam a significant node of India’s naval-industrial base.

## Constraints to acknowledge

Time and cost overruns in complex programmes, historical difficulty in transitioning laboratory prototypes into series production, and continued import dependence in aero-engines, advanced sensors and semiconductors — the areas where indigenisation remains genuinely unfinished.

## Conclusion

DRDO’s contribution to national development operates through four channels: it converts defence spending from an import bill into domestic industrial activity, it seeds a private manufacturing base through technology transfer and open testing facilities, it generates civilian spin-offs, and it builds research capacity. The export figure of Rs. 38,424 crore in 2025-26 shows the model working. What remains is the hardest part of indigenisation — propulsion, advanced sensors and electronics — where sustained funding and industry partnership, rather than further institutional reform, will determine progress.

- Reform architecture:DAP 2020 (Defence Acquisition Procedure); DPM 2025 (Defence Procurement Manual, effective 1 November 2025); five Positive Indigenisation Lists banning import of over 5,000 items by set deadlines; SRIJAN indigenisation portal (2020); FDI at 74% automatic and 100% through government route for advanced technology; 75% of the defence capital budget reserved for domestic industry; 2025 declared the Year of Reforms.

## Introduction

The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) programme, begun with IRS-1A in 1988, gave India one of the world’s largest civilian Earth-observation constellations. Its defining characteristic is purpose: unlike programmes built primarily for science or commerce, IRS was designed from the outset as an operational resource-management system, feeding directly into agricultural, water, forest and disaster administration through the National Natural Resources Management System.

## Role of the IRS programme
- Institutional backbone. IRS data feeds the National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS), the framework through which satellite information enters resource planning across ministries, with the Department of Space as nodal agency.
- A constellation matched to tasks.Resourcesat for multispectral resource mapping; Cartosat for high-resolution cartography and stereo terrain modelling; Oceansat/EOS-06 for ocean colour, winds and fisheries; RISAT/EOS radar satellites for all-weather, day-and-night imaging; and now NISAR, launched 30 July 2025 aboard GSLV-F16 from SDSC-SHAR, the world’s first dual-frequency SAR satellite, imaging the globe every 12 days and detecting surface deformation below one centimetre.
- Data dissemination as public infrastructure.NRSC, Hyderabad acquires, processes and archives the data and disseminates it to government, academic and private users, with much of it freely accessible through the Bhuvan geoportal. This open-access model is what converts an expensive orbital asset into a resource a district planner or a start-up can actually use.
- Capacity building. The Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun, trains professionals in remote sensing and geo-informatics, including through outreach programmes, ensuring there are users capable of interpreting the data.

## How IRS satellites assist natural resource management
- Land and agriculture. Crop acreage and yield forecasting under FASAL; horticulture assessment under CHAMAN; drought monitoring under NADAMS; soil resource mapping through the Soil and Land Use Survey of India; wasteland and land-degradation inventories. The Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (MNCFC), established in 2012, operationalises ISRO-developed techniques for crop forecasting within the agriculture ministry.
- Water resources. Groundwater prospect mapping using satellite-derived lithology, structure and geomorphology, supporting well siting under rural drinking water programmes; reservoir and snowmelt monitoring; India-WRIS for consolidated water data; watershed monitoring through Srishti and Drishti under WDC-PMKSY 2.0.
- Forests and biodiversity. The Forest Survey of India’s biennial India State of Forest Report rests on satellite interpretation; FSI operates a near-real-time forest fire alert system; biomass and carbon-stock estimation supports India’s climate reporting; e-Green Watch monitors compensatory afforestation.
- Ocean and coastal resources.INCOIS issues Potential Fishing Zone advisories from sea-surface-temperature and chlorophyll data derived from Oceansat, helping fishermen reduce search time and fuel; coastal land-use mapping, shoreline change detection and sediment monitoring support coastal zone management.
- Minerals and geology. Lineament and structural mapping guides mineral exploration targeting, reducing the cost of ground survey.
- Disaster management. Flood inundation mapping in the Godavari and Krishna basins; cyclone tracking via INSAT-3D/3DR; drought assessment in Rayalaseema; landslide and deformation monitoring; damage assessment for relief. Radar satellites are decisive here, since floods and cyclones occur precisely when cloud blocks optical sensors.
- AP application: the Real Time Governance Society’s AWARE platform integrates satellite, drone, IoT and CCTV feeds for real-time alerts, strengthened by a five-year MoU with ISRO’s SHAR, Sriharikota (June 2025) — a State drawing operational value directly from the national constellation.

## Conclusion

The IRS programme’s significance lies in having been built as operational infrastructure rather than as a scientific instrument: its data settles how much rice India will harvest, where a well should be dug, whether forest cover has changed and which villages a flood will reach. With NISAR adding all-weather, centimetre-sensitive observation and Bhuvan making much of the archive openly available, the programme’s next contribution will depend less on new satellites than on whether States and districts build the capacity to use what is already freely available.

## Value addition
- The IRS lineage: IRS-1A (1988, the first) –> IRS-1B/1C/1D –> Resourcesat (IRS-P6) –> Cartosat-1 (IRS-P5) –> Cartosat-2 series –> Oceansat (IRS-P4) –> RISAT radar series –> the current EOS naming convention (EOS-04 = RISAT-1A, EOS-06 = Oceansat-3) –> NISAR (2025).
- Institutions to name:NRSC Hyderabad (data acquisition and dissemination, Bhuvan); IIRS Dehradun (training); SAC Ahmedabad (payload and application development); MNCFC (crop forecasting); INCOIS Hyderabad (ocean services); NNRMS as the umbrella framework.
- Application programmes: FASAL, CHAMAN, NADAMS (National Agricultural Drought Assessment and Monitoring System), Rice-Fallow Area Mapping, Bhuvan-PDMC for Per Drop More Crop, SVAMITVA, Srishti and Drishti.
- NISAR quick facts: joint ISRO-NASA mission; NASA L-band plus ISRO S-band SAR; 12-metre unfurlable mesh reflector; about 2,392 kg; sun-synchronous orbit near 747 km; global coverage every 12 days; detects deformation below one centimetre; first GSLV flight to a sun-synchronous polar orbit.
- Why radar matters for India specifically: the monsoon, when floods and crop stress peak, is exactly when cloud cover blinds optical satellites — so SAR is not a refinement but a necessity for an operational system.
- AP linkage: Godavari and Krishna delta flood mapping; Rayalaseema drought assessment; Coringa mangroves and Kolleru Lake (Ramsar) monitoring; INCOIS advisories for Andhra fishermen; RTGS AWARE and the RTGS–SHAR MoU.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh’s forests — concentrated in the Eastern Ghats, the Nallamala range and the Godavari catchment — face pressure from agricultural expansion, resource extraction, infrastructure and increasingly from fire. According to the India State of Forest Report 2023 (Forest Survey of India), the State’s forest cover declined from 30,223.62 sq km in 2021 to 30,084.96 sq km in 2023, a reduction of 138.66 sq km. The more significant story, however, is degradation — the conversion of dense forest to open forest within retained boundaries — which the headline area figure does not capture.

Infrastructure & irrigation projects | Fuelwood, grazing & NTFP extraction .

## Primary reasons for deforestation
- Agricultural expansion and encroachment — the leading driver. Forest land has been converted for permanent cultivation and horticulture, particularly for cashew, mango and, in the Godavari districts, oil palm. In tribal areas of the Eastern Ghats, podu (shifting cultivation) contributes,

though its impact is often overstated relative to commercial conversion. Encroachment has periodically intensified where communities anticipated regularisation of occupied land.

- Forest fires — disproportionately significant in AP. Andhra Pradesh recorded 1,073 large forest fire events in 2023-24, among the highest counts in the country (Forest Survey of India). Most are anthropogenic — lit to clear undergrowth, promote fresh grass for grazing, or aid collection of non-timber forest produce such as mahua — and spread uncontrolled in the dry season. Fire is primarily a degradation driver: it kills regeneration and saplings while leaving mature trees standing, so canopy density falls without the area being formally deforested. This is why AP’s fire problem is larger than its forest-cover statistics suggest.
- Mining and quarrying. Extraction in mineral-rich belts of the Eastern Ghats — including bauxite, limestone, laterite and granite — clears forest for pits, overburden dumps, haul roads and processing units. Bauxite proposals in the Visakhapatnam and Alluri Sitharama Raju agency areas have been particularly contested, since they fall in Fifth Schedule tribal areas where consent requirements under PESA and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 apply. Associated dust and drainage affect adjoining forest health.
- Infrastructure and irrigation projects. Roads, transmission corridors, urban expansion and irrigation projects require diversion of forest land under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam (the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, as amended in 2023). Beyond the land directly taken, new roads open previously inaccessible forest to further pressure — an indirect effect usually larger than the direct one. Submergence under reservoir projects in the Godavari and Krishna basins has also caused loss.
- Fuelwood, grazing and NTFP over-extraction. Continuing dependence of forest-fringe communities on fuelwood, uncontrolled livestock grazing that prevents natural regeneration, and unsustainable collection of minor forest produce cumulatively degrade forest quality without registering as area loss.
- Industrial plantation demand. Paper mill-linked raw material demand has historically encouraged conversion of natural forest to monoculture plantation — which retains “tree cover” while losing biodiversity, an important distinction.
- Climate stress as a multiplier. Higher temperatures, longer dry spells and erratic rainfall lengthen the fire season and reduce regeneration success, compounding every driver above.

## The legal and institutional framework
- Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 (amended 2023) governs diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes, requiring central approval and compensatory afforestation.
- CAMPA funds compensatory afforestation, with e-Green Watch for monitoring — addressing the long-standing problem that afforestation was recorded on paper but unverifiable on the ground.
- Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises individual and Community Forest Resource rights, empowering gram sabhas to protect and manage forests — the strongest legal instrument available for community-based protection.
- Vana Samrakshana Samithis (VSS) are Andhra Pradesh’s Joint Forest Management institutions, involving fringe communities in protection and benefit-sharing.
- Forest Survey of India’s fire alert system pushes near-real-time SMS alerts to field staff, and Bhuvan provides the geospatial monitoring base.

## Way forward

Strengthen fire management through early detection, fire lines and community fire-watchers, given AP’s exceptional fire count; recognise and implement CFR rights at scale so communities have a legal stake; regulate mining in Fifth Schedule areas with genuine gram sabha consent; promote agroforestry and alternative livelihoods in buffer zones to reduce extraction pressure; ensure compensatory afforestation prioritises native species over monoculture; and expand LPG access to reduce fuelwood dependence.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s forest loss is driven less by any single catastrophic cause than by the accumulation of agricultural conversion, exceptional fire incidence, mining in the Eastern Ghats, and steady extraction pressure from fringe communities. Because much of this manifests as degradation rather than clearance, area statistics understate the ecological change. Effective response therefore requires fire management and community rights recognition at least as much as it requires restrictions on diversion.

## Value addition
- Distinguish your sources: the India State of Forest Report 2023 (Forest Survey of India) — official, biennial, satellite-based — records AP forest cover falling from 30,223.62 sq km (2021) to 30,084.96 sq km (2023), a decline of 138.66 sq km. Global Forest Watch (World Resources Institute) — a non-governmental platform measuring tree cover, a broader category including plantations — reports different figures. Naming which source produced which figure is itself a mark of rigour.
- Fire data: AP recorded 1,073 large forest fire events in 2023-24, among the highest in India (FSI). India’s national forest and tree cover is about 25.17% of geographical area (ISFR 2023), against the National Forest Policy 1988 target of 33%.
- Key legal instruments:Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 (amended 2023); Forest Rights Act, 2006 with Community Forest Resource rights; PESA, 1996 for Fifth Schedule areas; Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; CAMPA and e-Green Watch.
- AP protected areas to name:Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (India’s largest); Papikonda National Park; Sri Venkateswara National Park; Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary (mangroves); Rollapadu (Great Indian Bustard); Kambalakonda; Kolleru Lake (Ramsar site).
- Restoration instruments:National Mission for a Green India; Nagar Van Yojana for urban forests; MISHTI for mangroves; Green Credit Programme; agroforestry under the sub-mission on agroforestry.
- The concept to name:forest degradation — reduction in canopy density, biomass, biodiversity or ecosystem service capacity without conversion to non-forest use. It is systematically under-measured because area-based statistics cannot capture it.

## Introduction

Mining and related subsurface activity can generate seismic events by altering the stress state and pore fluid pressure of rock at depth. The essential distinction is between induced seismicity — where human activity creates the stress that causes failure — and triggered seismicity — where human activity merely advances the timing of a failure that pre-existing tectonic stress would eventually have produced anyway. Most significant events associated with mining and reservoirs fall in the second category, which is why they can be much larger than the energy humans directly introduce.

perturbation (pore pressure / unloading) , with the caption small change --> releases large stored energy .

## How mining and related activity generate seismicity
- Stress redistribution from excavation. Removing large volumes of rock — particularly in deep or open-cast mining — unloads the surrounding mass and redistributes stress onto adjacent rock and faults. The resulting failure may occur at the excavation face (a rockburst) or on a nearby fault.
- Pore fluid pressure — the dominant mechanism. Injecting fluid, or impounding water above a fault, raises pore pressure within the rock. This reduces the effective normal stress clamping the fault shut, allowing slip under tectonic stress that was already present. This is why very small pressure changes can release very large energy: the human contribution is the trigger, not the energy source. The mechanism applies equally to mine dewatering and re-flooding, wastewater injection, and reservoir impoundment.
- Mine collapse and subsidence. Roof falls, pillar failure and goaf collapse in underground workings produce seismic signals, generally shallow and of low magnitude but capable of damaging surface structures because of their proximity.
- Blasting. Produces high-frequency vibration; damaging locally, but it does not cause tectonic earthquakes.
- Reservoir-triggered seismicity (RTS). Impoundment behind a large dam adds a load and, more importantly, raises pore pressure through the underlying rock mass. RTS is the best-documented category of human-associated seismicity worldwide.

## The Indian evidence — Koyna

The most significant Indian case is Koyna in Maharashtra, where impoundment of the Shivajisagar reservoir in 1962 was followed by increasing seismicity and, on 11 December 1967, an earthquake of magnitude about 6.3 that caused substantial casualties and damage. Seismic activity in the Koyna-Warna region has continued for six decades, making it the longest-recorded and most-studied case of reservoir-triggered seismicity in the world. The Ministry of Earth Sciences has established a dedicated borehole geophysics research laboratory at Koyna, drilling deep boreholes into the seismogenic zone to observe an active fault directly — one of only a handful of such scientific efforts globally.

Other Indian instances of RTS have been reported at reservoirs including Kariba-class projects elsewhere and, in India, at several large impoundments in the peninsula. Mining-associated seismicity has been recorded in deep coal and metal mining regions, though of much lower magnitude.

A necessary qualification for a “critical” answer: attributing any specific earthquake to mining is difficult. India’s peninsular region is tectonically active in a stable-continental-region sense — Latur (1993) and Jabalpur (1997) occurred in areas without any mining or reservoir trigger. Correlation in time and space is suggestive but not conclusive, and this uncertainty is precisely why monitoring baselines matter.

## Regulating mining to minimise seismic risk
- Baseline seismic monitoring before operations begin. Without pre-project seismicity data, later events cannot be attributed or excluded. Requiring a baseline network for large mines and reservoirs is the single most important regulatory measure.
- Site characterisation. Geological and geophysical investigation to map faults, stress orientation and rock mass properties; siting decisions should avoid critically stressed faults.
- The “traffic light” protocol. Operations proceed while seismicity remains below defined magnitude thresholds (green), require modification at intermediate levels (amber), and are suspended above a threshold (red). Widely adopted internationally for injection and geothermal operations, it is the standard instrument for managing induced seismicity.
- Controlled extraction and blasting. Regulating extraction rate, sequence and geometry; pillar design to avoid sudden collapse; controlled blasting with limits on peak particle velocity at nearby structures, as specified by DGMS.
- Fluid management. Regulating rate and pressure of dewatering, re-injection and tailings impoundment, since pore pressure change is the dominant mechanism.
- Reservoir operating rules. Gradual first filling and controlled rates of water level change, as rapid changes are more strongly associated with triggered events than absolute level.
- Mine closure and post-closure monitoring. Backfilling voids, and continued monitoring after abandonment, since flooding of closed mines has been associated with delayed seismicity.
- Institutional framework in India: the Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS) under the Ministry of Labour and Employment regulates mine safety and blasting; the National Center for Seismology (NCS), Ministry of Earth Sciences, operates the national seismological network and issues earthquake information; the Indian Bureau of Mines oversees mining plans and conservation; the MMDR Act, 1957 and the Mines Act, 1952 provide the statutory base; EIA clearance requires assessment of geological and seismic implications; and the National Disaster Management Authority issues guidelines on earthquake management including seismic zoning and building codes (IS 1893).
- Community measures: structural safety audits of nearby settlements, grievance mechanisms, transparent disclosure of monitoring data, and compensation frameworks — since the affected population is typically not the beneficiary of the operation.

## Conclusion

Mining and reservoir impoundment do not create the energy released in significant earthquakes; they alter stress and pore pressure sufficiently to release energy already stored tectonically — which is why small human perturbations can be followed by large events, as at Koyna. Regulation should therefore concentrate on the variables humans actually control: baseline monitoring, site characterisation away from critically stressed faults, controlled rates of extraction and fluid pressure change, traffic-light suspension protocols, and continued monitoring after closure.

## Value addition
- The conceptual distinction to lead with:induced seismicity — human activity supplies the stress causing failure; triggered seismicity — human activity advances the timing of failure driven by pre-existing tectonic stress. Most large associated events are triggered, which is why they exceed the energy humans introduce.
- Koyna: reservoir impounded 1962; M 6.3 earthquake on 11 December 1967; continuing seismicity for six decades; the world’s longest-recorded case of reservoir-triggered seismicity; Ministry of Earth Sciences borehole geophysics laboratory drilling into the seismogenic zone to study an active fault in situ.
- Institutions:National Center for Seismology (NCS), Ministry of Earth Sciences — national seismological network and earthquake reporting; DGMS for mine safety and blasting standards; Indian Bureau of Mines; NDMA guidelines; IS 1893 seismic design code; NCESS and IIT/CSIR-NGRI research support.
- Seismic zoning: India is divided into Zones II to V under IS 1893, Zone V being the most severe (North-East, Kutch, Andaman & Nicobar, parts of the Himalaya). Andhra Pradesh lies largely in Zones II and III, so its principal seismic exposure is moderate — but reservoir and mining projects can raise local risk regardless of regional zoning.
- Other human causes of seismicity worldwide: wastewater injection associated with oil and gas operations; enhanced geothermal systems; deep mining; large reservoir impoundment; underground nuclear testing; and, at very small scale, groundwater extraction and CO2 sequestration.
- Terminology:rockburst; goaf collapse; peak particle velocity (the standard blasting vibration limit); effective stress; pore pressure; traffic light protocol; stable continental region seismicity — the category to which Latur and Jabalpur belong.
- AP relevance: seismic Zones II-III; large reservoirs in the Krishna and Godavari basins including Srisailam and Nagarjuna Sagar, and the Polavaram project — all requiring baseline seismic monitoring; mining in the Eastern Ghats bauxite, limestone and granite belts; APSDMA and RTGS AWARE for hazard monitoring.

Sources used: MoEFCC on the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) and its missions, the EIA Notification 2006, and the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam 1980 as amended 2023; MNRE on installed solar and non-fossil capacity as on 31 March 2026 and the June 2025 50% milestone; PIB on the Panchamrit commitments and PM E-DRIVE; Bureau of Energy Efficiency on PAT and the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme; Central Pollution Control Board and the Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981 and Environment (Protection) Act 1986 for pollution control board functions; Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023, and FSI forest fire alert data for Andhra Pradesh; Global Forest Watch (World Resources Institute) for tree-cover loss estimates, cited as a non-governmental source; Ministry of Earth Sciences and the National Center for Seismology on Koyna reservoir-triggered seismicity and the borehole geophysics laboratory; DGMS and the Indian Bureau of Mines; Supreme Court of India, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Taj Trapezium case, 1996); ICAR on climate impacts on wheat yield; Government of Andhra Pradesh (APPCB, APSDMA, Vana Samrakshana Samithis, APCNF).

## Introduction

Sustainable development was defined by the Brundtland Commission report, Our Common Future (1987), as “development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.” It rests on three interdependent pillars — economic growth, social equity and environmental protection. For a country in India’s position, industrialising rapidly while carrying a large development deficit, the concept is not an abstraction but the central policy question.

## The concept and its principles
- Intergenerational equity — the present may not foreclose the options of the future.
- Intragenerational equity — benefits and burdens must be fairly distributed within the present generation.
- The precautionary principle — absence of full scientific certainty is not grounds for postponing action.
- Polluter pays — environmental costs must be internalised by those who cause them.
- Institutionalised globally through the Rio Earth Summit (1992), Agenda 21, the Millennium Development Goals (2000-15) and the 2030 Agenda with its 17 SDGs (2015).

## Relevance in the context of modern industrialisation — the question’s actual demand
- The historical tension. Industrialisation in Europe and North America proceeded without environmental constraint; today’s industrialising economies are asked to grow while decarbonising. This asymmetry underpins India’s insistence on Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC) and on climate justice — the position that historical emitters bear primary responsibility, and that developing countries require carbon space and finance to industrialise.
- Where industrialisation and sustainability now align. This alignment is genuinely new: solar power is cheaper than new coal, so clean generation is the least-cost industrial input, not a sacrifice. India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its NDC target. Similarly, energy efficiency under the PAT scheme reduces industrial costs while reducing emissions.
- Where the tension remains.Hard-to-abate sectors — steel, cement, fertiliser, refining — cannot be electrified with current technology and account for a large share of industrial emissions. The National Green Hydrogen Mission (Rs. 19,744 crore, 5 MMT by 2030) exists precisely because these industries need a non-electric decarbonisation route.
- The material-intensity problem. Clean industrialisation is not dematerialised: it requires lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare earths, concentrated in a few countries. The National Critical Mineral Mission (2025), with 1,200 GSI exploration projects by 2030-31, acknowledges that the transition substitutes one resource dependency for another.
- Instruments applying sustainability to Indian industry: the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022; Extended Producer Responsibility across plastics, e-waste, batteries and tyres; the Green Credit Programme; PLI schemes for solar modules and batteries; PM E-DRIVE (Rs. 10,900 crore, from October 2024, replacing FAME-II) for transport; and the National Manufacturing Mission announced in Budget 2025-26.
- India’s measured position: India ranked 99th of 167 countries in the Sustainable Development Report 2025 with a score of 67 — entering the top 100 for the first time, from 109th in 2024 and 112th in 2023.

## Critical evaluation of the concept itself — where most answers stop short
- It is elastic to the point of vagueness. “Sustainable development” is invoked by environmentalists and extractive industries alike, because the phrase itself specifies no trade-off rule. Its very acceptability derives from its ambiguity.
- The growth assumption. The concept presumes continued economic growth can be decoupled from resource use. Relative decoupling (less resource use per unit of output) is well documented; absolute decoupling (falling total resource use with rising output) is not, at the global scale. This is the strongest critique available.
- Weak versus strong sustainability.Weak sustainability treats natural capital as substitutable by manufactured capital — a forest may be exchanged for a factory of equal value. Strong sustainability holds that certain natural capital is critical and non-substitutable, since no amount of manufactured capital replaces a stable climate or a functioning aquifer. Most policy operates on weak assumptions while environmental reality behaves according to strong ones.
- Greenwashing. Sustainability reporting without verified outcomes; India’s response is BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting), mandatory for the largest listed companies.
- The equity question within industrialisation. Environmental costs of industry — air pollution, land acquisition, water extraction — fall on those least benefiting from it. Sustainable development is meaningful only if it addresses this distribution, not merely the aggregate.

## Conclusion

Sustainable development remains the only available framework for reconciling industrialisation with ecological limits, and its relevance to India has increased rather than diminished — because clean technology has become cost-competitive, making the choice commercial rather than sacrificial. But it is not a resolved concept: it assumes decoupling that has not been demonstrated at global scale, and its ambiguity permits its use as cover. For India, the workable position is neither to abandon industrialisation nor to accept the historical polluters’ timeline, but to industrialise on the least-carbon-intensive path available while pressing the CBDR-RC claim to finance and technology.

## Value addition
- Origins and milestones:Brundtland Report, Our Common Future (1987); Rio Earth Summit (1992) with Agenda 21, UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD; Johannesburg (2002); Rio+20 (2012); 2030 Agenda and the 17 SDGs (2015).
- India’s SDG performance:99th of 167 in the Sustainable Development Report 2025 with a score of 67 — first entry into the top 100, from 109th (2024) and 112th (2023); NITI Aayog’s SDG India Index tracks State-level progress.
- Key concepts to deploy: weak versus strong sustainability; relative versus absolute decoupling; planetary boundaries (Rockström); doughnut economics (Raworth — a safe and just space between a social foundation and an ecological ceiling); circular economy; just transition.
- India’s climate position:CBDR-RC; climate justice; per capita emissions far below the global average; Panchamrit commitments at COP26; net zero by 2070; LiFE as the demand-side contribution.
- Industrial sustainability instruments: PAT scheme and energy saving certificates; Carbon Credit Trading Scheme; EPR regimes; Green Credit Programme; BRSR disclosure; Zero Liquid Discharge norms; National Green Hydrogen Mission for hard-to-abate sectors.
- AP-specific:Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 (160 GW renewable target, 22 GW pumped storage); APCNF as a sustainable agriculture model; Sri City and Visakhapatnam industrial clusters as test cases for green industrialisation; the WEF-AP Centre for Energy and Cyber Resilience, Amaravati.

## Introduction
There is a significant relationship between deforestation and the emergence of infectious (especially zoonotic) diseases.

## Relationship
- **Habitat destruction** forces wildlife into closer contact with humans and livestock, facilitating spillover of pathogens (zoonoses).
- **Loss of biodiversity** disrupts natural checks on disease vectors.
- **Edge effects**: forest fragmentation increases human-wildlife interface (e.g., Nipah, Ebola, and vector-borne diseases like malaria).
- Changed ecosystems favour disease vectors (mosquitoes).
- Disruption of ecological balance amplifies pathogen transmission.

## Examples
- Emergence of Nipah, Ebola and increased malaria/Lyme disease linked to deforestation.

## Way forward
- Forest conservation, One Health approach and biodiversity protection.

## Conclusion
Deforestation increases the emergence of infectious diseases by heightening human-wildlife contact and disrupting ecosystems; conserving forests and adopting a One Health approach are vital to prevent future outbreaks.

## Introduction
Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is a process to evaluate the environmental consequences of a proposed project before approval.

## What is EIA
- A planning tool to identify, predict and mitigate the environmental effects of development projects, ensuring sustainable decisions.

## Key stages
- **Screening**: whether a project requires EIA.
- **Scoping**: identifying key impacts and terms of reference.
- **Baseline data collection**: existing environmental conditions.
- **Impact prediction and assessment**.
- **Mitigation and Environmental Management Plan (EMP)**.
- **Public consultation/hearing**.
- **Appraisal and decision** (clearance).
- **Monitoring and compliance** post-clearance.

## Significance
- Balances development with environmental protection.

## Conclusion
EIA, through screening, scoping, assessment, public consultation and monitoring, integrates environmental concerns into project planning—an essential safeguard for sustainable development when implemented rigorously.

## Introduction

Natural resources are materials and energy occurring in nature that can be used to satisfy human needs. India’s endowment is exceptionally diverse — from Himalayan glaciers to tropical rainforest, from the Thar desert to a 7,500-km coastline — but it supports about 18% of the world’s population on roughly 2.4% of its land area, which makes conservation a matter of necessity rather than choice.

renewability (renewable / non-renewable) , By origin (biotic / abiotic) , By development status (actual / potential /

reserve / stock) .

## Classification of natural resources

By renewability - Renewable — replenished naturally within human timescales: solar, wind, water, forests, soil (slowly), biodiversity. Caveat worth stating: renewability is conditional on the rate of use — a forest harvested faster than it regenerates behaves as non-renewable. - Non-renewable (exhaustible) — finite stocks formed over geological time: coal, petroleum, natural gas, and all minerals.

By origin - Biotic — derived from living organisms: forests, wildlife, fisheries, crops, and fossil fuels (biotic in origin though non-renewable in use). - Abiotic — from non-living sources: land, water, air, minerals, solar radiation.

By development status - Actual resources — surveyed, quantified and currently in use. - Potential resources — known to exist but not yet usable, such as identified but unexploited mineral deposits. - Reserve — the extractable portion of an actual resource under present technology and prices. - Stock — materials whose use awaits technology, such as hydrogen as a fuel until electrolysis became viable.

## India’s major natural resources and their conservation

1. Land and soil - The resource: about 328 million hectares of geographical area, with roughly 140 million hectares under net sown area — among the world’s largest arable bases. Major soils: alluvial, black regur, red, laterite, desert, mountain and saline. - Pressures: erosion, salinisation, desertification, nutrient depletion and diversion to non-agricultural use. - Conservation:Soil Health Card Scheme; WDC-PMKSY 2.0 watershed treatment (Rs. 8,134 crore, 49.50 lakh ha, 2021-26); National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture; National Mission on Natural Farming; India’s commitment to restore degraded land under the UNCCD Bonn Challenge pledge; the Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas by ISRO/SAC.

2. Water - The resource: India has about 4% of the world’s freshwater for 18% of its population; the utilisable resource is a fraction of total precipitation because much runs off unused. - Pressures: groundwater over-extraction (India is the world’s largest user), pollution, erratic monsoon, and inter-state disputes. - Conservation:Jal Jeevan Mission (rural tap water); Atal Bhujal Yojana (participatory groundwater management); Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain; National Water Mission (20% water-use efficiency improvement); Per Drop More Crop micro-irrigation; Namami Gange; Amrit Dharohar for wetlands; Master Plan for Artificial Recharge (CGWB).

3. Forests and biodiversity - The resource: forest and tree cover of 8,27,357 sq km — 25.17% of geographical area (ISFR 2023), comprising forest cover of 7,15,343 sq km (21.76%) and tree cover of 1,12,014 sq km (3.41%), an increase of 1,445 sq km over 2021. India holds four biodiversity hotspots and is a megadiverse country. - Pressures: diversion, encroachment, fire, invasive species, grazing. - Conservation:National Mission for a Green India; Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980; CAMPA and e-Green Watch; Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 with Project Tiger, Project Elephant and Project Dolphin; Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023); Forest Rights Act, 2006 with Community Forest Resource rights; MISHTI for mangroves; Nagar Van Yojana; Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam.

4. Mineral resources - The resource: strong in coal, iron ore, bauxite and limestone; deficient in petroleum, copper and critical minerals. - Conservation: MMDR Act, 1957 with auction-based allocation; National Mineral Policy, 2019 asserting inter-generational equity; Star Rating of Mines; mine closure plans with financial assurance; National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) including recycling as a supply route.

5. Energy resources - Conservation and transition: non-fossil capacity of 283.46 GW as on 31 March 2026, with 50% non-fossil installed capacity reached in June 2025, five years ahead of the NDC target (MNRE); PM Surya Ghar and PM-KUSUM; PAT scheme and Standards and Labelling for efficiency; National Green Hydrogen Mission; PM E-DRIVE; Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 with the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme.

6. Marine and coastal resources - The resource: a 7,500-km coastline and an Exclusive Economic Zone of about 2.02 million sq km; fisheries, minerals, hydrocarbons and shipping. - Conservation:Coastal Regulation Zone notifications; Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana; Deep Ocean Mission; Marine Protected Areas; MISHTI mangrove restoration.

## Cross-cutting frameworks

Mission LIFE for demand-side behaviour; Extended Producer Responsibility across plastics, e-waste, batteries and tyres; the Green Credit Programme; the National Action Plan on Climate Change with eight missions and State Action Plans; and the SDG India Index for monitoring.

AP instances: the Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 (160 GW renewable target including 22 GW pumped storage); APCNF covering over 1.77 million farmers in agroecological transition; Vana Samrakshana Samithis for community forest management; Coringa mangroves and Kolleru Lake (Ramsar) as coastal and wetland assets; and mineral wealth in barytes, limestone and beach sands.

## Conclusion

India’s natural resources are classified most usefully on three axes — renewability, origin and development status — because each implies a different conservation logic: renewable resources require rate limits, non-renewable ones require efficiency and substitution, and potential resources require exploration. India’s conservation architecture now spans all of them, with the clean energy transition running ahead of target and forest cover marginally increasing. The persistent deficits are in groundwater, soil health and critical mineral security — the resources where extraction has outpaced regeneration or discovery.

## Value addition
- Forest data (ISFR 2023): forest and tree cover 8,27,357 sq km = 25.17% of geographical area; forest cover 7,15,343 sq km (21.76%); tree cover 1,12,014 sq km (3.41%); an increase of 1,445 sq km over the 2021 assessment; National Forest Policy 1988 target is 33%.
- India’s proportional position — the framing statistic: roughly 2.4% of world land area, 4% of freshwater, 18% of world population — the single most effective way to convey the pressure on Indian resources.
- Classification axes: renewability (renewable / non-renewable); origin (biotic / abiotic); development status (actual / potential / reserve / stock); ownership (individual / community / national / international, the last including the common heritage of mankind — oceans beyond national jurisdiction, Antarctica, outer space).
- India’s biodiversity credentials: one of 17 megadiverse countries; four biodiversity hotspots — Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Sundaland (Nicobar Islands); party to the CBD, Nagoya Protocol and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework with its “30 by 30” target.

## Introduction

Integrated Solid Waste Management (ISWM) is a framework for managing waste through a coordinated combination of techniques, selected to be environmentally effective, economically affordable and socially acceptable. Its central insight is that no single technology solves the waste problem: composting, recycling, energy recovery and landfilling each handle a different fraction, and the system’s performance depends on how they are combined and sequenced.

## Key principles of ISWM
- Sustainability. Systems must be viable over the long term across three dimensions — environmental protection, financial affordability for municipalities and citizens, and social acceptability. Technologies that create future liabilities or unaffordable operating costs fail this test, which is why capital-intensive waste-to-energy plants have underperformed in Indian cities.
- The waste hierarchy. The operational blueprint for decision-making, prioritising options by resource conservation — developed below.
- Stakeholder responsibility and participation. Waste management is a shared function: government regulates and provides infrastructure, the private sector supplies services and technology, and citizens perform source segregation, without which no downstream system works. The SWM Rules, 2016 make this legally explicit by placing duties on waste generators themselves.
- Polluter Pays Principle. Those generating waste bear the cost of managing it. In India this takes two forms: user charges on households and bulk generators under the SWM Rules, and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) on producers under the Plastic Waste, E-Waste, Battery Waste and Tyre Waste Rules — shifting end-of-life cost from the municipality to the manufacturer.
- Proximity principle. Waste should be treated as close to its source as practicable, minimising transport cost, emissions and the risk of a single distant facility becoming a point of failure. This is the technical basis for decentralised composting at ward level rather than a single centralised plant.
- Precautionary and integrated planning principles — treating the entire waste stream and its full life cycle rather than individual fractions.

## The role of the waste hierarchy

DISPOSE (landfill) , with an arrow down the side labelled “decreasing environmental preference, increasing cost per tonne”.

- Prevention and reduction — the highest tier. Waste not generated requires no management at all. Instruments: product design for durability and repairability; packaging reduction; the ban on identified single-use plastic items (July 2022); Mission LIFE’s themes on reducing waste and single-use plastic; and consumer behaviour change.
- Reuse. Using an item again in its existing form, without reprocessing — refillable containers, repair rather than replacement, second-hand markets, and the right to repair framework being developed in India. Reuse retains the energy already embodied in manufacture, which is why it ranks above recycling.
- Recycling. Reprocessing materials into new products — paper, glass, metals and plastics. Its precondition is source segregation, since mixed waste yields contaminated and low-value material. Material Recovery Facilities and the integration of waste-pickers are the operational requirements.
- Recovery. Extracting value where recycling is not possible: composting and vermicomposting for the organic fraction, biomethanation producing bio-CNG under SATAT and GOBARdhan, refuse-derived fuel from high-calorific rejects for co-firing in cement kilns, and waste-to-energy for suitable residual fractions.
- Disposal — the last resort. Only inert residue that cannot be treated should reach an engineered sanitary landfill with liner, leachate collection and treatment, gas capture and daily cover. Under the SWM Rules, 2016, mixed waste may not be landfilled.

Why the hierarchy matters as a decision rule: it prevents the common error of treating waste management as a disposal problem to be solved by building a bigger facility. By ranking options, it directs investment upward — toward segregation, composting and recycling — where the environmental return per rupee is highest.

## The Indian regulatory expression
- Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 — mandatory source segregation into three streams (wet, dry, domestic hazardous); duties on waste generators including bulk generators; user fees; no mixed waste to landfill; and integration of waste-pickers.
- Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0 (from 1 October 2021) targeting garbage-free cities by 2026, covering used water, plastic waste, construction and demolition waste and legacy dumpsite remediation.
- EPR regimes under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022, Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 and tyre waste rules.
- Swachh Survekshan and the Star Rating Protocol for Garbage Free Cities, which create competitive pressure between municipalities.
- Current position: India generates about 1,70,339 tonnes per day of municipal solid waste, of which roughly 92% is collected and about 54% processed, with 24% landfilled (CPCB, 2021-22) — showing that the hierarchy’s upper tiers remain substantially under-used.

AP instances: the Swachh Andhra Corporation, established to implement solid waste management projects and public awareness under the Swachh Bharat Mission; the State Solid Waste Management Policy (2018), which mandates need-based assessment for common regional sanitary landfills serving groups of municipalities on a cost-sharing model — an application of the proximity principle scaled to what small municipalities can actually afford; and Visakhapatnam’s GPS-enabled collection and consistent Swachh Survekshan performance.

## Conclusion

ISWM’s principles and the waste hierarchy together supply what municipal waste management most often lacks — a rule for deciding what to invest in first. The hierarchy directs resources toward prevention, segregation and recovery rather than toward disposal capacity, and India’s rules now embed this legally through mandatory source segregation, user charges and Extended Producer Responsibility. The gap is in execution: with about 54% of waste processed against 92% collected, the constraint lies precisely at the hierarchy’s upper tiers, where household behaviour and municipal capacity meet.

## Value addition
- The five ISWM principles to name: sustainability; waste hierarchy; stakeholder responsibility and participation; polluter pays; proximity.
- The hierarchy in order: Prevent –> Reuse –> Recycle –> Recover –> Dispose. Extended in circular economy usage to Refuse, Rethink, Reduce, Reuse, Repair, Refurbish, Remanufacture, Repurpose, Recycle, Recover.
- Indian data (CPCB, 2021-22): generation 1,70,339 TPD; collection about 92%; processing 54%; landfilled 24%; about 645 operational landfills against 2,452 dumpsites; legacy waste remediation of about 1,437 lakh tonnes by September 2025 under SBM-U 2.0, reclaiming over 7,600 acres.
- Rules embedding the principles:SWM Rules 2016 (source segregation, user fees, generator duties, waste-picker integration); Plastic Waste Management Rules with EPR and the July 2022 single-use plastic ban; E-Waste Rules 2022; Battery Waste Rules 2022; Construction and Demolition Waste Rules 2016; Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016.
- Why Indian waste suits composting over incineration: 30-55% organic content with high moisture gives low calorific value, so mass-burn incineration performs poorly and often requires auxiliary fuel — the technical reason the hierarchy’s “recover” tier should mean composting and biomethanation first, energy recovery second.
- Circular economy linkage: the hierarchy’s upper tiers are the circular economy in practice; India participates in the Global Alliance on Circular Economy and Resource Efficiency (GACERE); Mission LIFE addresses the demand-side behaviour the hierarchy depends on.
- AP-specific:Swachh Andhra Corporation; State SWM Policy 2018 with common regional sanitary landfills on a cost-sharing model; Visakhapatnam’s GPS-enabled collection and Swachh Survekshan record; coastal plastic leakage along the 1,053-km coastline.
